MUJAHID:v1p96/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p96/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p96/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses rafath as sexual intercourse.

MUJAHID:v1p96/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p96/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p96/r2.claim: Mujahid interprets seeking what God prescribed as seeking offspring, adding that if one wife does not bear, another may.

MUJAHID:v1p96/r3.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p96/r3.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p96/r3.claim: Mujahid repeats that sexual relations are forbidden during retreat in mosques.

MUJAHID:v1p96/r4.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p96/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
MUJAHID:v1p96/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says a person in retreat must not have intercourse with women.

MUQATIL:2:187/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r1.claim: The permission for marital intercourse on Ramadan nights was a concession for believers after Umar's conduct.

MUQATIL:2:187/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r2.claim: Rafath means intercourse, and spouses are garments for one another in the sense that each is the other's repose.

MUQATIL:2:187/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r3.claim: The self-betrayal refers to Umar's intercourse with his wife; khiyāna here means sin or disobedience.

MUQATIL:2:187/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r4.claim: Muqatil glosses the parallel uses of khiyāna in 66:10 and 5:13 as disobedience.

MUQATIL:2:187/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r5.claim: God forgave them by leaving them unpunished, and intercourse is permitted throughout the whole night.

MUQATIL:2:187/r6.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r6.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r6.claim: The command to seek what God prescribed means seeking offspring, and it was revealed concerning Ṣirma b. Anas.

MUQATIL:2:187/r7.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r7.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r7.claim: The white thread is the first crosswise light of dawn, distinguishing daylight from the darkness of night.

MUQATIL:2:187/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r8.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r8.claim: The ban on intercourse during retreat was revealed about Ali, Ammar b. Yasir, and Abu Ubayda, who left the mosque at night and returned after sex and washing.

MUQATIL:2:187/r9.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:187/r9.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:187/r9.claim: Intercourse with women is forbidden both night and day while one is in mosque retreat; these are God's limits, meant to protect against sins during retreat.

FARRA:v1p114/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p114/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p114/r4.claim: Abdullah's reading has فلا رفوث ولا فسوق; رفوث means intercourse, and it is nominative because أحل is passive.

FARRA:v1p114/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p114/r5.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p114/r5.claim: الآن باشروهن refers to the newly revealed permission, previously unavailable; ما كتب الله لكم is explained as offspring or read واتبعوا, and Ibn Abbas says the two readings mean the same.

FARRA:v1p114/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p114/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p114/r6.claim: When a man asked whether the white and black threads were literal, the Prophet replied that he had a broad nape and explained them as night and day.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r1.claim: Before this verse, sleeping after part of the night barred food, drink, and marital relations until the next night; some Muslims ate or had intercourse, so God granted a concession.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r2.claim: He glosses rifath as sexual intercourse with women.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r3.speaker: عكرمة مولى ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r3.claim: An unnamed Anṣari Companion fell asleep before his wife could prepare food, then fasted without eating and nearly collapsed; mercy was revealed in his case.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r4.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r4.claim: What God prescribed to seek is offspring.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r5.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r5.claim: What God prescribed to seek is the concession He granted.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r6.claim: Asked whether to read ابتغوا or اتبعوا, he allowed either but said to keep the first reading.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r7.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p70/r7.claim: People in retreat used to leave the mosque, have relations with their wives, and return; God forbade this.

AKHFASH:v1p139/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p139/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p139/r1.claim: A masculine demonstrative after feminine فتنة is explained by an understood masculine noun: this matter you were hastening.

AKHFASH:v1p139/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p139/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p139/r2.claim: In الرفث إلى نسائكم, إلى is used because rafath here has the meaning of ifḍāʾ; normally one says rafatha bi-imraʾatihi.

AKHFASH:v1p139/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p139/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p139/r3.claim: Arabic usage can put bi in place of إلى or على, as in أحسن بي for أحسن إلي, غما بغم for غما على غم, and تأمنه بقنطار for على قنطار.

AKHFASH:v1p139/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p139/r4.speaker: الشاعر
AKHFASH:v1p139/r4.claim: The poet’s علي is used for عني, providing evidence that Arabic prepositions can substitute for one another.

AKHFASH:v1p139/r5.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p139/r5.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p139/r5.claim: خلوا إلى شياطينهم can be compared with both خلوت إليه and خلوت به; إلى may also mean مع, as in من أنصاري إلى الله, while من can mean على in ونصرناه من القوم.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r1.claim: Rafath means intercourse; rafath of speech is explicit mention of sexual matters that should be euphemized.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r2.claim: “You were betraying yourselves” means violating the prohibition God had imposed on you.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r3.claim: “Seek what God wrote for you” means offspring; this is an instruction of etiquette, not an obligation.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r4.claim: The commands to eat and drink grant permission.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r5.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r5.claim: The white thread is daylight and the black thread is night; they become distinguishable at the second dawn.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r6.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p74#2/r6.claim: ʿĀkifū means stay in the mosques; an ʿākif is someone who remains in the mosque and has vowed retreat there.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r1.claim: Ahilla means “made lawful” or “permitted,” laylat al-siyam means during the night of fasting, and rafath is a euphemism here for intercourse; al-Tabari also mentions Abdullah's recitation. Elsewhere rafath can mean obscene speech.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas explains rafath as intercourse, saying God is gracious and speaks euphemistically.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r3.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas glosses rafath as sexual relations.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r4.claim: Qatada glosses rafath as approaching or having intercourse with women.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r6.speaker: سالم بن عبد الله
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r6.claim: Salim ibn Abdullah likewise says rafath means intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r7.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p229#2/r7.claim: Al-Suddi says rafath here means intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p231/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r1.claim: One explanation of spouses being garments is bodily closeness: each covers the other in bed, like clothing on the body; the poem of Nabigha ibn Ja'da illustrates the image.

TAB-FULL:v3p231/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r2.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r2.claim: Al-Rabi glosses each spouse as a cover or quilt for the other.

TAB-FULL:v3p231/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r3.claim: A second explanation is that each spouse is the other's tranquility and place of repose, as night is called clothing in 25:47 and a spouse is made so one may dwell with her in 7:189.

TAB-FULL:v3p231/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r4.claim: Mujahid says spouses are a place of rest and tranquility for each other.

TAB-FULL:v3p231/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p231/r5.claim: A further possible sense is that each spouse conceals the other's sexual intimacy from other people's sight.

TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r1.claim: The self-betrayal comprised two things: sexual relations with wives and eating or drinking during the period when those acts were forbidden.

TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abi Layla reports the earlier rule: after sleeping before the evening meal, fasting people could neither eat nor have relations; reports about Umar and an Ansari led to this permission.

TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r3.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r3.claim: In another account, the elderly Ansari Sirma slept before eating and woke to continue fasting; Umar also had relations after his wife slept, and the verse lifted both hardships.

TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r4.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
TAB-FULL:v3p233#2/r4.claim: Muadh reports that people stopped eating, drinking, and having relations after sleep; Abu Sirma became exhausted after labor, while another man violated the rule concerning women, and the verse followed.

TAB-FULL:v3p233/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r1.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r1.claim: Al-Suddi explains the garment image as spouses being tranquility for each other.

TAB-FULL:v3p233/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r2.claim: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd interprets the image as sexual intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p233/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p233/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says each spouse is the other's tranquility.

TAB-FULL:v3p236/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r1.speaker: البراء
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r1.claim: Al-Bara recounts an Ansari who worked, fell asleep before iftar, and awoke exhausted; the permission to eat and drink until dawn was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p236/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r2.speaker: البراء
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r2.claim: A second al-Bara report names Qays ibn Sirma: after work he slept before eating, became severely hungry, and the verse allowing night relations and food was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p236/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p236/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says early Muslims could eat only until the evening prayer and then had to fast through sleep until the next night; some, including Umar, broke the rules, so the verse permitted relations, food, and drink until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p237/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن كعب بن مالك
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r1.claim: Ka'b ibn Malik reports that after his wife slept Umar had intercourse with her, and Ka'b did likewise; Umar told the Prophet, after which this permission was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p237/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r2.speaker: ثابت
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r2.claim: Thabit reports that Umar had intercourse with his wife on a Ramadan night and felt distressed, so the permission was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p237/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p237/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas recounts Umar's remorse after intercourse under the old rule; God then revealed forgiveness and allowed intercourse, food, and drink until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p238/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r1.claim: Mujahid says earlier a person who slept after sunset could neither eat, drink, nor have relations until the next night; those who broke the rule were forgiven and allowed these acts throughout the night.

TAB-FULL:v3p238/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r2.claim: Ikrima reports that an unnamed Ansari fell asleep while his wife prepared food, then became faint while fasting; the dispensation was revealed for him.

TAB-FULL:v3p238/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p238/r3.claim: Qatada describes the early fast as three days each month and then Ramadan: eating, drinking, and sex became forbidden after sleep, but the verse allowed all three until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p240/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r1.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r1.claim: Qatada says anyone who slept after nightfall had previously been barred from food, drink, and sex until the following night; violations prompted God's concession.

TAB-FULL:v3p240/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r2.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r2.claim: Al-Suddi says the Christians' Ramadan rule against eating, drinking, or sex after sleep had been imposed on Muslims; after Abu Qays became exhausted and Umar and others confessed to intercourse, the verse permitted these acts until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p240/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p240/r3.claim: Al-Suddi glosses self-betrayal as intercourse with wives and “then have relations” as sexual intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p241/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r1.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r1.claim: Ataa says the earlier rule barred food, drink, and sex after sleeping; an Ansari who had relations after sleep said he had betrayed himself, and revelation allowed all three until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p241/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r2.claim: Mujahid repeats that people who slept after sunset had violated the ban on sex, food, and drink, which was then lifted for the entire night.

TAB-FULL:v3p241/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r3.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r3.claim: Ikrima relates Umar having relations after his wife slept and says the eat-and-drink permission concerned Abu Qays ibn Sirma, who ate after sleeping.

TAB-FULL:v3p241/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r4.speaker: محمد بن يحيى بن حبان
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r4.claim: Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Habban reports that the elderly Sirma ibn Anas fell asleep before eating after fasting and work, so the permission to eat and drink until dawn was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p241/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p241/r5.claim: In Arabic mubashara literally means skin touching skin; here it euphemistically means intercourse, permitted on Ramadan nights until dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r1.claim: Mujahid says “seek what God ordained for you” means seek offspring; reports also attribute this interpretation to al-Hakam, Ikrima, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Abbas, and al-Rabi.

TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r2.speaker: الأوزاعي
TAB-FULL:v3p244#2/r2.claim: Al-Awzai reports Mujahid's view that mubashara in the Qur'an means intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas explains mubashara as intercourse, with God graciously using a euphemism.

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r2.claim: Another Ibn Abbas gloss translates “now have relations” as “marry them.”

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r3.claim: A further Ibn Abbas report glosses mubashara as sexual relations.

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r4.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r4.claim: Ataa says mubashara means intercourse, and that every Qur'anic occurrence of mubashara means the act of intercourse itself; Abd Allah ibn Kathir is reported to agree.

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r5.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas, in a report through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, says mubashara means intercourse, though God may use whichever euphemism He wills.

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r6.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r6.claim: Al-Suddi glosses the command to have relations as “have intercourse with them.”

TAB-FULL:v3p244/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p244/r7.claim: Mujahid and Ataa both gloss mubashara in the Book as intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd says “seek what God ordained” means sexual intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r2.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim says it means offspring.

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r3.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through Abu al-Jawza interprets what was ordained as Laylat al-Qadr.

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r4.claim: Qatada interprets the phrase as pursuing what God made lawful and the concession He granted; he also reports a reading with “follow” instead of “seek.”

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r5.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r5.claim: Ataa asked Ibn Abbas whether to read “seek” or “follow”; Ibn Abbas accepted either but advised keeping the first reading.

TAB-FULL:v3p246/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p246/r6.claim: Al-Tabari says the wording broadly means seek what God decreed and made available, including offspring, Laylat al-Qadr, or lawful things; offspring best fits the context of intercourse and has the clearest surface support.

TAB-FULL:v3p248/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r1.claim: One interpretation identifies the white thread as daylight and the black thread as night's darkness: eating, drinking, and intercourse may continue until dawn light emerges.

TAB-FULL:v3p248/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r2.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r2.claim: Al-Hasan glosses the white and black threads as night and day.

TAB-FULL:v3p248/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r3.claim: Qatada says the early false dawn should not end the pre-dawn meal: wait for the unmistakable dawn spreading horizontally across the horizon.

TAB-FULL:v3p248/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p248/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the white and black threads mean day and night; when dawn becomes clear, food, drink, and intercourse stop, and the fast continues until night.

TAB-FULL:v3p250/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p250/r1.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
TAB-FULL:v3p250/r1.claim: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash rebukes a literal reading as night's departure and day's arrival; Adi reports the Prophet's clarification that the threads mean daylight and night.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r1.claim: Sahl ibn Sa'd says the original wording lacked “from dawn”; some men tied black and white threads to their legs until God added the phrase to clarify that the threads mean night and day.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r2.claim: True dawn is a diffuse whiteness spreading through the sky and lighting roads, unlike the vertical, bright false dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r3.speaker: أبو مجلز
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r3.claim: Abu Majliz says the bright streak in the sky is false dawn; true dawn appears when the horizon opens and becomes clear.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r4.speaker: مسلم
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r4.claim: Muslim says people did not count the dawn as true until it filled homes and roads.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas distinguishes two dawns: the one rising in the sky changes no ruling, but dawn visible over the mountain tops prohibits drinking.

TAB-FULL:v3p252/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r6.speaker: محمد بن عبد الرحمن بن ثوبان
TAB-FULL:v3p252/r6.claim: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban says the wolf-tail-like dawn prohibits nothing; the spread dawn across the horizon permits prayer and prohibits fasting.

TAB-FULL:v3p253/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r1.speaker: محمد
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r1.claim: The Prophet says neither Bilal's call nor the elongated false dawn should stop the pre-dawn meal; only the dawn spread across the horizon does so.

TAB-FULL:v3p253/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r2.speaker: محمد
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r2.claim: In another report, the Prophet says not to be deceived by Bilal's call or the early whiteness until dawn appears and breaks open.

TAB-FULL:v3p253/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r3.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r3.claim: Another reported interpretation takes the white thread to mean sunlight and the black thread to mean night.

TAB-FULL:v3p253/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r4.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r4.claim: Ibrahim al-Taymi recounts Hudhayfa continuing to eat after the feared dawn had appeared and delaying prayer, supporting the view that day begins only at sunrise.

TAB-FULL:v3p253/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r5.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v3p253/r5.claim: Ali reportedly said after praying dawn prayer that this was when the white thread became distinct from the black.

TAB-FULL:v3p256/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r1.speaker: البراء
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r1.claim: Al-Bara reports eating a late pre-dawn meal with Ibn Masud, who urged him to drink even though he had already eaten; they then went out while people were praying.

TAB-FULL:v3p256/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r2.speaker: عامر بن مطر
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r2.claim: Amir ibn Matar says Ibn Masud shared leftover pre-dawn food with him, then they went to prayer after it had been called.

TAB-FULL:v3p256/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r3.speaker: سالم مولى أبي حذيفة
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r3.claim: Salim says Abu Bakr first gestured for him to stop eating, then looked toward dawn and finally asked for food and ate before praying.

TAB-FULL:v3p256/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r4.speaker: إبراهيم
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r4.claim: Conflicting reports from Ibrahim place suhur by day, by night, or between the second call and the prayer's commencement.

TAB-FULL:v3p256/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r5.speaker: حبان بن الحارث
TAB-FULL:v3p256/r5.claim: Hibban reports that he ate suhur with Ali and then went out as the prayer was being established.

TAB-FULL:v3p258/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r1.claim: Ali is reported to have prayed dawn and said this was when the white thread became distinct from the black.

TAB-FULL:v3p258/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r2.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r2.claim: Those identifying dawn with sunrise argue that day begins at sunrise as it ends at sunset; starting it at dawn would imply it ends at twilight, contrary to consensus, and reports show the Prophet eating after dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p258/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r3.speaker: حذيفة
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r3.claim: Hudhayfa says he ate suhur with the Prophet and describes the time as day although the sun had not risen.

TAB-FULL:v3p258/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r4.speaker: حذيفة
TAB-FULL:v3p258/r4.claim: Another report says the Prophet ate while dawn was near and visible, but the sun had not yet risen.

TAB-FULL:v3p259/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r1.claim: The Prophet reportedly told a person hearing the call with a vessel in hand to finish drinking; one version says the caller sounded when dawn had begun.

TAB-FULL:v3p259/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r2.speaker: أبو أمامة
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r2.claim: Abu Umama reports that when prayer was called with a vessel in Umar's hand, the Prophet permitted him to drink.

TAB-FULL:v3p259/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r3.speaker: بلال
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r3.claim: Bilal reports that the Prophet drank when Bilal came to announce dawn prayer and then shared the vessel before they went to prayer.

TAB-FULL:v3p259/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the Prophet's explicit explanation that the white thread is daybreak and the black thread is night, which matches ordinary Arabic usage; reports of drinking before prayer do not prove drinking after dawn, since the prayer followed dawn and its call preceded it.

TAB-FULL:v3p259/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p259/r5.claim: Al-Tabari reads Hudhayfa's “it is dawn” as meaning close to dawn rather than literally after dawn; Arabic may call something by the name of what it resembles.

TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r1.claim: The white thread marks the beginning of dawn, when God sets the fast’s boundary.

TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r2.claim: The white thread is an early part of dawn; when it appears, prayer becomes due and food and drink become forbidden to the fasting person.

TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r3.claim: The verse rules out eating until sunrise: it sets the start of abstention at the first dawn light, and delaying it would have no principled boundary against delaying it farther.

TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r4.claim: If sunrise marked the day’s beginning, consistency would make fasting continue until the sun’s light and twilight disappeared; transmitted consensus rejects that endpoint.

TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p261#2/r5.claim: He derives fajr from the verb for water bursting forth and flowing.

TAB-FULL:v3p261/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p261/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p261/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd describes the white thread as the line beneath the night that uncovers it, and the black thread as what lies above it.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r1.claim: A continuous faster is starving himself outside obedience, since the fast ends at night and one is free to eat or not thereafter.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r2.claim: A report from ʿUmar says the fasting person has broken the fast when night comes, day recedes, and the sun sets.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r3.speaker: أبو أوفى
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r3.claim: Abu Awfa reports that the Prophet insisted on breaking the fast after sunset and said that the fast ends as night comes from the east.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r4.speaker: رفيع
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r4.claim: Rafiʿ says the obligation lasts only until night; afterward one may eat or choose not to eat.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r5.speaker: أبو العالية
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r5.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya says God prescribed daytime fasting, while at night people may eat or refrain voluntarily.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r6.speaker: أبو العالية
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r6.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya reads the verse’s limit as making the person free to eat or not once night arrives.

TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r7.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p263#2/r7.claim: ʿAisha understood “complete the fast until night” as disapproval of continuous fasting.

TAB-FULL:v3p263/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p263/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p263/r1.claim: The first signs of sunlight at sunrise are called dawn because their light bursts forth and spreads over paths, like water springing from its source.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r1.speaker: هشام بن عروة
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r1.claim: ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr reportedly continued fasting for seven days, then five, then three as he aged.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r2.speaker: عبد الملك
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r2.claim: Ibn Abi Yaʿmar reportedly broke his fast only once each month.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r3.speaker: عامر بن عبد الله بن الزبير
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r3.claim: ʿAmir continued across two Ramadan nights and said ghee sustained him by moistening his veins, unlike water which left his body.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r4.claim: He explains that some who continued did so to seek bodily austerity and strength, like ʿUmar’s call to rugged living to prevent comfort from producing cowardice and avoidance of enemies.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r5.speaker: عمرو بن ميمون
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r5.claim: Seeing Ibn Abi Nuʿaym continue until he could no longer stand, ʿAmr ibn Maymun said the Companions would have stoned him for it.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r6.claim: Many people of merit discouraged continuous fasting, and abundant transmitted Prophetic reports prohibit it; al-Tabari cites examples instead of listing them all.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r7.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r7.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet forbade continuous fasting and explained that his own nourishment was unlike theirs.

TAB-FULL:v3p265/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r8.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p265/r8.claim: He notes a report that the Prophet permitted continuous fasting from one pre-dawn meal to the next.

TAB-FULL:v3p267/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r1.claim: Abu Saʿid reports the Prophet forbade continuous fasting, allowing anyone who insists to continue only until dawn; the Prophet said he was specially fed and given drink.

TAB-FULL:v3p267/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r2.speaker: أم ولد حاطب بن أبي بلتعة
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r2.claim: When she declined the Prophet’s food because she was fasting, he pointed her to the Prophet’s family practice of continuing from one dawn to the next.

TAB-FULL:v3p267/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r3.claim: The command means to abstain from what God prohibited from discernible dawn until night, after which those things become lawful again until the next dawn.

TAB-FULL:v3p267/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p267/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd calls the passage the four boundaries and recites it from the permission of night intimacy through the command to complete fasting until night.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r1.claim: “Do not be intimate” means do not have intercourse while engaged in retreat in the mosques; iʿtikaf is staying and confining oneself to something.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r2.claim: Al-Tirmah’s verse uses ʿukuf to mean remaining or residing.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r3.claim: Al-Farazdaq likewise uses ʿakaf to describe people remaining around an idol.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says intercourse with women is prohibited by night and day, during Ramadan or outside it, until the retreat ends.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r5.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r5.claim: ʿAtaʾ interprets the prohibited intimacy as intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r6.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak says people used to have intercourse during retreat before this prohibition was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p268/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r7.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v3p268/r7.claim: Al-Dahhak also says a person leaving the mosque during retreat could previously have intercourse, but then was told not to approach women while in retreat.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r1.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r1.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses the prohibited intimacy as intercourse.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r2.speaker: مالك بن أنس
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r2.claim: Malik prohibits an iʿtikaf participant from touching, embracing, kissing, or taking any pleasure with his wife.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says the prohibition includes intercourse and every other form of skin-to-skin contact.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers intercourse and acts equivalent in sexual pleasure and requiring ritual bathing; the wording cannot prohibit every kind of contact because Aisha groomed the Prophet during retreat.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r5.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r5.claim: Aisha reports that while the Prophet was in retreat he brought his head near her so she could groom it.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r6.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r6.claim: Aisha says the Prophet entered the home only for a human need, but extended his head from the mosque for her to groom.

TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r7.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p271#2/r7.claim: Aisha reports grooming the Prophet’s head while he was in retreat in the mosque and she was menstruating.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r1.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r1.claim: Al-Rabiʿ says people had intercourse with their wives while in retreat, so God forbade it.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r2.claim: Qatada says people leaving the mosque during retreat would have intercourse with their wives; God prohibited this until the retreat ended.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says a person in retreat fasts and may not have relations with women while retreating.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r4.claim: Mujahid glosses the retreat as residence in God’s house and says one who leaves home for it should not approach women.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says that one who leaves home for God’s house should not approach women.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r6.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r6.claim: Qatada says people used to leave retreat, have intercourse, and return to the mosque; the verse forbade it.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says retreatants would leave to relieve themselves, have intercourse, bathe, then return; they were prohibited from this.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r8.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r8.claim: Mujahid says the prohibition addressed intercourse in mosques, where the Ansar used to have sex, and glosses retreat as residence.

TAB-FULL:v3p271/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r9.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v3p271/r9.claim: ʿAtaʾ identifies the forbidden direct intimacy as intercourse; he personally disliked kisses or touching in the mosque as well.

TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r1.claim: God’s limits here are the rules just explained: eating, drinking, and intercourse during Ramadan’s daytime without excuse, and intercourse during retreat in mosques; people must stay away from them.

TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r2.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r2.claim: Al-Suddi interprets God’s limits as His conditions.

TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r3.claim: Al-Tabari says “conditions” is close, but limits more precisely delimit and distinguish forbidden matters from unrestricted lawful ones.

TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v3p274#2/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets God’s limits as His disobedience, meaning intimacy during retreat.

TAB-FULL:v3p274/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r1.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r1.claim: Aisha reports washing the Prophet’s head while he was in retreat and she was menstruating.

TAB-FULL:v3p274/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r2.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r2.claim: Aisha’s report through Malik says the Prophet would extend his head for her to groom while he was in retreat.

TAB-FULL:v3p274/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p274/r3.claim: Since Aisha’s grooming reports are sound, the verse cannot prohibit every meaning of physical contact; because intercourse is agreed to be forbidden, the ban includes it and equivalent sexual pleasure.

TAB-FULL:v3p275/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p275/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p275/r1.claim: Just as God clarified fasting obligations, limits, times, travel and illness allowances, and retreat restrictions, He explains His rulings, lawful and unlawful matters, commands, and prohibitions through scripture and the Messenger.

TAB-FULL:v3p275/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p275/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p275/r2.claim: God clarifies these rules so people will avoid His prohibitions and sins and avert His displeasure by abandoning what He forbade.

ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r2.claim: Al-rafath is a broad term for what a man seeks with a woman, used here euphemistically for intercourse.

ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p255#2/r3.claim: At the beginning of the fasting obligation, intercourse at night and eating or drinking after the last evening prayer and sleep were forbidden; God allowed them until dawn.

ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r1.claim: One interpretation of spouses being garments is that they embrace one another; another says each finds rest and intimacy with the other.

ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r2.claim: Arabic calls a wife a garment or waist-wrapper; two anonymous poems use لباس and إزاري as terms for a wife.

ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r3.speaker: قالوا
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r3.claim: Some explain ‘seek what God prescribed for you’ as seeking children.

ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r4.claim: He prefers that the command means following the Qur’an in what it permits and commands.

ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p256/r5.claim: The black thread is the dark horizontal dawn and the white thread the bright dawn filling the horizon; the image means night becoming day, with fasting beginning at clear dawn.

ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r1.claim: Intercourse is forbidden during mosque retreat; the retreating worshipper stays in a congregational mosque and leaves only for necessary needs.

ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r2.claim: God’s boundaries are the prohibitions against violating them; the related Arabic root denotes a gatekeeper or anything that prevents passage, as in mourning, iron, and a property boundary.

ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p257/r3.claim: ‘Thus God makes His signs clear’ refers to the kind of clarification just given: He explains what He has commanded.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r1.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r1.claim: Mu'adh reports that fasting initially prohibited food, drink, and sex only after a person slept; after Umar had intercourse with his wife after sleeping and told the Prophet, the verse permitting night intercourse was revealed.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses rafath as sexual intercourse; the source lists Ata, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and others in agreement.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says spouses are a source of tranquility for one another; Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Muqatil are reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r4.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r4.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas interprets the spouses' clothing metaphor as each being a covering or blanket for the other.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNABIHATIM:v1p315/r5.claim: Ka'b ibn Malik recounts that people once had to abstain from food and drink after sleeping during a fast; Umar and Ka'b each had intercourse after their wives had slept, then Umar informed the Prophet and this verse was revealed.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r1.claim: Mujahid explains “you were betraying yourselves” as “you were wronging yourselves.”

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r2.claim: Al-Suddi explains the phrase as secretly having intercourse with their wives in violation of the former rule.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas connects God's pardon to what Umar had done, saying God revealed His forgiveness in these words.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says “be intimate with them” means intercourse, expressed by God euphemistically; Mujahid, Ata, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Suddi, and others agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r5.claim: One interpretation of “seek what God has written for you” is to seek offspring; many early authorities are reported to share this view.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r6.claim: A second view from Ibn Abbas interprets what God has written as Laylat al-Qadr.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p316/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the white and black threads as day and night: intimacy, eating, and drinking were permitted until dawn became clear, after which they were forbidden.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r1.speaker: ابن جريج
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r1.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the command to eat and drink was revealed concerning Abu Qays ibn Sirma of the Khazraj.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r2.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r2.claim: Adi ibn Hatim misunderstood the threads literally and watched two threads; the Prophet clarified that dawn means the whiteness of day and blackness of night.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r3.speaker: سهل بن سعد
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r3.claim: Sahl says the words “of dawn” were added after men tied white and black threads to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them; the clarification means night and day.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r4.speaker: عطاء
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r4.claim: A report from Ata describes dawn as the white dawn, with the transmitted wording apparently incomplete after “the one beneath it.”

IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r5.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p318/r5.claim: The Prophet forbade uninterrupted fasting for two days, likened it to Christian practice, and instructed Muslims to complete the fast until night and then break it.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r1.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r1.claim: The Prophet says the fast is over when night comes, day departs, and the sun has set.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says intercourse is forbidden to anyone in retreat in a mosque, by night or day, until the retreat ends; Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Ata, Qatada, Mujahid, and others agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r3.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r3.claim: When asked whether men who sleep in the mosque and become ritually impure should be reported to the ruler, Ibn Umar says they are the people in retreat.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God's boundaries as obedience to God.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r5.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r5.claim: Al-Suddi's second interpretation takes God's boundaries as His stipulations or conditions.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r6.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets God's boundaries as disobedience, specifically intercourse during retreat; Muqatil is reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r7.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r7.claim: Muqatil glosses “do not approach them” as “do not have intercourse.”

IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r8.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v1p319/r8.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains “thus” as “in this way God makes His signs clear.”

IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r1.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r1.claim: Muqatil says God clarifies His signs so people will avoid sins.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r2.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r2.claim: Muqatil says every person in retreat must fast for as long as the retreat lasts.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r3.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v1p320/r3.claim: Mujahid glosses “so that they may be mindful” as “they obey.”

NAHHAS:v1p288/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p288/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v1p288/r2.claim: Al-Rafath covers everything a man desires from a woman; the clauses about clothing and commands are parsed as coordinated.

THALABI:v2p76/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p76/r3.speaker: المفسرون
THALABI:v2p76/r3.claim: Initially, after iftar people could eat, drink, and have sex until the late evening prayer or sleep; afterward these were forbidden until the next night.

THALABI:v2p76/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p76/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
THALABI:v2p76/r4.claim: After having sex with his wife following the late prayer, Umar repented to the Prophet; other men confessed similar conduct, and the verse then permitted intimacy on fasting nights.

THALABI:v2p76/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p76/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود والأعمش
THALABI:v2p76/r5.claim: They read الرفوث; both rafath forms are euphemisms for intercourse, and Ibn Abbas says God's Qur'anic terms for touching, meeting, and intimacy mean intercourse.

THALABI:v2p77/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r1.speaker: القتيبي
THALABI:v2p77/r1.claim: Al-Qutaybi says rafath explicitly names what should be euphemized in sex talk and derives from obscenity or coarse speech.

THALABI:v2p77/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p77/r10.claim: To betray oneself refers to wronging oneself with intimacy after the late prayer; God then forgave and erased their sins.

THALABI:v2p77/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r11.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p77/r11.claim: Al-an marks a time that spans both past and coming time, while bashiruhunna means have intercourse because skin touches skin.

THALABI:v2p77/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r2.speaker: العجاج
THALABI:v2p77/r2.claim: Al-Ajjaj's verse uses rafath in speech, illustrating the term's association with coarse talk.

THALABI:v2p77/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r3.speaker: الزجاج
THALABI:v2p77/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines rafath as a comprehensive term for men's desires toward women.

THALABI:v2p77/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v2p77/r4.claim: The spouses are garments in the sense of being a place of rest and repose, as night is called a garment and a spouse is made for repose.

THALABI:v2p77/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r5.speaker: أصحاب المعاني
THALABI:v2p77/r5.claim: They explain the garment metaphor by spouses sleeping unclothed together, each body close against the other like an inner garment.

THALABI:v2p77/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r6.speaker: النابغة بني جعدة
THALABI:v2p77/r6.claim: Al-Nabigha ibn Ja'da's poem calls a woman لباسا, supporting the metaphor for spouses joined in bed.

THALABI:v2p77/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r7.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
THALABI:v2p77/r7.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas paraphrases the spouses as each other's covering blanket.

THALABI:v2p77/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r8.speaker: بعضهم وأبو زيد
THALABI:v2p77/r8.claim: Another view says each spouse covers the other from forbidden conduct and from public view during sex; Abu Zayd explains the phrase as referring to intercourse.

THALABI:v2p77/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p77/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة
THALABI:v2p77/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda says a wife may be called a man's garment, bedding, or waist wrap, as in a poem addressed to Umar.

THALABI:v2p78/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p78/r1.claim: ابتغوا means seek or do; ما كتب الله لكم means what God decreed or wrote in the Preserved Tablet.

THALABI:v2p78/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r2.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v2p78/r2.claim: Most commentators understand what God ordained as offspring; Mujahid urges seeking children, while Ibn Zayd reads it as lawful intercourse.

THALABI:v2p78/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r3.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v2p78/r3.claim: Qatada understands the phrase as seeking the concession God prescribed.

THALABI:v2p78/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r4.speaker: معاذ بن جبل وأبو الجوزاء عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p78/r4.claim: They interpret what God prescribed as Laylat al-Qadr.

THALABI:v2p78/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p78/r5.claim: The author prefers the offspring interpretation because it follows the permission of intercourse and is framed as permission or encouragement, supported by a Prophetic call to marry and multiply.

THALABI:v2p78/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r6.speaker: أهل الظاهر
THALABI:v2p78/r6.claim: The literalists say the command to seek what God wrote is obligatory, citing a report about al-Hawla, who asks Aisha why her husband avoids intimacy.

THALABI:v2p78/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p78/r7.speaker: أنس بن مالك
THALABI:v2p78/r7.claim: In the al-Hawla report, the Prophet tells the wife to listen to and obey her husband, then promises merit for household care, pregnancy, labor, and nursing.

THALABI:v2p79/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v2p79/r1.claim: The continuation of the al-Hawla report promises men rewards for approaching, embracing, kissing, and having intercourse with their wives, and forgiveness through ritual washing.

THALABI:v2p79/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r2.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
THALABI:v2p79/r2.claim: Muadh identifies the Anṣari man in the dawn-food occasion as Abu Sirma, al-Bara Qays ibn Sirma.

THALABI:v2p79/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r3.speaker: عكرمة والسدي
THALABI:v2p79/r3.claim: Ikrima and al-Suddi give his name as Abu Qays ibn Sirma.

THALABI:v2p79/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r4.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
THALABI:v2p79/r4.claim: Muqatil ibn Hayyan names him Sirma ibn Iyas.

THALABI:v2p79/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r5.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v2p79/r5.claim: Al-Kalbi gives the man's fuller genealogy as Abu Qays Sirma ibn Anas ibn Abi Sirma ibn Malik ibn Adi al-Najjar.

THALABI:v2p79/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p79/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p79/r6.claim: The Anṣari fasted while working, slept before his wife finished preparing food, refused to eat after waking under the old rule, and fainted from exhaustion the next day; the revelation then allowed eating and drinking at night until dawn.

THALABI:v2p80/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r1.speaker: الشاعر
THALABI:v2p80/r1.claim: A poem likens dawn's beginning light to a white thread and the dark night to a black one.

THALABI:v2p80/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r2.speaker: أبو داود
THALABI:v2p80/r2.claim: Abu Dawud's verse describes daybreak as a thread of light.

THALABI:v2p80/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r3.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
THALABI:v2p80/r3.claim: Adi ibn Hatim says he literally watched black and white hairs; the Prophet laughed and clarified the image as daylight against night.

THALABI:v2p80/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r4.speaker: سهل بن سعد
THALABI:v2p80/r4.claim: Sahl reports that before من الفجر was revealed, some men used actual threads to judge when to stop eating; the added phrase clarified that night and day were intended.

THALABI:v2p80/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p80/r5.claim: Dawn is the first splitting of light, named from water bursting forth; the false dawn rises vertically without spreading, while the true dawn spreads across the horizon.

THALABI:v2p80/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p80/r6.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
THALABI:v2p80/r6.claim: The Prophet says not to stop eating because of Bilal's call or the vertical false dawn, but at the spreading dawn along the horizon.

THALABI:v2p81/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي أوفى
THALABI:v2p81/r1.claim: The Prophet's party delayed iftar until sunset despite a companion's doubt; when night arrives, day recedes, and the sun sets, the faster has completed the fast whether or not he eats.

THALABI:v2p81/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p81/r2.claim: I'tikaf fundamentally means staying and residing; the cited Qur'anic phrase describes people remaining at idols.

THALABI:v2p81/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r3.speaker: الفرزدق
THALABI:v2p81/r3.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line likens people gathered around cooking pots to people devoted around an idol, illustrating the root of i'tikaf.

THALABI:v2p81/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p81/r4.claim: I'tikaf is confining oneself in a mosque for worship of God.

THALABI:v2p81/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r5.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء والضحاك والربيع
THALABI:v2p81/r5.claim: They limit the prohibited intimacy of i'tikaf to intercourse, which invalidates the retreat.

THALABI:v2p81/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r6.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والكلبي
THALABI:v2p81/r6.claim: They report that some companions left the mosque during retreat to have sex with their wives, then bathe and return, and were forbidden intercourse day and night until retreat ended.

THALABI:v2p81/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r7.speaker: أبو زيد
THALABI:v2p81/r7.claim: Abu Zayd takes direct intimacy broadly to include intercourse, touching, kissing, and other pleasures.

THALABI:v2p81/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p81/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p81/r8.claim: Intercourse invalidates i'tikaf by consensus; pleasurable touching or kissing without intercourse is disliked but does not invalidate it for most jurists.

THALABI:v2p82/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r1.speaker: مالك بن أنس
THALABI:v2p82/r1.claim: Malik holds that non-intercourse direct intimacy invalidates i'tikaf.

THALABI:v2p82/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r2.speaker: ابن جريج عن عطاء
THALABI:v2p82/r2.claim: Ata says the forbidden act is intercourse itself, though he dislikes even kissing or touching in the mosque.

THALABI:v2p82/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r3.speaker: عائشة
THALABI:v2p82/r3.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet, while in retreat, would extend his head out of the mosque for her to comb.

THALABI:v2p82/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r4.speaker: ابن عباس عن سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v2p82/r4.claim: A Prophetic report says a person in retreat is kept from sins and receives the reward of all good-doers.

THALABI:v2p82/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r5.speaker: علي بن الحسين عن أبيه
THALABI:v2p82/r5.claim: A Prophetic report promises the reward of two pilgrimages and two minor pilgrimages for ten days of Ramadan i'tikaf.

THALABI:v2p82/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r6.speaker: السدي وشهر بن حوشب والضحاك
THALABI:v2p82/r6.claim: They gloss God's limits as His conditions, obligations, or prohibitions.

THALABI:v2p82/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r7.speaker: المفضل بن سلمة والخليل والزجاج
THALABI:v2p82/r7.claim: They define a limit as a boundary or endpoint that distinguishes or prevents transgression; the author adds that the root means restraint and cites Arabic usage.

THALABI:v2p82/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p82/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p82/r8.claim: Do not approach the limits means do not commit the prohibited acts; God clarifies the signs so people avoid His anger and punishment.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r1.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi interpret spouses as garments to mean that they are one another's repose, as night is called a garment in 78:10.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r10.claim: The white thread means daylight's light, the second dawn, and the black thread means night's darkness before it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r11.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r11.claim: After Adi ibn Hatim watched two literal threads under his pillow, the Prophet explained that the verse means daylight's whiteness and night's blackness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r12.claim: The first dawn light is called a thread because it initially appears stretched out like one.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r2.claim: Before this concession, night intimacy and eating or drinking were allowed only before a person slept and forbidden afterward.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r3.claim: The occasion included Umar having intercourse after his wife said she had slept, and Abu Qays ibn Sarma falling asleep before eating after work; both told the Prophet, and the verse was revealed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r4.claim: The forgiveness in the verse either pardons their sins or removes the ban on intimacy and food after sleep.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r5.claim: Bashiruhunna means intercourse; its root is joining skin to skin, and the command clarifies what happened with Umar.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r6.claim: Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Suddi interpret seeking what God prescribed as seeking a child.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets seeking what God prescribed as seeking Laylat al-Qadr.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r8.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r8.claim: Qatada interprets it as seeking what God made lawful and permitted.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r9.speaker: سهل بن سعد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244#2/r9.claim: Sahl ibn Sad reports that some men tied literal white and black threads to their legs and kept eating until they could distinguish them; the words min al-fajr clarified that they meant day and night.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r1.claim: Ibn Masud read both al-rafath and al-rufuth; the word denotes intercourse and originally means obscene speech.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r2.claim: The word euphemistically denotes intercourse because saying it outside its proper context would be indecent; al-Ajjaj's verse witnesses its use for obscene talk.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p244/r3.claim: One interpretation makes spouses garments for each other: each joins the other and provides covering like a worn garment; al-Nabigha al-Jadi's verse illustrates this image.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r1.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r1.claim: The cited poem calls dawn's bright light the white thread and nighttime darkness the black thread.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r10.speaker: الجمهور
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r10.claim: Most interpreters understand the prohibited intimacy during retreat in the mosque to mean intercourse.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r11.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r11.claim: Ibn Zayd and Malik understand the prohibition during mosque retreat to include touching and kissing short of intercourse.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r12.claim: God's limits are either boundaries He defines by mention and explanation or limits because He prescribes penalties for many prohibitions.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r13.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r13.claim: The signs here may mean signs of acts of worship or religious obligations and rulings.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r2.claim: In ordinary Arabic, khayt can denote a color.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r3.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r3.claim: Hudhayfa, with similar reports from Ali and Ibn Masud, identifies the white thread with sunlight; al-Mawardi says consensus rejects this view.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r4.speaker: حذيفة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r4.claim: Zirr ibn Hubaysh reports Hudhayfa saying the Prophet ate suhur while arrow targets were visible and called it dawn before sunrise; al-Mawardi presents this against the consensus.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r5.claim: The Prophet says the false dawn, like a wolf's tail, neither forbids food nor permits prayer; the broad dawn across the horizon permits prayer and forbids food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r6.claim: Fajr derives from a verb meaning that water flowed forth; dawn is named for the emergence of light from the sun's rising place.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r7.claim: The agreed fasting period in which food and drink are forbidden runs from the second dawn until sunset.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r8.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says the greatest fasting reward belongs to those who break their fast nearest to nightfall.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p246/r9.claim: Completing the fast until night means fasting until the sun sets.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r1.claim: God gains nothing from created qualities; whether a servant performs worship or enjoys permitted ordinary companionship, permission leaves God without need.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r2.claim: The verse followed a lapse by Umar and made that concession available to all Muslims until the Resurrection.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r3.claim: God apportioned Ramadan nights and days between His due and the servant’s lawful needs: fasting is His due, while eating and drinking are the servant’s share.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r4.claim: The ban on intimacy during retreat signifies that the place of divine presence is sanctified from personal appetites; absorption in God should not return to self-interest.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r5.claim: God guards sacred times against mixing serious devotion with play.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r6.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r6.claim: Aisha told the Prophet that she loved him and loved being near him.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r7.speaker: رسول الله
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r7.claim: The Prophet replied that Aisha should leave him to worship his Lord.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r8.speaker: رسول الله
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r8.claim: The Prophet described having a private time in which nothing but God could occupy him.

QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p91/r9.claim: When bringing disputes before people, remember that God sees inward secrets even when human judges see only outward appearances.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p48/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p48/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p48/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says fasting initially barred food and marital relations from the night prayer until the next night; some Muslims, including ʿUmar, broke that restriction and complained.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r1.speaker: البراء بن عازب
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r1.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that before the concession, people could eat and have relations after breaking the fast only until they slept; Qays b. Ṣirma fainted after sleeping hungry, and ʿUmar also reported a lapse.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r2.speaker: البراء
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p50/r2.claim: In a second version, one who slept before eating could not eat that night or the next day; Qays b. Ṣirma slept hungry after asking his wife for food, and the revelation brought great relief.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r1.claim: Sahl b. Saʿd says some tied white and black threads to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them; the phrase “from dawn” clarified that the verse meant night and day.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r2.speaker: القاسم بن محمد
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p52/r2.claim: Al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad says the first fasting rule ran from one evening to the next; sleeping barred food and marital relations, until God granted relief after ʿUmar and Ṣirma’s cases.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r1.claim: At the beginning of the fasting obligation, intercourse was forbidden on fasting nights and eating or drinking after the last evening prayer; God then permitted all of it until dawn.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r2.claim: The singular ليلة الصيام stands in place of the plural nights; al-Abbas ibn Mirdas supplies a poetic parallel.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r3.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r3.claim: Rafath means intercourse, though its root meaning is obscene speech, as the line cited by al-Zajjaj shows.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r4.claim: Rafath is a comprehensive word for everything a man desires from a woman.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r6.claim: Because God uses modest euphemism, Qur'anic references to touching, contact, consummation, entering, and rafath mean intercourse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r7.speaker: الزجاجي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r7.claim: No Arabic term was originally exclusive to intercourse; frequent use can make a word effectively literal, as with مباضعة, whose root means cutting flesh.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r8.speaker: الزجاجي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p596/r8.claim: Other common intercourse expressions—غشيها, وطئها, قربها, and بطنها—originally denote other actions; even فرج is a euphemism.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r1.claim: He rejects the claim that ناك ينيك نيكا is an explicit, literal intercourse term: it too is metaphorical, since Arabs say drowsiness “possessed” an eye to mean it clung to it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r2.claim: The root of that expression means sticking or persisting; he postpones discussion of nikah to 2:221.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r3.claim: Rafath ila your wives means reaching or being intimate with them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r4.speaker: الأخفش
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r4.claim: The preposition إلى governs rafath because the verb is used with the sense of الإفضاء.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r5.claim: Clothing covers the body; spouses are each other's clothing because their bodies join in intercourse and each is like the garment the other wears, as al-Jaʿdi's poem illustrates.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r6.claim: Arab usage also calls a wife clothing, bedding, waist-wrapper, mother of children, dwelling, or shelter; cited poetry uses izar for wives and includes أم بيت and ربضا.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r7.speaker: الربيع
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r7.claim: He glosses the spouses as bedding for one another: she is a bed and he a coverlet.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r8.speaker: ابن زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r8.claim: He takes the image as intercourse: each spouse shields the other from people's sight; the source says this position is distinctive to humans, with a report that humans and crocodiles, and perhaps bears, mate belly-to-belly.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p598/r9.claim: He interprets clothing as mutual comfort or repose; Mujahid and Qatada share this view.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r1.claim: The spouses mingle through cohabitation; either spouse can scarcely endure separation from the other.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r2.claim: Another explanation is that each spouse protects the other from what is forbidden; a prophetic report says marriage secures two-thirds of one's religion.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r3.claim: The singular لباس after plural هن is used as a verbal noun; the sense is that they are mutually clothed or joined to one another.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r4.claim: The forms خانه and اختانه mean to fail or betray; a sword that misses its stroke has betrayed, and fortune betrays when it turns worse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p601/r5.claim: Treachery is failing a trust or breaking a covenant; 8:58 uses it for treaty breach and 8:27 for disobedience toward God and the Messenger.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r1.claim: “Betraying yourselves” means disobeying God; Ibn Abbas says it concerns what God entrusted to them, namely their intercourse on fasting nights.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r2.claim: Umar had intercourse with his wife after the evening prayer, wept after bathing, sought permission from the Prophet, and other men confessed the same; the verse was revealed for them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r3.claim: The command “now approach them” grants permission; approach here means intercourse because the two skins touch and join.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r4.claim: “Seek what God has prescribed for you” means seek children through intercourse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r5.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r5.claim: He interprets what God prescribed as the concession granted to you.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r6.speaker: معاذ بن جبل وابن عباس في رواية أبي الجوزاء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r6.claim: They interpret what God prescribed as Laylat al-Qadr.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r7.claim: All of these interpretations fit the verse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r8.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p603/r8.claim: He prefers that what God prescribed is the Qur'an: follow its directions about what is permitted and commanded.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r1.claim: Eating and drinking are permitted until dawn distinguishes the white thread from the black; the Prophet explained this to ʿAdi ibn Hatim as daylight's whiteness versus nighttime's darkness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r2.speaker: أكثر أهل التفسير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r2.claim: The majority of exegetes understand the two threads as the light of day and darkness of night; Umayya and Abu Dawud use this imagery in poetry.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r3.speaker: الأكثرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r3.claim: They say the threads are the interwoven light and darkness at daybreak, like two skeins; grey hair is also described as black and white mixed, in a verse cited from al-Asmaʿi.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r4.claim: An anonymous poet likens remnants of night spread over dawn garments to twisted yarn, illustrating the interwoven black and white appearance.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r5.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p604/r5.claim: He says the two threads are two dawns: the dark horizontal false dawn and the bright dawn filling the horizon; they are called threads for their extended shape.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r1.claim: Fajr derives from water breaking or flowing; al-Azhari says its root is splitting, and dawn is light splitting the night like water breaking through a basin.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r2.speaker: سهل بن سعد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r2.claim: He reports that people initially tied black and white threads to their legs and ate until they could see them; “from dawn” clarified that the verse meant night and day.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p607/r3.claim: Because intercourse and eating remain permitted until dawn breaks, someone who becomes junub before dawn may still fast and wash afterward; this refutes those who say otherwise.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r1.claim: Some people in retreat left the mosque, had intercourse, and returned; intercourse was therefore prohibited during iʿtikaf.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r2.claim: Intercourse invalidates iʿtikaf; touching intended for pleasure is disliked but does not invalidate it, while contact without that intent is not disliked.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r3.claim: “Those are God's limits” refers to the rulings just stated; a limit is a separation or endpoint.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r4.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r4.claim: The language also uses limits for boundaries of lands and the sanctuary.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r5.speaker: أهل اللغة
