WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r5.claim: The root conveys prevention: a deprived person is barred from provision, a gatekeeper prevents entry, and a boundary prevents trespass; cited poetry uses حداد for a keeper and احددها for restrain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r6.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r6.claim: One category of God's limits sets the bounds of permitted and forbidden foods, drinks, marriage, and other conduct; people must not exceed them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r7.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r7.claim: The other category comprises penalties for transgression, such as theft, adultery, and slander; these deter sins, while the first category marks God's non-crossable endpoints.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r8.claim: He endorses al-Azhari's sound account: the first limits are forbidden boundaries and the second are deterrents; a verbal noun may name either the acted-on thing or agent, as in نسج اليمن and ضرب الأمير.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p609/r9.claim: “Do not approach them” means do not enter those prohibited bounds, confirming that they are forbidden.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p612/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p612/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p612/r1.claim: God explains His signs to people in the manner of the explanation just given.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r10.claim: The stated limits are God's prohibitions, which people must not commit; this clarification aims to help them avoid forbidden acts.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r4.claim: At first, intercourse during fasting nights and eating or drinking after the last evening prayer were forbidden; God later permitted all of them until dawn.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r5.claim: Rafath means intercourse; spouses are garments for one another, meaning bedding or covering during intercourse.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r6.claim: Umar ibn al-Khattab and others had intercourse during Ramadan nights, then asked the Messenger, and the permission was revealed.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r7.claim: God's pardon forgave conduct before the permission, while what God prescribed to seek means the child destined for the couple.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r8.claim: Eating and drinking remain allowed throughout the night until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct from night's blackness; the phrase specifies that the thread is dawn.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:186-187/r9.claim: Fasting then means abstaining from these acts until night, and intercourse is forbidden during mosque retreat because it invalidates it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r1.claim: Rafath is a euphemism for sexual intercourse; Ibn Abbas says the Qur'anic terms for intimate contact likewise refer to intercourse.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r2.speaker: الزجاج
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj says rafath broadly covers everything men desire from women.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r3.claim: At first, after breaking the fast one could eat, drink, and have intercourse only until the night prayer or sleep; then these acts were forbidden until the next night.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p206/r4.claim: After Umar had intercourse after the night prayer, he regretted it and asked the Prophet for relief; the Prophet replied that Umar was not worthy of that conduct, and others confessed similar acts before the verse was revealed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r1.claim: The revelation followed an exhausting day of work by an unnamed account's Abu Sirma ibn Qays, or Abu Qays ibn Sirma according to Ikrima, or Abu Qays Sirma ibn Anas according to al-Kalbi; he fell asleep before eating and became dangerously weak.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r2.claim: The white and black threads mean daylight and nighttime darkness; they were likened to threads because each first appears as an extended line.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r3.speaker: سهل بن سعد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r3.claim: Sahl says the phrase was first revealed without 'of dawn'; some tied white and black threads to their legs, so the clarification 'of dawn' specified natural light and dark.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r4.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207#2/r4.claim: Adi put a black and white cord beneath his pillow and watched them unsuccessfully; the Prophet explained that the words mean night's blackness and day's whiteness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r1.claim: Spouses are garments for one another, meaning sources of comfort; the author supports this with the verse that God made a mate so one could find repose in her.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r2.claim: Other explanations compare spouses to a shared garment during sleep, or say each veils the other from what is forbidden; Rabi ibn Anas instead calls them bedding and coverlet.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r3.claim: Abu Ubayda and others say a woman may be called one's garment, bedding, or waist-wrapper; a hadith says marriage protects two thirds of one's religion.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r4.speaker: البراء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r4.claim: Al-Bara says that when Ramadan fasting was first prescribed, men abstained from wives throughout the month, and some wronged themselves by breaking that restriction.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r5.claim: The former restriction was a betrayal and injustice to oneself; God relented, erased the sin, and then permitted intercourse.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r6.claim: Bashiruhunna means have lawful intercourse; it is called direct contact because the partners' skin touches.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r7.claim: Most exegetes understand 'seek what God wrote for you' as seeking a child; Mujahid says seek offspring, even with another wife if one does not conceive.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r8.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r8.claim: Qatada interprets the phrase as seeking the dispensation God ordained: eating, drinking, and intercourse during the fast's nights.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r9.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p207/r9.claim: Muadh interprets what God wrote as Laylat al-Qadr.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r1.claim: Fasting begins at true dawn, when eating and drinking cease, and ends at sunset, when the fast is broken.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r2.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r2.claim: Umar reports the Prophet's rule that the fast is broken once night comes from the east, day recedes in the west, and the sun sets.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r3.claim: I'tikaf is remaining in a mosque in worship; it is a recommended practice, valid in any mosque, and not outside one.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r4.claim: The ban addresses intercourse during i'tikaf, which is prohibited and invalidates the retreat; intercourse was forbidden day and night for the companions who left the mosque for it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r5.speaker: عائشة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r5.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet observed the final ten days of Ramadan in i'tikaf until his death, and his wives continued the practice after him.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r6.claim: Most scholars, and al-Shafii's stronger view, consider kissing or touching with desire disliked but not invalidating i'tikaf; Malik says it invalidates it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r7.claim: Another view says emission invalidates the retreat, while touch without emission does not, by analogy with fasting.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r8.speaker: عائشة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p209/r8.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet would bring his head near her while in i'tikaf so she could groom him, and he entered the house only for a human need; the author uses this for non-desirous touch.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r1.claim: The stated limits are the fasting and i'tikaf rulings just described; 'limits' means what God has forbidden people to violate.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r2.speaker: السدي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r2.claim: Al-Suddi glosses God's limits as His conditions; Shahr ibn Hawshab calls them His obligations.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r3.claim: The Arabic root of hadd is prevention, as a gatekeeper is called a haddad because he prevents entry.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p210/r4.claim: Do not approach the limits means do not commit the prohibited acts; God clarifies His signs so people may avoid them and escape punishment.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r1.claim: A report says people could eat, drink, and have intercourse after sunset until sleeping or the night prayer, then these acts were forbidden until the next evening; Ibn Abbas's report is graded weak because of Atiyya al-Awfi and those below him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r2.claim: In the reported occasion, Umar had intercourse after the night prayer, regretted it, confessed to the Prophet, and other men also admitted doing so before the verse was revealed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r3.claim: A reading makes the wording mean that God permitted intercourse on the night of fasting.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r4.claim: Abdullah's reading الرفوث means explicit speech about what should ordinarily be stated euphemistically.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p255#2/r5.claim: While in pilgrimage consecration, Ibn Abbas recited a poem with a sexual allusion; when challenged, he said rafath means what occurs with women.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r1.claim: Rafath euphemistically denotes intercourse, since intercourse is rarely free of something covered by that term.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r2.claim: The blunt, disapproving term rafath highlights their conduct before permission, which is also called betraying themselves.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r3.claim: Rafath is followed by إلى because the verb includes the sense of intimacy and union.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p256/r4.claim: The clothing metaphor describes the spouses' close embrace, with each enveloping the other; al-Jaʿdī's poem illustrates it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r1.claim: The white thread is the first dawn light stretched across the horizon; the black thread is the twilight of night alongside it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r2.claim: Abu Dawud's line about dawn's thread supplies poetic evidence for this image.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r3.claim: From dawn explains the white thread and suffices to clarify the black one; من can also mean that it is part of, and the beginning of, dawn.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r4.claim: Adding من dawn turns the expression from metaphor into a vivid simile, just as specifying the source of a lion comparison makes it a simile.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257#2/r5.claim: The added phrase signals the otherwise unclear metaphor and makes the comparison unmistakable, yielding an emphatic simile.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r1.claim: The clause about spouses being garments explains why intercourse was permitted: their intimate closeness makes abstention difficult.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r10.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r10.claim: An interpretation as seeking Laylat al-Qadr and its reward is dismissed by the author as a nearly baseless novelty in exegesis.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r2.claim: Betraying yourselves means wronging yourselves and depriving them of their share of good; the augmented form intensifies the sense of khiyana.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r3.claim: God turned toward them when they repented from what they had prohibitedly done.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r4.claim: Seek the offspring God allotted and recorded through intercourse, rather than seeking pleasure alone, since procreation is a purpose of marriage.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r5.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r5.claim: One interpretation makes the phrase a prohibition of coitus interruptus with free wives.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r6.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r6.claim: Another interpretation commands seeking the lawful place of intercourse rather than a forbidden one.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r7.speaker: قتادة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p257/r7.claim: Qatada interprets the words as seeking the permission God granted after the earlier prohibition.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد الساعدي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r1.claim: A report says people tied white and black threads to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them; the phrase من الفجر then clarified that the threads meant day and night.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r2.claim: Most jurists and theologians, including Abu Ali and Abu Hashim, reject this report because they disallow delaying clarification of a command.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r3.claim: Those who allow delayed clarification say the initial wording still informs the listener of an obligation and prompts readiness to act once its meaning is clarified.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258#2/r4.claim: The command to complete the fast until night supports daytime intention for Ramadan, delaying the purificatory bath until dawn, and rejecting continuous fasting.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r1.claim: Without من الفجر, readers would not know that the two threads are figurative; adding it makes the wording an emphatic simile rather than metaphor.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r2.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r2.claim: Adi reports that he put two cords under his pillow and could not distinguish them at night; the Prophet laughed and said his pillow must be broad, or that his nape was broad, meaning daybreak and night.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r3.claim: The author says Adi missed the textual clarification and treats the Prophet's reference to his broad nape as a sign of dullness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p258/r4.claim: An anonymous Bedouin poem uses a broad nape as an image of foolishness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r1.claim: Believers are within the sphere of truth; they are told not to cross its boundary, then more emphatically not even to approach it, so they stay far from falsehood.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r2.claim: The Prophet compares God's prohibitions to a king's protected pasture: someone grazing around it may soon enter it; the author equates grazing nearby with approaching the boundary.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259#2/r3.claim: God's boundaries can specifically mean prohibitions and bans, as illustrated by the restriction on marital intercourse during iʿtikaf.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r1.claim: Iʿtikaf means keeping oneself in a mosque for worship.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r2.claim: Here direct contact means intercourse, as in the earlier permission; a further view includes lustful touching, and intercourse or touching or kissing followed by emission invalidates iʿtikaf.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r3.speaker: قتادة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r3.claim: Qatada says a man in iʿtikaf used to leave, have intercourse with his wife, and return to the mosque, which God then forbade.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r4.claim: The passage indicates iʿtikaf must take place in a mosque, without limiting it to a particular mosque; other views restrict it to a prophet's mosque or a congregational mosque, while the majority require a mosque where congregational prayer is held.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r5.speaker: مجاهد
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r5.claim: Mujahid read في المسجد in the singular.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p259/r6.claim: Those boundaries refer to the rulings just mentioned.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r1.claim: “Made lawful” implies that intercourse had previously been forbidden; layl is an accusative time expression and a generic singular.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r10.claim: The opening of the verse abrogates the earlier rule against intercourse after sleep.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r11.speaker: النحاس ومكي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r11.claim: They transmit a version in which ʿUmar slept and then had intercourse; Ibn ʿAṭiyya considers this unlikely for ʿUmar.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r12.speaker: صرمة بن قيس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r12.claim: A report says Ṣirma slept before eating and continued fasting without food until he nearly collapsed the next day; this occasioned the permission to eat and drink.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r13.claim: Clothing is the basic meaning of libās, extended by analogy to the closeness, mixture, and attachment of spouses.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r2.speaker: عامر الرامي الحضرمي المحاربي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r2.claim: A line of poetry is cited as evidence for the generic use of singular layl.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r3.claim: They explain rafath as a euphemism for sexual intercourse, since God speaks euphemistically.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r4.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd uses rafūth in place of rafath.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r5.claim: Outside this verse, rafath can mean obscene speech; the cited poem illustrates that sense.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r6.speaker: أبو إسحاق
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r6.claim: Abū Isḥāq defines rafath to include the man’s approaches to a woman, such as touching, kissing, and intercourse.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r7.claim: The euphemism can also include speech about such sexual matters; a Prophetic report uses rafath for obscene conduct during pilgrimage.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r8.claim: The verse was revealed after Muslims, including ʿUmar in one account, had intercourse after sleeping or after the night prayer, both previously forbidden; ʿUmar apologized to the Prophet, and a similar event involved Kaʿb ibn Mālik.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r9.speaker: السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p256#2/r9.claim: Al-Suddī says ʿUmar’s incident involved a slave girl.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r1.speaker: النابغة الجعدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r1.claim: A poem compares a woman’s closeness to her companion with clothing, illustrating the metaphor.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r10.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r10.claim: Qatāda interprets it as seeking the dispensation and expanded permission, a good interpretation in Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s view.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r11.speaker: الحسن ومعاوية بن قرة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r11.claim: They are reported to read “follow” instead of “seek”; Ibn ʿAbbās allowed the reading, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the received “seek” reading.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r12.claim: He prefers ibtaghū from the root of seeking over the alternate reading itbaʿū, though Ibn ʿAbbās permitted that reading.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r13.claim: The dawn boundary requires enough time for dawn to become visible before eating becomes forbidden; the phrase until it becomes clear sets that limit.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r14.claim: The two threads metaphorically describe the thin initial whiteness of dawn and the surrounding darkness; the cited line uses the same image.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r15.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r15.claim: Abū Dāwūd’s poem describes a thread of dawn appearing, as evidence for the metaphor.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r16.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r16.claim: Some exegetes say the thread means color, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this does not work throughout the language.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r17.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r17.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r17.claim: All scholars understand the phrase as the light of day and darkness of night, as the Prophet explicitly explained to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r18.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r18.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r18.claim: The first min marks the starting point, the second is partitive, and fajr is named for water bursting forth gradually.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r19.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r19.speaker: سهل بن سعد وغيره من الصحابة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r19.claim: They report that the verse first descended without “from dawn”; after some people tied white and black threads, that clarification was revealed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r2.speaker: الربيع وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r2.claim: Al-Rabīʿ and others explain spouses as clothing because they shelter and bring peace to one another.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r20.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r20.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r20.claim: A further report says a year passed between the two stages of the revelation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r3.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r3.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī explain “clothing” as a source of tranquility, each spouse finding repose with the other.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r4.claim: The acts are called self-betrayal because sin’s eventual consequence is that the offender betrays and harms himself.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r5.claim: “He turned toward you” means He pardoned the sin committed; “pardoned you” may reinforce that pardon or mean He lifted the prospective restriction.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r6.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r6.claim: “Now be intimate with them” is a euphemism for intercourse, derived from the word for skin.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r7.claim: The word “now” was discussed earlier in the story of the cow.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r8.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والحكم بن عتيبة وعكرمة والحسن والسدي والربيع والضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r8.claim: They interpret seeking what God prescribed as seeking offspring.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r9.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p257/r9.claim: Another report interprets the command as seeking Laylat al-Qadr.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r1.claim: ʿAdī placed two threads on his pillow; the Prophet replied in one version that his pillow was broad, and in another that his nape was broad.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r10.claim: He accepts the linguistic position that day starts at dawn but finds this verse inconclusive proof; its argument is given under the discussion of day and night.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r11.speaker: مالك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r11.claim: According to Mālik, someone who eats while unsure whether dawn has broken must make up the fast.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r12.claim: Completing the fast to night is obligatory; when the endpoint is of the same kind as the preceding interval it is included, but an unlike endpoint is excluded.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r13.speaker: عائشة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r13.claim: ʿĀʾisha understands “until night” to prohibit continuous fasting; the Prophet practiced it but forbade people, while some scholars also practiced it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r14.claim: Some understood the earlier rule in 2:183 as prohibiting eating and intercourse after sleep or after the night prayer, and this verse abrogated it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r15.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r15.claim: The night marking the end of fasting begins when the sun’s disk disappears; the well-known Mālikī position requires make-up and expiation if sunset is uncertain.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r2.claim: The two remarks about ʿAdī have two possible interpretations, though the passage does not specify them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r3.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r3.claim: The majority, followed by the towns and supported by sound reports, require abstention at the first horizontal dawn spreading across the horizon.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r4.claim: According to the majority, fasting begins as soon as the first light spreads across the horizon, supported by reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Samura ibn Jundub.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r5.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح والأعمش وغيرهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r5.claim: A group including ʿAṭāʾ and al-Aʿmash requires abstention only once dawn is discernible on roads and mountain tops.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r6.speaker: حذيفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r6.claim: Ḥudhayfa says he ate the pre-dawn meal with the Prophet while it was already day, before the sun had risen.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r7.claim: ʿAlī reportedly prayed dawn prayer with the people and then announced that the white thread was now distinct from the black.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r8.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r8.claim: Al-Ṭabarī explains the later-dawn view by saying its proponents start daytime at sunrise because it also ends at sunset.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r9.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p258/r9.claim: Al-Khalīl says daytime begins at dawn, citing the command to pray at the two ends of the day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r1.claim: Abū Zayd’s collection gives a view requiring only make-up, by analogy with uncertainty about dawn; a group of scholars held it too.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r10.speaker: قوم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r10.claim: Some require one of the three mosques to which people travel, based on the relevant report.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r11.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r11.claim: Another group permits retreat only in a mosque of a prophet.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r12.speaker: مالك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r12.claim: Mālik requires at least a day and a night; whoever vows either owes the other as well.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r13.speaker: سحنون
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r13.claim: Saḥnūn says a vow of one night of retreat does not bind the person to anything.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r14.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r14.claim: A group says whichever period is vowed is fulfilled without requiring a longer period.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r16.speaker: غيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r16.claim: Others allow retreat without fasting; a report from ʿĀʾisha also permits retreat outside a mosque.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r17.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r17.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r17.claim: “Those” points back to the preceding commands and prohibitions; divine limits are barriers between what is permitted and forbidden.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r18.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r18.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r18.claim: The word for a gatekeeper is related to a barrier, as is a term for a woman who refrains from adornment.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r19.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r19.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r19.claim: The verses are signs guiding to truth; “perhaps” expresses hope relative to humans, while the general wording applies specifically to those God enables to receive guidance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r2.speaker: إسحاق والحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r2.claim: Isḥāq and al-Ḥasan say no make-up is due, treating the person like one who forgot.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r3.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r3.claim: One group limits the prohibition during retreat to sexual intercourse.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r4.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r4.claim: The majority include intercourse and lesser forms of sexual pleasure in the prohibition during retreat.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r5.claim: ʿĀkifūn means people who remain attached and devoted to a place or thing; two poems illustrate that usage.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r6.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r6.claim: Qatāda is reported to read ʿākifūn without the alif.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r7.speaker: الأعمش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r7.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads “in the mosque” in the singular and identifies it as the Sacred Mosque.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r8.speaker: مالك وجماعة معه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r8.claim: Mālik and others require retreat to take place in mosques where Friday prayer is held.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r9.speaker: مالك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p259/r9.claim: Another position attributed to Mālik permits any mosque, with departure for Friday prayer and necessary errands.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r1.claim: A report raised through Ali ibn Ibrahim's father to Abu Abd Allah says Ramadan nights initially barred eating after sleep, and intercourse was forbidden by night and day.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r2.claim: The report says the elderly fasting Mat'am ibn Jubayr slept before iftar when his wife was late with food; he thought eating was forbidden and later fainted while digging the trench, moving the Prophet to pity.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r3.claim: Young men secretly had intercourse at night in Ramadan, and the verse then permitted night intercourse and food after sleep until dawn.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r4.claim: General transmitters give the Anṣari's name variously as Qays b. Sirma, Abu Sirma, Abu Qays b. Sirma, or Sirma b. Iyas; his long workday and missed iftar left him exhausted.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
TABRISI:2:187#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi report that Qays told the Prophet he had worked all day, slept before eating, and awoke believing food forbidden; Umar and other men admitted comparable conduct, including intercourse after evening prayer.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r6.claim: The verse explains the fast's timing and rules: rafath means intercourse; Ibn Abbas treats rafath, clothing, direct contact, and ifḍā as euphemisms for it, while al-Zajjaj calls rafath a comprehensive term for a man's desires of a woman.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#2/r7.claim: Calling the night singular refers to the nights of the month in which the following day is fasted; the wording implies intercourse had earlier been forbidden.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r8.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله
TABRISI:2:187#2/r8.claim: Abu Ja'far and Abu Abd Allah reportedly considered intercourse disliked on the first night of every month, except Ramadan's first night, when this verse makes it recommended; the author favors its generic application to all Ramadan nights.

TABRISI:2:187#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
TABRISI:2:187#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada interpret spouses as clothing because each is a source of rest and shelter for the other.

TABRISI:2:187#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#3/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#3/r1.claim: The prior rule forbidding intercourse and eating after sleep explains the phrase about betraying themselves: they sinned by violating it, so the later permission is a divine favor.

TABRISI:2:187#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#3/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#3/r2.claim: Another interpretation of self-betrayal is depriving oneself of lawful desire and pleasure by avoiding what had been prohibited.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#4/r1.claim: Repentance here means either accepting their repentance or granting a concession and removing the former restriction; pardon means forgiveness or ending that prohibition.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#4/r2.claim: The command to approach wives at night functions as permission to have intercourse.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r3.speaker: الحسن وأكثر المفسرين
TABRISI:2:187#4/r3.claim: Al-Hasan and most exegetes read what God prescribed as offspring: one has intercourse hoping for a child who worships and praises God.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#4/r4.claim: A second view takes what God prescribed as lawful things stated in scripture; God loves people to accept his concessions as they accept obligations.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#4/r5.claim: Eating and drinking are permitted until the true dawn makes day distinct from night; the comparison is with the threadlike first light, not its later spread.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r6.speaker: ابن دريد
TABRISI:2:187#4/r6.claim: Ibn Durayd takes مِن in مِن الفجر partitivally, meaning a portion of dawn; another grammatical analysis takes it as explanatory.

TABRISI:2:187#4/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#4/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#4/r7.claim: A report says Adi b. Hatim placed white and black hairs as literal threads to judge dawn; the Prophet laughed and explained that the words mean day and night.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r1.claim: The fast ends when night begins, after sunset; as a precaution, one may wait for eastern redness to disappear and darkness to approach, while on flat land sunset suffices.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r10.claim: The verse shows that God intends all people to attain piety.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r2.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة
TABRISI:2:187#5/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada limit forbidden contact during retreat to intercourse.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r3.speaker: مالك وابن زيد
TABRISI:2:187#5/r3.claim: Malik and Ibn Zayd include intercourse and all lesser intimacy such as kissing; the author says this is his school's position.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r4.claim: His school permits i'tikaf only in the four named mosques; other jurists allow it in any mosque, while Malik requires a congregational mosque.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r5.claim: His school requires fasting for valid i'tikaf, as do Abu Hanifa and Malik; al-Shafi'i allows it without fasting.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r6.claim: His school requires three days; Abu Hanifa requires a day, Malik ten days, and al-Shafi'i allows any length, even an hour.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r7.claim: The verse bars sexual intimacy throughout the retreat, by night as well as by day, since the prohibition is attached to the state of i'tikaf.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r8.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:2:187#5/r8.claim: Al-Hasan interprets God's limits here as his sacred prohibitions; al-Dahhak calls them sins, and al-Zajjaj says they are what God forbids.

TABRISI:2:187#5/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187#5/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187#5/r9.claim: Do not approach the limits means do not commit them; alternatively, do not violate God's obligations. The explanation aims to produce obedience to commands and prohibitions.

TABRISI:2:187/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r1.claim: رفث here unambiguously means intercourse, though its original sense is indecent speech; the poet al-Ajjaj uses it for talk.

TABRISI:2:187/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r10.claim: I'tikaf linguistically means staying put; in law it is remaining in a specified place for worship. God's boundaries are prohibitions and limits that prevent transgression.

TABRISI:2:187/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r11.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:2:187/r11.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines God's boundaries as what God forbids people to violate; the Arabic root of hadd is prevention or separation.

TABRISI:2:187/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r12.claim: Hadd also names a sword's edge, a house boundary, or an end that keeps things from entering or leaving their proper bounds.

TABRISI:2:187/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r2.speaker: الأخفش
TABRISI:2:187/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash says إلى governs rafath because the word carries the sense of ifḍā, intimacy or reaching.

TABRISI:2:187/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r3.claim: Clothing covers bodies; Arabs also call a wife clothing or a waist-wrapper, as the cited poetry witnesses.

TABRISI:2:187/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r4.claim: اختيان is a form of betrayal; eye-treachery is furtive looking at what is forbidden, and the root concerns withholding a right.

TABRISI:2:187/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r5.claim: Direct contact means skin touching skin; ابتغاء is seeking the desired thing.

TABRISI:2:187/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r6.claim: The white thread is dawn's whiteness, the black thread night; day begins with the second, broader dawn.

TABRISI:2:187/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r7.speaker: أبو داود
TABRISI:2:187/r7.claim: Abu Dawud's poem uses خيط to describe the streak of light at dawn.

TABRISI:2:187/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:187/r8.claim: The blackness of night explains such usages as whispered conversation, the dark complexion of Iraq's land, and a person's visible form; بيضة الإسلام means its foundation or protected core.

TABRISI:2:187/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:187/r9.speaker: الطرماح
TABRISI:2:187/r9.claim: Al-Tirimmāḥ's verse describes women of the night keeping vigil as mourners; عكوف witnesses remaining in place.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r1.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r1.claim: Before this ruling, sleeping before the evening meal barred a fasting person from eating or intercourse; an Ansari slept hungry, while Umar had intercourse after mistakenly thinking his sleeping wife was feigning sleep, and the verse relaxed both restrictions.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r2.speaker: البراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r2.claim: The Ansari in the occasion report was Qays ibn Sirma.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r3.speaker: القاسم بن محمد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r3.claim: The Ansari was called Sirma ibn Anas; Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla instead names him Sirma ibn Malik.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r4.claim: Other identifications of the Ansari are Damra ibn Anas and Abu Qays ibn Amr, both recorded by Abu Bakr al-Khatib.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r5.speaker: ابن عمر وابن عباس ومجاهد وعطاء والحسن وابن جبير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p190#2/r5.claim: Rafath in this verse means sexual intercourse, according to these authorities and others.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r1.claim: The spouses are garments for one another in the sense that they are a source of repose, as night is called a garment.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r10.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r10.claim: What God prescribed means the permission or concession granted to them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r11.speaker: أبو الجوزاء عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r11.claim: What God prescribed means the Night of Decree.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r12.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r12.claim: What God prescribed is the Qur'an: follow it, since what it permits and commands is what one should seek.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r2.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r2.claim: The garment image also signifies spouses joining unclothed, with each person's skin touching the other's; Arabic calls a woman a garment or waist-wrapper.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r3.speaker: النابغة الجعدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r3.claim: His verse uses garment as a metaphor for the woman beside her partner.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r4.claim: An unnamed poet uses izar, literally a waist-wrapper, to mean his wife.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r5.claim: You were betraying yourselves by committing what had been forbidden.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r6.claim: The self-betrayal refers to Umar, who had intercourse with his wife, then blamed himself and wept after bathing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r7.claim: Mubashara literally means skin touching skin.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r8.claim: In this verse, mubashara means intercourse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r9.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p191/r9.claim: What God prescribed for you means offspring; the wording directs people to intercourse that can produce children.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r1.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r1.claim: Adi misunderstood the white and black threads as literal cords under his pillow; the Prophet laughed and explained that they mean daylight and night.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r2.speaker: سهل بن سعد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r2.claim: The phrase “of dawn” was revealed later because people tied black and white threads to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r3.speaker: أحمد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r3.claim: Ahmad's apparent position is that a person uncertain about dawn keeps eating until sunrise is certain.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r4.speaker: مالك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r4.claim: Malik disliked eating once dawn was uncertain and required a make-up fast if the person ate.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r5.speaker: الشافعي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p192/r5.claim: Al-Shafi'i held that eating while uncertain about dawn incurs no liability.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r1.speaker: الأكثرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r1.claim: The prohibition on approaching wives during mosque retreat means intercourse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r2.claim: The prohibition also covers touching and kissing, not just intercourse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r3.claim: Men in retreat would leave the mosque and touch their wives; God warned them against this.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r4.claim: I'tikaf literally means staying; it is recommended and becomes obligatory when vowed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r5.claim: Valid i'tikaf requires a mosque where congregational prayer is held, while a woman's mosque need not hold congregation; Ahmad transmitted two views on whether fasting is required.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r6.claim: The boundaries in the verse refer to sexual relations with wives.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r7.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r7.claim: God's limits are the prohibitions He set; they may not be crossed, and the root of the word means prevention.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r8.speaker: الأعشى
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r8.claim: His poem uses haddad for a keeper who prevents access to what is guarded.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p193/r9.claim: The related words for mourning, restricting one's gaze, and iron all evoke restraint or prevention.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r1.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r1.claim: Most exegetes say the first Muslim fasting rule barred eating, drinking, and intercourse after sleep or the last evening prayer, and this verse abrogated that rule.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r2.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r2.claim: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani says that restriction never belonged to Muslim law; it belonged to the Christians' law, which this verse abrogates, consistent with his denial of abrogation in Islamic law.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r3.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r3.claim: The majority argues that 2:183 compares Muslim fasting to earlier fasting, where the nighttime restriction existed, so the same restriction initially applied to Muslims.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r4.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r4.claim: The majority argues that saying nighttime intercourse was made lawful would be pointless if it had already been lawful from the start.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r5.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r5.claim: The majority reads the believers' self-betrayal as evidence that they had been breaking a prohibition, not doing something already lawful.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r6.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r6.claim: The majority takes God's turning toward and forgiving them to imply that they had sinned by doing what had been prohibited.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r7.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r7.claim: The majority says the command to be intimate now would have no point if the permission already existed.

RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r8.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v5p87#2/r8.claim: The majority also cites reports about the verse's occasion of revelation as evidence that the restriction had applied in Muslim law.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r1.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r1.claim: Abu Muslim replies that fasting laws need resemble one another only in their basic obligation, not every detail.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r2.claim: Razi calls the first majority proof weak: comparison with earlier fasting requires only shared obligation, not identical rules.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r3.claim: Abu Muslim says the permission addresses Muslims by contrast with other communities, for whom the rule remained forbidden.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r4.claim: Razi calls the second majority proof weak because the phrase can mean that something forbidden to earlier communities was made lawful for Muslims.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r5.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r5.claim: Abu Muslim says believers inferred that the earlier rule continued because the new fasting command did not expressly remove it, and 2:183's comparison reinforced this suspicion; they therefore abstained and deprived themselves until God clarified the dispensation.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r6.claim: Razi calls the third proof weak because a plausible but mistaken suspicion of continuity explains their caution; ikhtiyān means depriving themselves of pleasures and interests.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r7.claim: The root kh-w-n here means deficiency: khāna, ikhtāna, and takhawwana are synonymous forms; believers would have denied themselves nighttime pleasures as Christians did after sleeping.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r8.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r8.claim: Abu Muslim distinguishes human repentance as returning to God in worship from God's repentance as returning to the servant with mercy and beneficence; pardon means overlooking, and the verse describes easing a prior burden.

RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p88/r9.claim: Razi calls the fourth majority proof weak: repentance and pardon can describe God's merciful removal of a heavy burden imposed on earlier people, as 7:157 says.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r1.claim: The phrase refers to the night associated with fasting in general, not one particular night.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r3.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r3.claim: A poem cited by al-Zajjaj uses rafath for lewd talk, supporting its sense of obscenity.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r4.claim: When asked whether his verse recited during pilgrimage was rafath, Ibn Abbas answered that rafath means what occurs with women.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r5.claim: Rafath first meant obscene speech, then intimate speech with women, and finally became a euphemism for intercourse and related acts.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r6.claim: The verse calls intercourse rafath because the pre-permission conduct was repugnant, as its description as self-betrayal also shows.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r7.speaker: الأخفش
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r7.claim: The preposition ila follows rafath because the word carries the sense of mutual intimacy, as in the verse about spouses drawing close.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r8.claim: Because layla is an adverbial time span, the wording makes intercourse lawful throughout the night and itself abrogates the earlier restriction.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89#2/r9.claim: An alternative reading says the first clause only permits intercourse at night; on that reading, the command to eat and drink performs the abrogation.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r1.claim: Razi calls the fifth proof weak: believers refrained because of their mistaken suspicion that the earlier restriction continued, then the verse removed that doubt and commanded intimacy.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r10.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r10.claim: Al-Wahidi says the singular phrase night of fasting stands for the plural nights of fasting, a singular used with collective meaning; he introduces a line by Abbas ibn Mirdas as evidence.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r11.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r11.claim: Al-Wahidi cites Abbas ibn Mirdas's poetry as evidence for using a singular noun where a plural is intended.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r2.claim: The sixth proof is weak: a solitary report cannot establish a legally prescribed rule or its abrogation, and the reports' confession detail conflicts with the verse's apparent sense of concealed intercourse.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r3.claim: The reported occasion says a tired Anṣari who had worked all day in the date palms came home after fasting, fell asleep before eating, and awoke unable to eat; Umar also reports having intercourse after the evening prayer, and the verse was revealed after men disclosed what they had done.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r4.speaker: معاذ
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r4.claim: Muadh identifies the tired Anṣari in the occasion report as Abu Sirma.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r5.speaker: البراء
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r5.claim: Al-Bara identifies the tired Anṣari as Qays ibn Sirma.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r6.speaker: الكلبي
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r6.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies him as Abu Qays ibn Sirma.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r7.claim: Another version calls him Sirma ibn Anas; the account also says Umar confessed to intercourse after the last evening prayer and the Prophet responded that he had not been worthy of doing so.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r8.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r8.claim: Al-Kashshaf explains the reading of uḥilla lakum laylata al-ṣiyām al-rafath as meaning Allah made intimacy lawful.

RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r9.speaker: عبد الله
RAZI-FULL:v5p89/r9.claim: Abdullah is reported to read al-rafath as al-rufūth.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r1.claim: One explanation compares spouses to garments because they embrace and each body covers the other like clothing.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r2.speaker: الربيع
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r2.claim: Al-Rabi paraphrases the metaphor as spouses being bedding and covering for each other.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says each spouse covers the other from people's sight during intercourse.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r4.claim: Another explanation is that spouses shield one another from unlawful conduct; the report says marriage protects two thirds of one's religion.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r5.claim: A further explanation is that a husband keeps his wife uniquely for himself, as he does his clothing, and their whole bodies meet.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r6.claim: The metaphor may mean a wife protects the household from many harms, just as clothing shields a person from heat, cold, and other injuries.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r7.speaker: الأصم
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r7.claim: Al-Asamm says spouses cover one another in concealing the forbidden acts they commit; al-Razi rejects this because the description is a divine blessing.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r8.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r8.claim: Al-Wahidi explains singular libas after plural hunna as a verbal noun meaning that the spouses are closely associated with each other.

RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r9.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v5p90/r9.claim: Al-Kashshaf treats the garment clause as an explanation of the permission: intimacy makes abstinence difficult, so the concession follows.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r1.claim: A second interpretation makes the betrayal hypothetical: God knew that continued hardship would lead people to violate the restriction, so no violation had yet occurred.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r2.claim: The first interpretation avoids an unstated condition, while the second better explains the repeal as mercy preventing future violations; al-Razi presents arguments both ways.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r3.claim: For Abu Muslim, God turned toward the believers by granting permission and expanding what they could do.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r4.claim: Those who affirm abrogation must understand repentance as the people's repentance followed by God's acceptance.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r5.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r5.claim: For Abu Muslim, pardon means the easing of permission to eat, drink, and have sex all night; afw can mean expansion and relief.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r6.claim: Reports use afw for waived horse and slave alms, the later prayer time, and readily obtained wealth, so the word need not imply prior sin.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r7.claim: Abu Muslim's reading needs no omitted phrase, while abrogation proponents must supply forgiveness of sins; this favors Abu Muslim.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91#2/r8.claim: An imperative following a prohibition is read as permission by one group; those who normally take commands as obligatory say consensus establishes permission here.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r1.claim: The root kh-w-n covers failure to fulfill an obligation, a sword missing its strike, adverse change, betrayal of trust, and breach of covenant; this verse calls disobedience betrayal.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r2.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r2.claim: Ikhtiyan derives from khiyana like iktisab from kasb, with an added sense of intensity.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r3.claim: Context links the unspecified self-betrayal to intercourse: sex is mentioned immediately before and permitted immediately after.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r4.claim: One interpretation says some secretly had intercourse after evening and ate after sleeping; disobedience betrays self and God by bringing punishment.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r5.claim: If this interpretation describes actual conduct, only some people committed it; it establishes an earlier prohibition and its violation by some.

RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v5p91/r6.claim: Abu Muslim takes self-betrayal as failing to pursue what benefits oneself, not disobeying God; the wording says themselves, unlike verses that name God.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r1.claim: One reading is to seek children through intercourse, fulfilling marriage's purpose of procreation rather than mere pleasure; a Prophetic saying urges marrying and multiplying.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r10.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r10.claim: Mu'adh and Ibn Abbas, in a report through Abu al-Jawza, read this as seeking Laylat al-Qadr and its reward.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r11.claim: Mu'adh and Ibn Abbas, through Abu al-Jawza, interpret the phrase as seeking Laylat al-Qadr and its reward.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r12.claim: Most careful scholars considered the Laylat al-Qadr interpretation unlikely, but al-Razi accepts it: satisfying desire can free one to devote himself to worship and seek that night.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r2.claim: A second reading makes the clause prohibit coitus interruptus; reports disapprove of it, and al-Shafi'i requires a free wife's consent but permits it with an enslaved woman.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r3.speaker: علي
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r3.claim: Ali is reported to have disliked coitus interruptus.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r4.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet forbade withdrawal from a free wife without her permission.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r5.claim: A third reading is to seek the permitted place of intercourse and avoid forbidden places, compared with the command to approach women as God directed.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r6.claim: A fourth reading treats the clause as emphasis: pursue the intercourse newly permitted after being forbidden.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r7.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r7.claim: For Abu Muslim, seek the intercourse God had prescribed even though believers mistakenly thought it forbidden.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r8.claim: A sixth reading limits intercourse to circumstances and times God permits, given menstruation, postpartum bleeding, waiting periods, and apostasy.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92#2/r9.claim: A seventh reading limits intercourse to a wife or an enslaved woman, as prescribed in the verse on sexual restraint.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r1.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r1.claim: The majority identify mubashara with intercourse, named for the joining of two skins.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r2.claim: A report says the Prophet forbade a man to make direct bodily contact with a man and a woman with a woman.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r3.speaker: الأصم
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r3.claim: Al-Asamm defines mubashara as intercourse and acts short of it; exegetes consequently differed over whether the i'tikaf prohibition includes all contact.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r4.claim: Because mubashara derives from skin contact, it can include intercourse, acts short of penetration, embraces, and touching.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r5.claim: In the first clause, mubashara means intercourse because the concession followed people's intercourse and rafath above means intercourse; permitting intercourse entails lesser contact.

RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p92/r6.claim: In i'tikaf, forbidding intercourse does not itself establish a ban on lesser contact, so exegetes can reasonably differ; al-Razi adopts the Qadi's analysis.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r1.claim: Kitab can mean made or established, as in God placing faith in hearts and the request to be made among witnesses.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r2.claim: Kitab can mean decreed, as in the statement that nothing befalls people except what God decreed for them and that God will prevail.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r3.claim: Kitab may mean what God recorded in the Preserved Tablet, since every event and ruling was written there.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r4.claim: Kitab may refer to what the Quran itself records by permitting these acts.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas read the verb as wabtaghu, with the hamza retained.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r6.speaker: الأعمش
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r6.claim: Al-A'mash read the verb as wabghu.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r7.claim: Food and drink are named separately because permission for intercourse alone would not clearly lift the earlier bans on eating and drinking after sleep.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r8.claim: Adi ibn Hatim took the threads literally, placed black and white cords under his pillow, and failed to distinguish them; the Prophet explained that they mean daylight and night.

RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p93/r9.claim: The expression certainly means the whiteness of dawn's beginning and the darkness of the night's end, though that raises a problem about false dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r1.speaker: الأعمش
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r1.claim: Al-A'mash permits eating, drinking, and intercourse from dawn until sunrise by analogy with the sunset endpoint; he reads the threads as day and night.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r10.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r10.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that when a fasting man admitted eating and drinking, the Prophet called him God's guest and told him to complete the fast; jurists use this to excuse forgetfulness.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r2.speaker: الأعمش
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r2.claim: Al-A'mash argues that night means the sun's absence, so the period before sunrise remains night, just as the post-sunset period does.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r3.claim: Other people accepted dawn as the start of day and analogized the end, delayed breaking the fast until redness vanished, or waited for stars; jurists rejected these positions and they died out.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r4.speaker: الأزهري
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r4.claim: Al-Azhari derives fajr from splitting: dawn is the night darkness split by morning light.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r5.claim: Min in min al-fajr may be partitive, since only part of dawn matters, or explanatory, identifying the white thread as dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r6.claim: Dawn can be known with certainty by sight or by knowing enough time has elapsed; under uncertainty, a likely dawn prohibits eating, while a likely continuing night permits it.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r7.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says no make-up fast is required when someone mistakenly eats before dawn or breaks fast before sunset, by analogy with forgetfulness.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r8.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r8.claim: Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in al-Muzani's transmission require a make-up fast after mistaken eating at dawn or breaking before sunset because the required fast was not completed.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r9.speaker: مالك
RAZI-FULL:v5p94#2/r9.claim: Malik also requires make-up for eating forgetfully, unlike the other jurists who rely on a Prophetic report excusing the forgetful person.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r1.claim: The phrase min al-fajr rules out false dawn: fajr is when light breaks forth, which occurs at true dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r2.claim: True dawn initially appears as a narrow, fine streak before spreading, so it can be compared to a thread.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r3.claim: Al-Razi finds the Adi ibn Hatim report unlikely because the metaphor should have been clear given the phrase min al-fajr.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r4.claim: Until marks the endpoint: permission for intercourse, eating, and drinking ends when dawn appears.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r5.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r5.claim: Abu Muslim says only intercourse, eating, and drinking invalidate the fast; vomiting, enemas, and nasal medication remain permissible because the verse names only three.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r6.speaker: الفقهاء
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r6.claim: Jurists reply that the verse names the appetitive acts; people dislike vomiting and enemas, and nasal medication is uncommon.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r7.claim: Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy held that someone still in major ritual impurity at dawn has no valid fast.

RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p94/r8.claim: The verse disproves that view because intercourse remains permitted until dawn, leaving no time to bathe before daybreak.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r1.claim: A third view excuses mistaken eating before dawn but requires make-up after mistaken early breaking, because the prior state was permissibility at night and prohibition during day.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r10.speaker: ابن الزبير
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r10.claim: Al-Tabari says Ibn al-Zubayr continuously fasted seven days, later five, and finally three as he aged.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r11.claim: Al-Shafi'i's wording treats the ban on continuous fasting as prohibitive; another interpretation makes it merely disliked because it abandons lawful acts, allowing Ibn al-Zubayr's practice.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r12.claim: If someone fears that too little food will weaken the next fast or other worship, he must eat enough to remove that fear.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
