RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r2.claim: When a person cannot decide whether dawn has arrived, eating, drinking, and intercourse are disliked but valid because night is presumed to continue.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r3.claim: Ila marks the fast's endpoint: night is outside the fast because it is a different kind from day; by contrast, elbows belong to the arm in the ablution verse.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r4.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r4.claim: Ahmad ibn Yahya says ila can include or exclude its endpoint, like eating a fish up to its head, which may or may not be eaten.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r5.claim: Reason confirms that night is outside fasting; including it would impose great hardship and would also require including the elbows in washing.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r6.speaker: عمر
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r6.claim: Umar reports the Prophet's rule that when night advances, day retreats, and the sun has set, the fasting person has completed the fast.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r7.claim: The no-continuous-fast reports imply that one should take something when the sun sets, though even a small amount leaves one free to continue eating.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r8.speaker: ابن عمر
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r8.claim: Ibn Umar reports the Prophet forbidding continuous fasting after a man asked why the Prophet did it while prohibiting it to others.

RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p95/r9.claim: The Prophet explained that he was unlike others and remained with his Lord, who fed and gave him drink; explanations include food from Paradise or confidence of divine provision.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r1.claim: Because the verse has explained fasting, readers might think i'tikaf bans intercourse only by day like fasting; it clarifies that intercourse is forbidden throughout i'tikaf.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r2.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r2.claim: Al-Shafi'i defines i'tikaf linguistically as remaining with anything, good or sinful, and legally as staying in God's house to draw near to Him; legal convention narrows the generic term.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r3.claim: I'tikaf is an ancient religious practice, as shown by the command to purify the House for worshippers and those in retreat.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r4.claim: Touch without desire is allowed during i'tikaf because Aisha used to comb the Prophet's hair while he was in retreat.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r5.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r5.claim: Al-Shafi'i prohibits touching with desire, kissing, and contact short of penetration in i'tikaf; his sounder view is that these acts invalidate it.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r6.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r6.claim: Abu Hanifa says such contact does not invalidate i'tikaf unless ejaculation occurs.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r7.claim: The literal sense of mubashara is skin contact, so the i'tikaf verse prohibits intercourse and other bodily contact.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r8.claim: Intercourse alone was intended in the earlier permission because its context and occasion indicate that meaning; here there are no such clues, so the literal broader sense remains.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96#2/r9.claim: Those denying invalidation analogize to fasting and pilgrimage, which these acts do not invalidate; al-Razi answers that the text overrides analogy.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r1.claim: Some define night by the disappearance of sunlight's effects, requiring either the loss of the red glow or full darkness and visible stars.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r2.claim: Umar's report rejects those delayed definitions of night, which jurists do not follow.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r3.speaker: الحنفية
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r3.claim: Hanafis use the command to complete the fast to argue that prior-night intention and specification are not conditions: fasting is abstention, which has occurred.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r4.speaker: الحنفية
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r4.claim: They invoke the removal of hardship and say that if this reasoning were not limited, it would also validate an obligatory fast begun after noon.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r5.claim: The Hanafis nevertheless invalidate intention after noon, using the principle that a lesser part follows the predominant portion; intention before noon counts.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r6.speaker: الحنفية
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r6.claim: Hanafis say the command to complete the fast applies to every fast, making completion of a voluntary fast obligatory.

RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r7.speaker: الشافعية
RAZI-FULL:v5p96/r7.claim: Shafi'is answer that the verse explains obligatory fasting, so its completion command concerns the obligatory fast alone.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r1.speaker: علي
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r1.claim: Ali is reported to allow i'tikaf only in the Sacred Mosque, interpreting the House named in the verse as the sole valid site.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r10.speaker: المزني
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r10.claim: Al-Muzani argues that if i'tikaf required fasting, it could not be valid in Ramadan: the Ramadan fast is owed for the month, and another concurrent fast is impossible.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r11.speaker: المزني
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r11.claim: Al-Muzani argues that if i'tikaf depended on fasting, it would end each night when fasting ends; it does not, so it can stand alone.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r12.speaker: ابن عمر
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r12.claim: Ibn Umar reports that the Prophet told a man to fulfill his pre-Islamic vow to observe i'tikaf for a night, although fasting at night is impossible.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r2.speaker: عطاء
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r2.claim: Ata permits i'tikaf only in the Sacred Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque, citing the superior prayer reward in those mosques.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r3.speaker: حذيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r3.claim: Hudhayfa permits it in those two mosques and Jerusalem's mosque, citing the report that journeys of religious intent are made to only three mosques.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r4.speaker: الزهري
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r4.claim: Al-Zuhri says i'tikaf is valid only in a congregational mosque.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r5.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r5.claim: Abu Hanifa requires a mosque with a regular imam and muezzin.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r6.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r6.claim: Al-Shafi'i permits i'tikaf in every mosque and prefers a congregational mosque to avoid leaving for Friday prayer; the verse's wording is general.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r7.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r7.claim: Al-Shafi'i permits i'tikaf without fasting but regards fasting alongside it as preferable.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r8.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r8.claim: Abu Hanifa requires fasting for a valid i'tikaf.

RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r9.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p97/r9.claim: Al-Shafi'i reasons that the verse recognizes nonfasting i'tikaf by prohibiting sexual contact for anyone in retreat; without valid i'tikaf, the restriction would not apply.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r1.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r1.claim: Al-Shafi'i sets no minimum duration for i'tikaf: even an hour fulfills a general vow, by analogy with a general vow to give charity.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r2.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r2.claim: Al-Shafi'i recommends a full day to avoid disagreement.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r3.claim: Abu Hanifa disallows i'tikaf shorter than a day, requiring entry before dawn and departure after sunset.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r4.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r4.claim: Al-Shafi'i argues that no particular duration is more warranted than another, so the minimum necessary time should count.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r5.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r5.claim: Abu Hanifa argues that a moment does not establish sustained self-restraint and would not distinguish retreat from simply waiting for prayer.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r6.claim: The phrase God's limits refers to all the rulings discussed from the beginning of the fasting verse onward, not just the single i'tikaf restriction.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r7.speaker: الليث
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r7.claim: Al-Layth defines hadd as a boundary or endpoint; related words describe one barred from provision, a gatekeeper, a property boundary, and iron that restrains.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r8.claim: God's limits are the measures He set, with specified bounds and defined qualities.

RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p98/r9.claim: The phrase do not approach seems to cover both permissions and prohibitions, while another verse says not to exceed the limits.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r1.claim: The strongest explanation is that obedience remains in the realm of truth; one must not cross its boundary and should stay farther away to avoid falling into error.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r2.claim: A Prophetic comparison says every king has protected pasture, God's protected pasture is His prohibitions, and grazing nearby risks trespassing.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r3.claim: Abu Muslim reads do not approach them as do not tamper with the limits, like the warning not to approach an orphan's property.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r4.claim: A contextual reading focuses on nearby prohibitions: intercourse in i'tikaf, food and drink by day, and intercourse outside lawful partners, place, and permitted times.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r5.claim: One reading says God explains other proofs of His religion and law just as He has explained commands and prohibitions here.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r6.claim: Abu Muslim takes signs to mean prescribed duties, as in the sura that names its ordinances and then details adultery's penalties.

RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v5p99/r7.claim: The closing praise may celebrate how a few words set out fasting rules fully and clearly, showing God's mercy in giving such an explanation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r1.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأبو ثور وأصحاب الرأي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r1.claim: Qurtubi says that if forgetful eating leaves a complete fast intact, deliberate intercourse afterward requires make-up and expiation as if there had been no lapse.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r10.claim: The verse names eating, drinking, and intercourse as nighttime permissions but does not mention touching; therefore it alone does not prohibit kissing or touching during a fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r11.claim: Maliki scholars discourage touching for someone unable to control himself, to prevent it leading to a fast-breaking act; Ibn Umar prohibited kissing and touching for this reason.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r2.claim: Qurtubi's scholars argue that the obligatory fast must last a complete day, so forgetful eating leaves make-up due under the command to complete the fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r3.claim: The Bukhari-Muslim wording commands continuing the fast but does not mention make-up, addressing freedom from blame and continuation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r4.claim: Qurtubi endorses the majority view that forgetful eating or drinking does not invalidate the fast and requires no make-up, based on Abu Hurayra's report; al-Daraqutni grades its chain sound and its transmitters reliable.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r5.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r5.claim: Ahmad says no make-up is due for forgetful eating, citing Abu Hurayra, and laughs at the claim that Malik required it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r6.speaker: ابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r6.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reads the Prophet's command to complete the fast as proof it remains entirely valid, with no make-up mentioned.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r7.claim: Qurtubi reasons that deliberate intercourse afterward still requires make-up and expiation, as if the forgetful person had not broken the fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r8.claim: Qurtubi's scholars infer make-up from the requirement of a complete day's fast in 2:187; they suggest the no-make-up hadith may concern voluntary fasting, while Bukhari and Muslim's version orders completion without discussing make-up.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r9.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#10/r9.claim: An explicit report says whoever breaks Ramadan by forgetfulness owes neither make-up nor expiation; al-Daraqutni says only trustworthy Ibn Marzuq transmits it from al-Ansari, resolving the ambiguity.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r1.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r1.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet kissed and touched his wives while fasting, rebutting those who categorically prohibit it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r10.speaker: اللخمي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r10.claim: Al-Lakhmi's principle is that expiation requires intent to break the fast's sanctity; habits and the likelihood of emission distinguish intent or recklessness from an unusual accident.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r11.claim: Qurtubi explains Malik's stricter view by habitual susceptibility and Ashhab's leniency by the common expectation of safety; their view on looking illustrates the distinction.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r2.claim: Ibn Masud and Urwa disliked kissing; a report says Ibn Masud required make-up, but the Prophetic report is evidence against them.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r3.speaker: أبو عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r3.claim: Abu Umar knows no one who permits kissing for someone who expects it to produce a fast-breaking result; ejaculation requires make-up but no expiation according to several jurists.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r4.speaker: أحمد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r4.claim: Ahmad requires make-up if kissing causes preseminal fluid or semen, but expiation only for intercourse with penetration, whether deliberate or forgetful.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r5.speaker: ابن القاسم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r5.claim: Ibn al-Qasim reports Malik requiring make-up after an erection with no emission; Ibn Wahb reports no make-up until preseminal fluid appears, and the school agrees there is no expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r6.speaker: أشهب وسحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r6.claim: Ashhab and Sahnun require no expiation for one kiss or touch causing ejaculation, but require it if repeated; Ibn al-Qasim requires it in all such cases except looking without repetition.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r7.speaker: الحسن البصري وعطاء وابن المبارك وأبو ثور وإسحق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r7.claim: These authorities, and Malik in al-Mudawwana, require expiation for ejaculation caused by kissing, touching, play, or sex without penetration.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r8.speaker: أشهب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r8.claim: Ashhab reasons one kiss is not itself invalidating and does not show intent to spill semen, while repetition indicates intent to violate the fast; repeated looking is analogous.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r9.speaker: اللخمي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#11/r9.claim: Al-Lakhmi says jurists agree that ejaculation caused by looking alone entails no expiation unless the gaze is repeated.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r1.speaker: أبو الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r1.claim: Qurtubi rejects a claimed consensus that one look never incurs expiation: Abu al-Hasan says one lustful look leading to ejaculation requires make-up and expiation, and al-Baji calls that correct.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r10.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r10.claim: Al-Shafi'i says that if a man withdraws from his wife as dawn begins, no make-up is due; al-Muzani disagrees because withdrawal completes intercourse, but Qurtubi favors al-Shafi'i.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r11.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r11.claim: The majority require and validate fasting for a menstruating woman who becomes pure before dawn but delays bathing until after it, whether deliberate or forgetful; Malik and Ibn al-Qasim agree.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r2.speaker: جابر بن زيد والثوري والشافعي وأبو ثور وأصحاب الرأي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r2.claim: These authorities say repeated looking that leads to ejaculation entails neither make-up nor expiation, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r3.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r3.claim: Ibn Nafi reports Malik requiring make-up but not expiation if a man looks at an unclothed woman with desire and ejaculates.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r4.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r4.claim: The majority say a person who enters dawn in major ritual impurity may fast; Ibn al-Arabi calls this settled consensus after earlier disagreement.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r5.claim: Abu Hurayra is reported to have said that one who wakes junub has no valid fast, a position with differing reports about whether he later retracted.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r6.claim: A third view attributed to Abu Hurayra distinguishes knowingly sleeping through dawn while junub from not knowing; Ata, Tawus, and Urwa transmit it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r7.speaker: الحسن والنخعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r7.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i say such a fast counts voluntarily but must be made up if obligatory.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r8.claim: Qurtubi prefers the majority on the strength of Aisha and Umm Salama's reports that the Prophet entered Ramadan dawn junub after intercourse, then bathed and fasted.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#12/r9.claim: The permission for intercourse until dawn necessarily allows dawn to arrive while a person is junub, since ritual bathing can occur afterward.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r1.speaker: عبد الملك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r1.claim: A menstruant who becomes pure before dawn but delays washing until after dawn has no valid fast, since part of the day was spent menstruating; this differs from janābah, which does not invalidate fasting.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r10.speaker: مالك والشافعي والثوري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r10.claim: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and al-Thawrī require no make-up fast after cupping, though they consider it disliked because it may weaken the fasting person.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r11.speaker: أنس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r11.claim: Anas says the Companions did not dislike cupping for a fasting person except because of the resulting weakness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r12.speaker: أبو عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r12.claim: Abū ʿUmar considers the cupping reports abrogated by Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that the Prophet cupped while fasting in iḥrām; the Farewell Pilgrimage was later than the conquest of Mecca, and the Prophet died before another Ramadan.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r13.claim: The command to complete fasting until night is obligatory; because night is the endpoint and belongs to a different kind of time, it is excluded from the fast, unlike a same-kind endpoint included in a purchase boundary.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r2.speaker: الأوزاعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r2.claim: She must make up the fast because she was negligent in performing the ritual wash.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r3.speaker: عبد الملك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r3.claim: Ibn al-Jallab reports a distinction: if there was enough time to wash before dawn, delay does not harm her fast, like a person in janābah; with too little time, the fast is invalid.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r4.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r4.claim: Mālik agrees that when purification occurred too late for a ritual wash, the day is a fast-breaking day, as when dawn arrives while she is menstruating.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r5.speaker: محمد بن مسلمة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r5.claim: Ibn Maslama says she should fast and make up the day, following al-Awzāʿī.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r6.speaker: محمد بن مسلمة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r6.claim: An anomalous report from Ibn Maslama requires both expiation and make-up when she deliberately delays washing until morning.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r7.claim: If a woman became pure at night but cannot tell whether it was before or after dawn, she fasts and makes up the day as a precaution, without expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r8.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r8.claim: Reports from Thawbān, Shaddād ibn Aws, and Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj transmit the Prophet’s statement that both the cupper and the person cupped break the fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r9.speaker: أحمد وإسحق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#13/r9.claim: Aḥmad and Isḥāq hold that cupping breaks the fast; Aḥmad authenticates the Shaddād report, and ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī authenticates the Rāfiʿ report.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r1.claim: Completing the fast requires retaining the intention; the Mudawwana treats a person who cancels it during the day, even without eating or drinking, as having broken the fast and owing make-up.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r10.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r10.claim: Mālik requires expiation and make-up if someone breaks the fast while unsure that sunset has arrived, unless sunset seemed more likely.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r11.speaker: ابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r11.claim: A person uncertain whether dawn has arrived must stop eating; if they eat while uncertain, make-up is due, though Ibn al-Mundhir reports another scholarly position requiring nothing until dawn is certain.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r12.speaker: مجاهد وجابر بن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r12.claim: Mujāhid and Jābir ibn Zayd say no make-up is due for eating while unsure whether dawn has arrived, because eating was still legally permitted on that presumption; al-Kiyā al-Ṭabarī answers that the case parallels eating on a possibly first night of Ramadan, which does require make-up.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r2.speaker: ابن حبيب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r2.claim: Ibn Ḥabīb holds that intention alone does not end the fast; only actually breaking it does.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r3.speaker: سحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r3.claim: Saḥnūn says expiation applies only to someone who formed the intention to break the fast before dawn; a daytime intention does no harm, though make-up is recommended.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r4.claim: The author calls Saḥnūn’s position sound.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r5.claim: Once night is visible, breaking the fast is legally prescribed whether or not one has eaten; sunset itself ends the fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r6.speaker: أبو إسحق الشيرازي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r6.claim: Al-Shīrāzī ruled that a sunset ends an oath not to break fast on either hot or cold food, while Ibn al-Ṣabbāgh said a person must eat something hot or cold; the author prefers al-Shīrāzī by the text and Sunnah.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r7.speaker: أكثر العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r7.claim: Most scholars require make-up when someone breaks the fast thinking the sun has set on a cloudy day and then sees it still above the horizon; Asmāʾ reports this happened in the Prophet’s time.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r8.speaker: عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r8.claim: One report from ʿUmar says no make-up is due after mistakenly breaking the fast before sunset; al-Ḥasan, Isḥāq, and the Ẓāhirīs agree, comparing the person to one who forgot.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#14/r9.claim: The author rejects the no-make-up position because the verse makes night the endpoint of fasting.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r1.claim: The same make-up ruling applies to a captive in enemy territory who ate assuming it was Shaʿbān and then learned it was Ramadan.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r2.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r2.claim: ʿĀʾisha says the phrase setting night as the fast’s endpoint entails forbidding continuous fasting across days.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير وإبراهيم التيمي وأبو الجوزاء وأبو الحسن الدينوري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r3.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, Abū al-Jawzāʾ, and others practiced multi-day continuous fasting; the account depicts its severe physical effects.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r4.claim: The apparent Qurʾānic wording and Sunnah forbid continuous fasting; the Prophet’s sunset report says the fast has ended when night arrives.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r5.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r5.claim: The Prophet forbade continuous fasting; after his Companions refused to stop, he continued with them for a day and another day until the new moon appeared, as a rebuke.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r6.speaker: جمهور العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r6.claim: Most scholars consider continuous fasting disliked because it weakens and exhausts the body; some prohibit it because it contradicts the apparent texts and imitates the People of the Book.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r7.speaker: أحمد وإسحق وابن وهب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r7.claim: Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ibn Wahb say a person choosing continuity may extend a fast only until the pre-dawn meal, not join one day directly to the next.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#15/r8.claim: Those permitting continuous fasting argue that the original prohibition protected new Muslims from overexertion and loss of strength needed for jihad; the Prophet’s exceptional practice was different, and later devout Muslims continued after faith and Muslim strength had grown.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r1.claim: The author says avoiding continuous fasting remains superior even after Islam’s strength and victory, because night is not a legally valid time for fasting and brings no reward as a fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r2.claim: The Prophet did not say that he continuously fasted; Companions inferred this, and he answered that he stayed overnight fed and given drink.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r3.claim: The author takes the Prophet’s statement literally as food and drink from Paradise; figurative spiritual nourishment is possible, but literal meaning stands absent evidence to displace it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r4.claim: When the Companions persisted, the Prophet joined them in his own customary way while they continued in their ordinary manner until weakened, disciplining them out of excessive self-hardship.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r5.claim: Even if “fed and given drink” means spiritual nourishment, the author says it would legally count as breaking the fast, just as backbiting or false testimony does.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r6.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r6.claim: The Prophet says one who does not abandon false speech and acting on it has no need to abandon food and drink; the author uses this to treat such conduct as legally breaking the fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r7.claim: The author concludes that the Prophet neither practiced nor commanded continuous fasting, and that leaving it is preferable.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#16/r8.claim: At iftar, it is recommended to begin with fresh dates, then dates, or sips of water; Anas’s report gives this order, and al-Dāraquṭnī calls its chain sound.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r1.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās gives a supplication to say when breaking the fast, asking God to accept it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r2.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet’s iftar prayer that thirst has gone, the veins are moist, and the reward is established; al-Dāraquṭnī says it is unique through Ḥusayn ibn Wāqid with a fair chain.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r3.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr reports the Prophet’s prayer for a host: may fasting people break their fast with you, the righteous eat your food, and angels pray for you.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r4.speaker: زيد بن خالد الجهني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r4.claim: The Prophet says feeding a fasting person earns the feeder the same reward without reducing the fasting person’s reward.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r5.claim: The Prophet says the fasting person has a supplication at iftar that is not rejected; Ibn Abī Mulayka heard Ibn ʿAmr pray for forgiveness at that time.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r6.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#17/r6.claim: The Prophet says a fasting person has two joys: breaking the fast and meeting the Lord with the reward of fasting.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r1.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r1.claim: Mālik disliked the six Shawwāl fasts to prevent the uninformed from attaching them to Ramadan; the feared practice arose in Khurasan, where people used Ramadan-style pre-dawn routines.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r10.claim: In legal usage iʿtikāf is adherence to a specified act of worship for a specified time, under specified conditions, in a specified place; it is unanimously non-obligatory and a recommended devotional act practiced by the Prophet, Companions, and wives.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r11.claim: A person makes iʿtikāf binding by undertaking it, while entering it is disliked for someone who fears being unable to meet its duties.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r12.claim: Scholars agree that iʿtikāf must occur in a mosque, based on the verse, but differ over which mosques qualify.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r13.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان وسعيد بن المسيب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r13.claim: Ḥudhayfa and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib restrict retreat to mosques built by prophets, namely the Sacred Mosque, the Prophet’s Mosque, and Jerusalem’s mosque.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r14.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r14.claim: ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, along with a group of jurists, require a mosque where Friday congregational prayer is held; this is one reported Mālik position.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r15.speaker: الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r15.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions allow retreat in any mosque with an imam and muezzin, reading the verse generally; this is also one Mālik position and the view of several other jurists.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r2.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r2.claim: Mutarrif reports that Mālik nevertheless fasted the six days privately.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r3.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r3.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī recommends fasting six days of Shawwāl; Abū Yūsuf dislikes it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r4.claim: The verse clarifies that intercourse invalidates iʿtikāf; scholars agree that deliberate vaginal intercourse by someone in retreat invalidates it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r5.speaker: الحسن البصري والزهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r5.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Zuhrī say deliberate intercourse during iʿtikāf incurs the same liability as intercourse during Ramadan.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r6.speaker: عطاء والشافعي وابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r6.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ibn al-Mundhir consider touch without intercourse disliked when intended for pleasure, but not when without desire; ʿĀʾisha’s combing the Prophet’s hair supports the latter permission.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r7.speaker: أبو عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r7.claim: Abū ʿUmar reports consensus that a person in iʿtikāf does not engage in direct intimacy or kissing.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r8.speaker: مالك والشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r8.claim: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī say such intimacy invalidates the retreat; al-Muzanī elsewhere says only intercourse that incurs the legal penalty invalidates it and chooses that view by analogy with their principles for pilgrimage and fasting.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#18/r9.claim: In grammar, “while you are in retreat” is a circumstantial clause; iʿtikāf literally means sticking to something, and cited verse and poetry illustrate remaining or staying.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r1.speaker: مالك وأبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r1.claim: Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa set the minimum retreat at a day and night: a vow for either a night or day includes both.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r2.speaker: سحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r2.claim: Saḥnūn says a vow to observe a night of iʿtikāf entails nothing.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r3.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions say a vow for a day requires only a day, while a vow for a night entails nothing, as Saḥnūn also holds.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r4.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r4.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī requires the vowed duration as stated, sets no upper limit, and allows a moment as the minimum; some Ḥanafī jurists also accept an hour.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r5.speaker: أحمد وداود بن علي وابن علية وابن المنذر وابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r5.claim: A view held in one report from Aḥmad and by Dāwūd, Ibn ʿUlayya, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn al-ʿArabī does not require fasting for iʿtikāf; the Prophet’s Ramadan retreat need not have been attached to a fast undertaken for iʿtikāf.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r6.speaker: مالك وأبو حنيفة وأحمد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r6.claim: Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, and Aḥmad in his other position require fasting for a valid retreat; reports also attribute this requirement to Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and ʿĀʾisha.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r7.speaker: القاسم بن محمد ونافع
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r7.claim: Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and Nāfiʿ say there is no iʿtikāf without fasting, reasoning that the Qurʾān mentions retreat alongside fasting; Mālik says this is the established practice among them.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r8.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#19/r8.claim: In Ibn ʿUmar’s report, ʿUmar asked about fulfilling a pre-Islamic vow to retreat at the Kaʿba for a night or day, and the Prophet told him to retreat and fast.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r1.claim: The word uhilla implies that intercourse had previously been prohibited at night and was then made lawful.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r2.speaker: أبو داود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abi Layla reports from companions that a person who slept before eating after sunset could not eat until morning; Umar and an Ansari encountered the hardship before this verse came.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r3.speaker: البراء بن عازب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r3.claim: Al-Bara says fasting companions who slept before iftar could not eat until the next evening; Qays ibn Sirma worked all day, fainted after missing food, and the verse brought relief.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r4.claim: Al-Bara also says men refrained from wives throughout Ramadan but violated the rule, so the clause about God knowing their self-betrayal was revealed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r5.claim: Ikhtiyan and khiyanah both mean betrayal; a sinner betrays himself by bringing punishment upon himself, though the root originally concerns failure to fulfill a trust.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r6.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r6.claim: Al-Tabari's account says Umar had sex with his sleeping wife after a late visit to the Prophet, and Ka'b ibn Malik did likewise; Umar confessed and asked for a dispensation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r7.claim: Al-Nahhas and Makki give a variant in which Umar slept, then had sex, informed the Prophet, and the self-betrayal clause was revealed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#2/r8.claim: Laylat al-siyam is an adverbial phrase, with laylah singular because it is a generic noun.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r1.speaker: الدارقطني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r1.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī says the report about ʿUmar’s vow is unique through Ibn Budayl from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, whom he considers weak.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r2.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r2.claim: A report attributed to ʿĀʾisha says the Prophet declared there is no iʿtikāf without fasting; al-Dāraquṭnī says its chain is unique through Suwayd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r3.speaker: أصحاب هذا القول
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r3.claim: Those not requiring a dedicated fast say any valid fast—Ramadan, a vow, or another type—suffices, just as a vowed prayer needs no ablution made specifically for it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r4.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r4.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that during retreat the Prophet brought his head near her so she could comb it, and entered the house only to relieve himself; a person must leave retreat only for an unavoidable need.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r5.claim: There is no disagreement that an iʿtikāf participant may leave for necessities such as clear illness or menstruation; promptly returning lets the retreat continue without penalty.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r6.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r6.claim: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfa restrict leaving retreat to the indispensable needs described above.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r7.speaker: سعيد بن جبير والحسن والنخعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r7.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, and al-Nakhaʿī allow visiting the sick and attending funerals; this is also attributed, without a sound chain, to ʿAlī.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r8.speaker: إسحق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r8.claim: Isḥāq distinguishes obligatory from voluntary iʿtikāf: neither sick visits nor funerals are allowed during the obligatory retreat, while conditions for these and Friday prayer may be stipulated for voluntary retreat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r9.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#20/r9.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī permits stipulating in advance that one may leave retreat to visit the sick, attend funerals, or meet other needs.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r1.speaker: أحمد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r1.claim: Two reports from Aḥmad differ over stipulating exits: one forbids it, while another says he hopes there is no harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r2.speaker: الأوزاعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r2.claim: Al-Awzāʿī agrees with Mālik that no exit condition may be stipulated for retreat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r3.speaker: ابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r3.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir says a person leaves retreat only for what is indispensable, the sort of need for which the Prophet himself left.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r4.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r4.claim: One group allows leaving for Friday prayer and returning after it without invalidating iʿtikāf; this was transmitted from Mālik by Ibn al-Jahm and is also Abū Ḥanīfa’s position, favored by Ibn al-ʿArabī and Ibn al-Mundhir.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r5.speaker: عبد الملك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r5.claim: Mālik’s well-known view requires a person vowing ten days to retreat in a congregational mosque, and retreat elsewhere is invalidated by leaving for Friday prayer; ʿAbd al-Malik instead allows leaving and returning without invalidation, which the author prefers because Friday prayer is obligatory and outweighs recommended retreat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r6.speaker: ابن خويز منداد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r6.claim: Ibn Khuwayz Mindād, reporting Mālik’s view, says committing a grave sin invalidates iʿtikāf because grave sin opposes worship and avoiding what God forbids is central to devotion.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r7.speaker: الأوزاعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r7.claim: Al-Awzāʿī follows the apparent report that the Prophet entered retreat after the dawn prayer; al-Thawrī, al-Layth in one view, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others also hold this.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r8.speaker: أبو ثور
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r8.claim: Abū Thawr limits entering after dawn to someone who vowed ten days; for longer retreats, he enters before sunset.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r9.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#21/r9.claim: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa, and their companions begin a vowed month before sunset on the preceding evening because its first night is part of the retreat; Mālik applies this to retreats of a day or more.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r1.claim: The author says ʿĀʾisha’s sound hadith settles the dispute over entry time.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r2.speaker: مالك وأحمد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r2.claim: Mālik and Aḥmad recommend that someone observing the last ten nights remain in the mosque on Eid eve and depart from it for the prayer ground.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r3.speaker: الشافعي والأوزاعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r3.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī and al-Awzāʿī say the retreat ends at sunset when Ramadan ends; Saḥnūn transmits this from Ibn al-Qāsim.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r4.speaker: سحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r4.claim: Saḥnūn says remaining through Eid eve is obligatory and leaving then invalidates the retreat; Ibn al-Mājishūn rejects this, since the month ends at sunset and valid retreats need not continue into Eid eve.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r5.claim: “Those are God’s limits” refers to the commands and prohibitions: limits are barriers preventing what belongs outside from entering, or what belongs inside from leaving; the term also names penalties and the woman who abstains from adornment during mourning.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#22/r6.claim: As God explains these limits, He explains all rulings so people may avoid transgressing them; signs guide to truth, while the apparent universal “so that they may” applies particularly to those God guides.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi take rafath as a euphemism for intercourse; al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari say it broadly covers what a man desires from his wife, while Ibn Arfa specifies intercourse.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r2.claim: Rafath can also mean explicit speech about intercourse or obscene speech; cited poetry uses the term in those senses.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r3.claim: The preposition ila after rafath is unusual; it is carried by analogy with ifda', meaning intimate contact, as in 4:21 and comparable constructions.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r4.claim: Qur'anic words can inherit a neighboring word's syntax through shared meaning: rahim is used with bi in the sense of ra'uf, and the poet says hamaltu bihi in the sense of conceived.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#3/r5.claim: The clause wives are clothing is a subject and predicate; nun is doubled because hunna parallels the plural marker in masculine forms.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r1.claim: Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di's poem illustrates the clothing image through spouses' intimate bodily closeness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r2.claim: Another explanation is that each spouse covers and protects the other from what is unlawful, or conceals their intimacy from people's eyes.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r3.speaker: أبو عبيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r3.claim: Abu Ubayd says a wife can be called one's clothing, bedding, or waist-wrap; in Umar's cited poem, izar means wife, though another view says self.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r4.speaker: الربيع
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r4.claim: Al-Rabi says wives are beds and husbands are covers; Mujahid explains that spouses are a source of tranquility for one another.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r5.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r5.claim: Mujahid glosses the clothing metaphor as mutual tranquility, with each spouse settling with the other.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r6.claim: Takhununa anfusakum can mean that some people assisted one another in prohibited sex or eating after sleep, like you kill yourselves can mean some kill others.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r7.claim: Alternatively, each person betrays himself because the harm of the betrayal returns to him.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r8.claim: Taaba alaykum may mean accepting repentance or easing the rule, as in 73:20; the word can also designate a concession in 4:92 and 9:117.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#4/r9.claim: Afa ankum may mean pardon for sin or expanded ease; a prophetic saying calls the end of the prayer time God's pardon, meaning facilitation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r1.claim: Qurtubi takes God's knowing as knowledge of their actual conduct, taaba as easing the rule afterward, and afa as making matters easy.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r10.speaker: الحسن البصري والحسن بن قرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r10.claim: They read the word as wattabi'u, follow; Ibn Abbas allowed this reading, but Qurtubi prefers ibtaghu, seek.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r11.claim: The command to eat and drink answers Qays's hardship, while the earlier command to approach wives answers Umar; Qurtubi begins with Umar's more important case.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r2.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r2.claim: Ibn al-Arabi remarks that Umar's self-betrayal became a law and a relief for the community, reflecting the honor of divine care.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r3.claim: Bashiruhunna is a euphemism for intercourse, now permitted; it is called direct contact because the two skins touch.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r4.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r4.claim: Ibn al-Arabi argues Umar's intercourse, rather than Qays's hunger, occasioned the verse: if Qays were central it would begin by permitting food.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r5.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والحكم بن عيينة وعكرمة والحسن والسدي والربيع والضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r5.claim: These authorities interpret what God prescribed as offspring, inferred from its placement after the permission for intercourse.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets what God prescribed as the Qur'an; al-Zajjaj says to seek the Qur'an's permissions and commands.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r7.speaker: ابن عباس ومعاذ بن جبل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r7.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas and Muadh interprets the phrase as seeking the Night of Decree.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r8.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r8.claim: Qatada interprets it as seeking God's dispensation and expanded ease; Ibn Atiyya calls this a good interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#5/r9.claim: A further view says the phrase means seeking what God has allotted of wives and slave women.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r1.claim: The Prophet's report presents true dawn as the horizontal light spreading across the horizon, setting the endpoint for eating.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r10.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r10.claim: Al-Tabari explains the later-dawn view by defining day as sunrise to sunset, but Qurtubi says the Prophet's night-darkness/day-whiteness explanation and 2:184 decide the issue.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r2.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r2.claim: The majority identify dawn with whiteness spreading horizontally across the horizon, as the reports and common practice establish.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r3.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r3.claim: The Prophet warned not to be deceived by Bilal's call or the false vertical whiteness; the true dawn spreads horizontally.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r4.claim: A report from Ibn Masud contrasts false dawn as a vertical gesture with true dawn indicated by fingers spread horizontally.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r5.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r5.claim: A mursal report distinguishes two dawns: a wolf-tail-like vertical light neither permits nor forbids, while horizontal dawn permits prayer and forbids food.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r6.claim: Another group says fasting begins only once dawn is visible in roads and homes; this is reported from Umar, Hudhayfa, Ibn Abbas, Talq, Ata, al-A'mash, and others.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r7.speaker: مسروق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r7.claim: Masruq says the early Muslims counted dawn only once its light filled houses.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r8.speaker: حذيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r8.claim: Hudhayfa says he ate suhur with the Prophet when it was effectively daytime though the sun had not risen.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r9.speaker: الدّارقطني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#6/r9.claim: A report from Talq ibn Ali says one may eat until the red dawn appears; al-Daraqutni calls Qays ibn Talq weak, and Abu Dawud says only Yamama transmit it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي بكر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r1.claim: A raised report from Hafsa says fasting is invalid without resolving to fast before dawn; Ibn Abi Bakr is described as trustworthy and of elevated transmission, while another version is Hafsa's own statement.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r2.claim: The two intention reports support the majority's dawn cutoff and require intention before dawn, contrary to Abu Hanifa; fasting is worship and requires intention, so post-dawn eating cannot be permitted.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r3.speaker: سهل بن سعد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r3.claim: Sahl says min al-fajr was added after people tied white and black threads and continued eating until they could distinguish them; they then understood the reference as daylight.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r4.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r4.claim: Adi ibn Hatim took the white and black threads literally; the Prophet joked about his broad nape and explained that they mean night-darkness and day-whiteness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r5.claim: The dawn is called a thread because its spreading whiteness appears extended; khayt can denote color, and fajr comes from a root meaning to break open or flow out.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r6.claim: Fajr names the first visible, spreading whiteness of morning from the sun's rising point, which Arabs called the white thread.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r7.speaker: أبو دواد الإيادي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r7.claim: Abu Dawad al-Iyadi's poem calls dawn's first light a bright thread, illustrating khayt.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r8.speaker: بشر بن أبي خازم أو عمرو بن معد يكرب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#7/r8.claim: A verse attributed uncertainly to Bishr ibn Abi Khazim or Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib calls dawn a split, another name for its appearance.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r1.speaker: الشماخ
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r1.claim: Al-Shammakh likens dawn splitting the night to a parted head; other poetry uses phrases for the clarity and first signs of morning.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r2.claim: A poem speaks of arriving before dawn's break while the morning star remains hidden, illustrating inbilaq al-fajr.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r3.claim: Night is the time for eating, drinking, and sex, while day is for fasting; outside a traveler or sick person, daytime allows none of these.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r4.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r4.claim: Malik says anyone who deliberately breaks Ramadan by eating, drinking, or intercourse owes both a make-up fast and expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r5.speaker: الشعبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r5.claim: Al-Sha'bi agrees with Malik that deliberate breaking by food, drink, or sex incurs expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r6.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#8/r6.claim: Al-Shafi'i and others restrict expiation to intercourse, relying on Abu Hurayra's report that explicitly describes sex with one's wife during Ramadan.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r1.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r1.claim: Malik, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Mundhir, and reports from Ata, al-Hasan, and al-Zuhri impose expiation for any deliberate fast-breaking because one report states it without restriction.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r10.speaker: أهل الظاهر وابن الماجشون وأحمد بن حنبل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r10.claim: They require make-up and expiation even for forgetful intercourse, reasoning the expiation report does not distinguish forgetfulness from intention; Ibn al-Mundhir says nothing is due.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r2.claim: Qurtubi rejects the claim that broad and intercourse-specific reports describe one event; their different wording indicates two distinct cases.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r3.claim: By al-Shafi'i's own principle, not asking for details despite differing circumstances should imply a general ruling; al-Shafi'i also imposes discretionary punishment for violating Ramadan's sanctity.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r4.speaker: مالك وأبو يوسف وأصحاب الرأي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r4.claim: These authorities require the wife who had sex with her husband in Ramadan to owe the same expiation as him.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r5.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r5.claim: Al-Shafi'i requires only one expiation, whether the wife consented or was coerced, because the Prophet answered with one and did not distinguish.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r6.speaker: أبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r6.claim: A report from Abu Hanifa says both owe expiation if she consented, but only the husband if he coerced her; Suhnun holds the same.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r7.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r7.claim: Malik says the husband owes two expiations, which a group of his followers regard as the settled doctrine.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r8.speaker: الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه وإسحق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r8.claim: They say a person who forgetfully has intercourse or eats while fasting owes neither make-up nor expiation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r9.speaker: مالك والليث والأوزاعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187#9/r9.claim: They require make-up but no expiation for forgetful intercourse or eating; Ata is also reported to hold this, though another report from him requires expiation for sex.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:187/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187/r6.speaker: السدي وأبو العالية والربيع
QURTUBI-FULL:2:187/r6.claim: Another view says earlier Christians, and early Muslims, could not eat, drink, or have sex after sleeping at night; 2:187 later abrogated that restriction.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r1.claim: The thread imagery becomes a representational comparison; min may instead be partitive because what first appears is only part of dawn.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r10.claim: The wording 'do not approach them' is stronger than the earlier 'do not transgress them'; the limits may also mean God's prohibitions.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r2.claim: A report says people used actual black and white threads to decide when to stop eating; if sound, it occurred before Ramadan or clarification was delayed until needed, or the clarification came after confusion arose.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r3.claim: Allowing intercourse until dawn shows that the ritual bath may be delayed until after dawn and the fast is valid for someone who enters dawn in a state of major ritual impurity.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r4.claim: Fasting ends at night, so continuous fasting through the night is forbidden.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r5.claim: I'tikaf means remaining in a mosque for worship; intercourse is forbidden during it and invalidates it because a prohibition in worship entails invalidity.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r6.claim: A man in retreat would leave the mosque, have intercourse with his wife, and return; the verse forbade this.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r7.claim: The verse establishes that i'tikaf is in a mosque without restricting it to any particular mosque.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r8.claim: God's limits are the rulings just stated; one must not even approach the boundary between right and wrong, lest one cross it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r9.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187#2/r9.claim: A prophetic parable says every king has a protected preserve, and whoever grazes near God's preserve may enter it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r10.claim: Calling the former conduct betrayal intensifies the charge; rafath is also read as rafuth.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r11.claim: The clothing metaphor explains permission: spouses have little patience for separation and closely envelop one another, like garments.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r12.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r12.speaker: الجعدي
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r12.claim: A line by al-Ja'di compares an embracing woman to clothing wrapped around her companion.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r13.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r13.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r13.claim: Another explanation of the clothing metaphor is that each spouse conceals the other's state and keeps the other from sexual wrongdoing.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r14.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r14.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r14.claim: People wrong themselves by exposing themselves to punishment and losing a share of reward; ikhtiyan is more intensive than khiyanah, like iktisab versus kasb.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r15.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r15.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r15.claim: God accepted their repentance and erased the trace of their former breach; permission to approach wives follows the repeal of the prohibition.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r16.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r16.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r16.claim: The permission supplies evidence that Qur'an can abrogate a Sunnah ruling; direct contact is a euphemism for intercourse.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r17.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r17.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r17.claim: What God ordained may mean offspring, making procreation the proper aim of sex; other views take it as a prohibition of coitus interruptus, avoidance of the proper place, or as the lawful place itself.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r18.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r18.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r18.claim: Dawn is pictured as a white thread appearing across the horizon against the remaining darkness; mentioning dawn with the white thread suffices to identify the black one.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r7.speaker: عمر
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r7.claim: After the evening prayer, Umar had intercourse and regretted it; other men admitted doing likewise, and the verse then permitted intimacy during fasting nights.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r8.claim: Before this ruling, Muslims could eat, drink, and have intercourse after sunset only until the late evening prayer or sleep.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:186-187/r9.claim: The night of fasting is the night that ends with a day of fasting; rafath is a euphemism for intercourse, and ila conveys the sense of sexual access.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r1.claim: Before the concession, after evening prayer or sleep a fasting man could no longer eat, drink, or have intercourse until the next night.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r2.speaker: عمر
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r2.claim: After intercourse with his wife following the late prayer, Umar wept, reproached himself, and told the Prophet; the concession was revealed.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r3.claim: رفث means intercourse; إلى takes the verb because it includes the sense of ifḍāʾ, and the euphemism reflects disapproval of what occurred before permission.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r4.claim: The spouses are garments because they embrace and envelop each other; alternatively, each protects the other from the forbidden.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r5.claim: The garment image explains the concession: intimate contact makes abstinence difficult, so intercourse was permitted at night.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r6.claim: They wronged themselves through intercourse, losing a share of good; ikhtiyān intensifies khiyāna, as iktisāb intensifies kasb.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r7.claim: God accepted their repentance when they repented of the prohibited act and pardoned what they had done before the concession.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p91#3/r8.claim: Now directly means have intercourse during fasting nights; mubāshara is named for the spouses' skin touching.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r1.claim: ما كتب الله لكم means seek the offspring assigned and recorded by God through intercourse, rather than satisfying desire alone; alternatively seek the lawful partner, not the forbidden.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r2.claim: The white thread is the first horizontal dawn light; the black thread is the stretched darkness of night.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r3.claim: Min of dawn identifies the white thread as dawn, implicitly clarifying the black one too; it may mean part of dawn, its beginning.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r4.claim: Adding min of dawn turns the metaphor into an explicit, eloquent comparison, as saying 'a lion of so-and-so' makes the intended comparison clear.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r5.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r5.claim: He put a white and black cord under his pillow and could not distinguish them; the Prophet explained that the phrase means daylight and night darkness.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r6.claim: The verse supports daytime intention for Ramadan fasting, delaying ritual washing until dawn, forbidding continuous fasting, requiring expiation for eating or drinking, and not invalidating fasting through major ritual impurity.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r7.claim: Intercourse is lawful on Ramadan nights only for someone not in retreat; the circumstantial clause also shows retreat is only in a mosque, with no mosque-specific restriction.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p92/r8.claim: The stated limits are God's defined rulings; do not approach them through violation or alteration, so that people may avoid prohibitions.

QASHANI:2:186-187/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:186-187/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:186-187/r3.claim: The fasting night is heedlessness within spiritual restraint; intimacy with wives signifies descending to the soul's necessary claims, which seekers illicitly took during disciplined travel before pardon.

QASHANI:2:186-187/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:186-187/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:186-187/r4.claim: After annihilation, at steadfast subsistence, the seeker may meet the soul's claims during heedlessness and use them to strengthen piety and fulfill God's commands.

QASHANI:2:186-187/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:186-187/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:186-187/r5.claim: Eating and drinking mean keeping company with the soul's gentleness until flashes of presence overcome heedlessness; then maintain presence until heedlessness returns, since livelihood requires it.

QASHANI:2:186-187/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:186-187/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:186-187/r6.claim: Do not approach the soul's claims while dwelling in the heart's mosques in presence, because they would disturb the seeker's spiritual time.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r5.speaker: العجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r5.claim: Al-ʿAjjaj's verse uses رفث for indecent speech.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r6.speaker: ابن عباس والزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Zajjaj, and others take رفث as a comprehensive term for what a man desires with a woman; Ibn Abbas's verse and his reply place this usage in sexual relations, including during pilgrimage discussion.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p174/r7.claim: A separate interpretation restricts رفث to intercourse and cites a poet describing women as avoiding men's sexual advances.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r3.speaker: البراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r3.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that after Ramadan fasting was prescribed, men who had wronged themselves through nighttime eating or intercourse prompted this verse; some had been allowed those acts only until sleeping or the night prayer.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r4.claim: Another account says ʿUmar, Kaʿb al-Anṣārī, and others had intercourse after the night prayer, while Qays b. Ṣirma slept before eating, fasted, and fainted; the verse then descended.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r5.speaker: بعض العلماء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r5.claim: Some scholars say a single lapse occasioned the verse, which became a concession for all Muslims until the end of time.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r6.claim: The passage completes the rules for circumstances faced by a fasting person and eases the earlier comparison with prior communities, whose fast forbade food, drink, and intercourse after sleep or night prayer.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p210/r7.claim: Permitting these acts from the start of night until dawn was kindness to Muslims and fulfills the preceding promise that God wills ease, not hardship.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r1.claim: The verb “was made lawful” implies prior prohibition, though intercourse and food had still been lawful early in the night before sleeping or the night prayer.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r2.speaker: author
