ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r2.claim: The majority read uḥilla passively with its agent omitted; an active reading makes God the understood agent or shifts from first to third person.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r3.claim: Laylat is grammatically an adverb but semantically gives the time of rafath; its syntactic governor is implicit because a verbal noun cannot front its complement under the stricter analysis.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r4.claim: The genitive “night of fasting” is licensed by loose association: fasting is intended at night and becomes actual during part of the night-to-day cycle.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r5.speaker: عبد الله
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r5.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads rafath as rafūth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r6.claim: Rafath euphemistically means intercourse; the word can name explicit sexual speech, and its shameful closeness to a vulgar term rebukes those who violated the earlier ban.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p211/r7.claim: The preposition ilā is used because rafath is construed with the sense of ifḍāʾ, intimate access; this yields a discreet Qurʾānic euphemism.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r1.claim: Al-nisāʾ is explained either as the plural of niswah or as a non-pattern plural of imraʾah, and is annexed to the addressees to mark wives or owned women as exclusive partners.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r2.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says a woman is a man’s clothing, bedding, and waist-wrap because of the closeness and intermingling between them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r3.speaker: الربيع
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r3.claim: Al-Rabīʿ glosses the spouses as each other’s quilt.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r4.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r4.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī read the spouses as mutual comfort and repose.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r5.claim: The clothing sentence is independent explanatory prose, showing why intercourse was permitted: spouses cannot endure separation because they intermingle like garments.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r6.claim: The verse mentions women as clothing first because it portrays men’s greater need and lesser patience, and the man as usually initiating intimacy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r7.claim: He identifies three rhetorical devices: semantic antithesis in making lawful what was previously forbidden, euphemism in rafath, and a striking clothing metaphor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r8.claim: Libās is singular because it functions like a verbal noun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p212/r9.claim: The syntax of ʿalima annakum varies by whether ʿalima is construed like “know” or in its original two-object construction; takhtānū is iftiʿāl with the sense of khānū.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r1.claim: Ikhtiyān may intensify betrayal: intercourse or eating after sleeping violated the rule and harmed the offenders’ own prospects for good.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r2.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r2.claim: Other glosses say they selfishly reserved forbidden pleasures for themselves, or took care of themselves by approaching their wives; takhawwana can mean to care for, with n replacing the more usual l.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r3.claim: Abū Muslim reads the phrase as failing to give the self its due, explaining why it says “yourselves” rather than “God.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r4.claim: He takes the betrayal as an actual past lapse, indicated by kāna and sound transmission; the hypothetical reading is weak because it lacks support and conflicts with “He turned toward you.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r5.claim: “He turned toward you” means He accepted their repentance after the forbidden acts; some instead understand it as easing the rule and granting permission.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r6.claim: “He pardoned you” means He forgave the sins and will not punish them; one report says repentance erases sin and pardon erases its trace, so the paired verbs intensify one sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r7.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p213/r7.claim: Another gloss takes pardon as leaving the prohibition behind or making the matter easy, as when something is said to be waived.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r1.claim: A Prophetic saying urges marriage and procreation, since the Prophet will take pride in the community’s numbers on Judgment Day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r10.claim: He prefers a reinforcing sense: pursue what God permits, namely intercourse throughout the Ramadan night; al-Aʿmash’s irregular “wa-atū” reading supports it but conflicts with the codex consonantal text.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r11.claim: Eating and drinking are also permission commands, reopening the three activities that had been forbidden during part of the fasting night until dawn appears.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r12.claim: The text links permission for intercourse to ʿUmar and others, and permission to eat to Qays b. Ṣirma or another report in the occasion of revelation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r2.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r2.claim: A second interpretation is to seek the lawful site of intercourse rather than a prohibited one.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r3.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r3.claim: Qatāda and Ibn Zayd say it means seeking the permission and concession granted after the restriction was lifted.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r4.speaker: معاذ بن جبل، ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r4.claim: A fourth view, attributed to Muʿādh and also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, reads it as seeking Laylat al-Qadr; al-Zamakhsharī calls this close to an eccentric interpretation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r5.claim: A fifth view from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zajjāj identifies what God prescribed as the Qurʾān and its commands; a variant reading wa-ttabiʿū supports it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r6.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r6.claim: Another view means the permitted conditions and times for intercourse, excluding menstruation, postpartum bleeding, waiting period, and apostasy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r7.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r7.claim: Another interpretation identifies the referent as wives and female slaves.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r8.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r8.claim: The phrase has also been read as a prohibition of coitus interruptus with free wives.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214#2/r9.claim: Kataba may mean made, decreed, or recorded in the Preserved Tablet or Qurʾān.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r1.claim: Al-ān means “at this time, this night”; bashirūhunna is a permission command because it follows a prohibition and consensus confirms its permissive sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r2.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r2.claim: The majority take mubāsharah as intercourse; another view includes intercourse and lesser bodily contact, from the idea of skin-to-skin contact.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r3.claim: Even if mubāsharah here means intercourse, its permission necessarily includes lesser acts.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r4.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة والحسن والضحاك والربيع والسدي والحكم بن عتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p214/r4.claim: Their first interpretation of “seek what God prescribed” is offspring decreed for the spouses; intercourse serves procreation, the purpose of marriage, not pleasure alone.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r1.claim: Sahl b. Saʿd reports that some Companions took the white and black threads literally, tying one of each to a foot until the clarification “of dawn” came.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r10.claim: This is the majority practice through the generations and accords with reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Samura b. Jundub.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r2.claim: A report says a Ramadan year passed between the initial wording and the words “of dawn.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says most jurists and theologians who reject delaying clarification until the time of need would not accept the report; those allowing delay say it still conveyed the duty to obey pending clarification.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says this is abrogation, not delayed clarification: Companions acted on the literal threads until “of dawn” replaced that reading with a figurative comparison.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r5.claim: The white thread is the light spreading horizontally at true dawn and the black thread is the remaining darkness; without “of dawn” the expression would be metaphor, while the added phrase marks a simile.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r6.claim: When ʿAdī b. Ḥātim misunderstood the comparison as literal threads, the Prophet laughed and said his pillow or nape must be broad, an idiom for dullness.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r7.claim: The poet’s “broad nape” line illustrates the idiom that a broad nape signals poor understanding; Arabs call anything fine, long, and threadlike a thread.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r8.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r8.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the phrase refers to two dawns: a dark horizontal false dawn and a bright dawn that fills the horizon.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p215/r9.claim: He identifies the white thread as true, spreading dawn rather than false dawn’s vertical light; dawn first appears fine, then spreads, and fasting begins with its first appearance.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r1.speaker: عثمان وحذيفة وابن عباس وطلق بن علي وعطاء والأعمش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r1.claim: They hold that fasting begins only once dawn can be distinguished on roads or mountaintops.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r2.speaker: علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r2.claim: ʿAlī reportedly prayed dawn with the people and then said the white thread had now become distinct from the black one.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r3.claim: Because the endpoint is discernibility rather than the first instant of dawn, one who eats or has intercourse while genuinely unsure and later learns dawn had begun owes no make-up fast.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās ate after two observers disagreed about whether dawn had appeared and ruled that he owed no make-up fast.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r5.speaker: الثوري وعبيد الله بن الحسن والشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r5.claim: Al-Thawrī, ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Ḥasan, and al-Shāfiʿī agree that eating amid doubt about dawn requires no make-up; Mālik requires it, and the two positions are reported from Abū Ḥanīfa.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r6.claim: Since intercourse remains lawful until dawn is discerned, ritual bathing may be delayed until after dawn; this refutes Abū Hurayra’s view, while al-Ḥasan invalidates the fast of one still in major impurity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r7.speaker: عائشة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r7.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet would enter dawn in major impurity after intercourse while fasting.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r8.claim: Where moonlight, clouds, or location prevent observing the horizon, one must act cautiously and refrain until certain dawn has entered.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r9.speaker: أبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p216/r9.claim: Abū Muslim says only intercourse, eating, and drinking break the fast; vomiting, enemas, and other cases remain permitted because the text names only those three.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r1.speaker: الفقهاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r1.claim: The jurists say the verse names eating, drinking, and intercourse because people desire them; vomiting and enemas are disliked and nasal medication is rare.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r2.claim: The first min marks a starting point; the second is partitive because the white thread is the first portion of dawn, though both prepositions can govern the same verb with distinct senses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r3.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r3.claim: On al-Zajjāj’s two-dawn reading, the second min may be partitive of both threads because fajr denotes a genus containing two dawns.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r4.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r4.claim: Another parsing makes min al-fajr a circumstantial or explanatory phrase for the white thread, whose clarification suffices to clarify the black thread too.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r5.claim: He explains omission of a matching “from night” after black thread as avoiding awkward repetition and because the black-thread phrase is secondary.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p217/r6.claim: The fast’s obligation was stated earlier; this verse adds its endpoint, night, which is outside the daytime category, though confirming day’s end entails entry into a portion of night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the People of the Book fasted from one evening meal to the next, and Muslims were ordered to differ by breaking fast at sunset.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r10.claim: Sexual intercourse that intentionally breaks the fast entails make-up by consensus; eating or drinking entails make-up for al-Shāfiʿī and make-up plus expiation for other jurists.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r11.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r11.claim: The majority treat forgetful intercourse like deliberate intercourse, though al-Shāfiʿī’s expiation ruling differs; forgetful eating or drinking leaves the fast intact for Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, while Mālik requires make-up.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r12.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r12.claim: One who merely resolves to stop fasting without acting remains fasting without make-up according to the majority; Ibn Ḥabīb and the Mudawwana’s report from Mālik require make-up.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r2.claim: Completing the fast is obligatory because fasting itself is obligatory; the earlier commands to intercourse, eating, and drinking merely permit what was allowed in principle.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r3.speaker: الراغب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r3.claim: Al-Rāghib claims the verse proves daytime intention, allowing ritual bathing to be delayed until dawn, and rejecting continuous fasting.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says daytime intention does not follow: the text commands completing an already begun fast, and its indication of delayed bathing comes from the prior discussion instead.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r5.claim: The endpoint at night does not by itself refute voluntary continuation; the Prophetic prohibition of wisāl is read by some as forbidden and by others as disliked.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r6.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير وإبراهيم التيمي وأبو الحوراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r6.claim: These early Muslims are reported to have practiced continuous fasting; Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ibn Wahb allowed it until dawn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r7.speaker: الجمهور وأبو حنيفة والشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r7.claim: If someone mistakenly breaks the fast thinking sunset has occurred and then sees the sun, the majority, Abū Ḥanīfa, and al-Shāfiʿī require make-up but no expiation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r8.speaker: إسحاق وأهل الظاهر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r8.claim: Isḥāq and the literalists say there is no make-up in that case, analogizing it to forgetfulness; this is also reported from ʿUmar.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r9.speaker: مالك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p218/r9.claim: Mālik requires both make-up and expiation when a person breaks the fast while uncertain about sunset; another reported position requires make-up alone by analogy with doubt at dawn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r1.claim: The wording apparently commands completion only of a fast already begun; although the Sunna separately requires a healthy person who began the day without fasting to abstain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r10.claim: If mubāsharah here included mere touching, intercourse would be prohibited a fortiori because it contains touching and more; the touching at issue is understood with desire.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r11.claim: In law, iʿtikāf means restraining oneself in a place for worship and nearness to God, and is an ancient religious practice.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r2.speaker: الحنفية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r2.claim: The Ḥanafīs include voluntary fasting under the general command to complete the fast; the Shāfiʿīs restrict it to obligatory fasting because the passage explains its rules.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r3.speaker: بعض أرباب الحقائق
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r3.claim: A mystical allegory divides Ramadan between God’s due, completing the fast until night, and human needs, eating and drinking until dawn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r4.claim: When intercourse was permitted at night, some retreatants left the mosque to have sex and returned after bathing; the verse forbids it during retreat both inside and outside the mosque.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r5.speaker: فرقة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r5.claim: One group limits the prohibited mubāsharah in retreat to intercourse, following the occasion of revelation and immediate context; the majority include pleasurable contact.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r6.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r6.claim: There is consensus that the prohibition is categorical and intercourse invalidates retreat; schools differ on whether lustful looking, touch, or kissing also invalidates it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r7.speaker: مالك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r7.claim: Mālik says lustful looking, touching, or kissing invalidates retreat; Abū Ḥanīfa conditions invalidation on ejaculation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r8.speaker: المزني عن الشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r8.claim: Al-Muzanī transmits from al-Shāfiʿī that such an act invalidates retreat if it would produce a comparable legal consequence with an unrelated woman.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r9.speaker: عائشة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p219/r9.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that she combed the Prophet’s head while he was in retreat in the mosque; scholars infer that nonlustful touch is allowed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r1.claim: Qatāda reads ʿākifūn without the alif, and the clause is a circumstantial phrase meaning “do not approach them while in this state.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r10.speaker: عبد الله وعائشة وإبراهيم وابن جبير وعروة وأبو جعفر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r10.claim: They restrict retreat to a mosque where congregational prayer is held; this is another opinion of Mālik.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r2.claim: Retreat is permissible and not obligatory by consensus; the Prophet practiced it, making it a Sunna, though this verse does not specify its recommendation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r3.speaker: علي وابن عمر وابن عباس وعائشة وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه ومالك والثوري والحسن بن صالح
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r3.claim: These authorities require fasting as a condition of retreat; a report from ʿĀʾisha calls fasting a Sunna of the retreatant.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r4.speaker: سعيد وإبراهيم وطاووس عن ابن عباس والشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r4.claim: These authorities say fasting is not a condition for retreat.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r5.speaker: الشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r5.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says any duration that counts as remaining in place qualifies as retreat; Mālik’s well-known minimum is ten days, with a report of one day and night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r6.speaker: الشافعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r6.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī allows retreat by night, day, or either alone, including a vow for only one night or one day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r7.speaker: سحنون وأبو حنيفة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r7.claim: Sahnūn says a vow of one night is not binding; Abū Ḥanīfa says a vow of days includes their nights.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r8.claim: The phrase “in the mosques” does not establish that a mosque is a condition of retreat: a restriction on intercourse during a state does not define where that state may occur.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r9.speaker: أبو قلابة وابن عيينة والشافعي وداود الطبري وابن المنذر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p220/r9.claim: They say retreat may take place in any mosque, a view also attributed to one opinion of Mālik.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r1.speaker: عبد الله وحذيفة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r1.claim: Some say retreat is valid only in one of the three holy mosques; another group limits it to a prophet’s mosque, a position Ibn al-Musayyab holds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r10.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya understands the limits as the boundaries between permissibility and prohibition.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r11.claim: Ascribing the limits to God emphasizes that they must not be confused; the phrase is neither indefinite nor marked by the definite article.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r12.claim: Forbidding people to approach a limit is stronger than merely forbidding transgression, fitting a passage focused on prohibitions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r2.speaker: الحارث عن علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r2.claim: Al-Ḥārith transmits from ʿAlī that retreat is only valid in the Sacred Mosque or the Prophet’s Mosque.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r3.claim: The verse expressly addresses men but is silent about women; Abū Ḥanīfa confines a woman to her home mosque, Mālik requires a congregational mosque, and al-Shāfiʿī permits any location.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r4.speaker: مجاهد والأعمش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r4.claim: Mujāhid and al-Aʿmash read “in the mosque” in the singular; al-Aʿmash means the Sacred Mosque, while the author takes the word generically and favors the plural reading.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r5.speaker: بعض الصوفية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r5.claim: Some Ṣūfīs say that the place of nearness is sacred and protected from the pursuit of bodily desires.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r6.claim: The demonstrative plus plural predicate cannot refer only to the single retreat prohibition; “God’s limits” encompasses the whole fasting passage, whose commands also entail prohibitions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r7.speaker: السدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r7.claim: Al-Suddī glosses God’s limits as His conditions or rules.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r8.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r8.claim: Shahr b. Ḥawshab glosses the limits as God’s obligations.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r9.speaker: الضحاك والزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p221/r9.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Zamakhsharī take the limits as sins, sacred prohibitions, or bans.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r1.claim: The Prophet compares God’s prohibitions to a king’s protected pasture: one who grazes near the boundary may soon enter it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r2.claim: The choice of “do not approach” suits a prohibition: elsewhere “do not transgress” follows divorce rules, while “transgress His limits” follows inheritance and family-law allocations, so each wording fits its context.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r3.claim: Abū Muslim reads “do not approach them” as forbidding alteration of the limits, by analogy with the ban on approaching an orphan’s property except in the best manner.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r4.claim: “In this way God makes His signs clear” means that, with brief eloquent wording, He explains fasting laws and other revealed legislation so people may be mindful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r5.speaker: أبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r5.claim: Abū Muslim takes God’s signs to mean the obligations He has explained, so people may obey what He revealed; this requires treating the kāf as extra.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r6.claim: He objects that Abū Muslim’s reading works only if the kāf is redundant; if it marks comparison, there must be both a comparator and a compared object.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r7.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya restricts “for people” to those whom God enables to receive guidance, citing verses about God’s leading astray.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p222/r8.claim: He sees no need for that restriction: God clarifies the signs to all people, but clear presentation does not mean everyone actually understands them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r2.claim: The Prophet urged opposition to Jews when encouraging the pre-dawn meal.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p224/r3.claim: When Companions isolated menstruating women in imitation of Jewish practice, he told them to do everything except intercourse; Jews then complained that he opposed all their customs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228#2/r1.claim: The prohibitions are God’s boundaries; forbidding even approaching them intensifies the command to keep distant, and clear signs and legal proofs are explained in hope of piety.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r6.claim: After requiring faith as the foundation of sound worship, God permits marital intercourse on fasting nights because spouses are garments for one another; He pardons past violations, commands intimacy and eating and drinking until dawn, requires fasting until night, and forbids intercourse during mosque retreat.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r1.claim: A view takes rafath as sexual intercourse itself, supported by two poetic examples; the author says these do not prove it because they may refer to preliminaries such as caressing or kissing.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r2.claim: While in consecration, Ibn ʿAbbās recited a flirtatious verse about women and asked whether the birds' omen proved it; when told he had committed rafath, he answered that rafath is only with women.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r3.claim: Kuntum takhtānūna is the predicate of inna, and takhtānūna is the predicate of kāna.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r4.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ reads kāna as past in both form and meaning, describing actual past lapses followed by repentance; the author objects to his alternative future reading expressed through narrative kāna.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r5.claim: Takhtānūna is from iftiʿāl of khiyānah, whose root has wāw, as shown by khāna/yakhūnu and khūn/khiyānah; zuhayr uses khānah in a line about a mount's back.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats ikhtiyān like iktisāb: the added form conveys greater intensity than the base khiyānah, consistent with added form suggesting added meaning.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r7.claim: A further gloss takes takhtānūna anfusakum as looking after or attending to yourselves through intercourse; takhawwanahu and takhawwalahu both mean to tend, with nūn substituted for the more common lām.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#2/r8.claim: If ʿalima means 'knew' and takes one object, anna and its clause fill it; if it takes two, the clause fills both for Sībawayh but only one for al-Akhfash, with the other omitted.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r1.claim: Hun(n)a libāsun lakum is an independent explanatory statement rather than a syntactically governed clause; putting it first highlights men's need for women and their initiating the relationship.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r2.claim: The garment metaphor means close intimacy; al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī's poem describes a lover embracing a woman until she becomes like clothing to him.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r3.claim: Al-ān ordinarily means the present, though it can denote nearby past or future; Abū al-Baqāʾ takes it here as the formerly prohibited time, now near enough to count as present.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r4.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means 'now We have permitted you intimacy'; the imperative implies an omitted perfect verb and al-ān keeps its ordinary present sense.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r5.claim: A reading wa-ittabiʿū is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, Muʿāwiyah b. Qurrah, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī; they gloss 'what God prescribed' as Laylat al-Qadr and following its reward.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#3/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the Laylat al-Qadr interpretation close to an innovation in exegesis.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r1.claim: Ḥattā marks the endpoint of eating and drinking; min al-khayṭ is an ablative of starting point governed by yatabayyana, understood as distinguishing the white thread from the black.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r2.claim: Min al-fajr may be partitive and attach to yatabayyana, or be a circumstantial phrase from al-abyaḍ with min explaining the kind; treating it as a specification is rejected.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r3.claim: The verse omits 'from the night' after the black thread because that is understood from the white thread; dawn alone anchors the legal rules on intimacy, food, and drink.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r4.claim: The image compares daylight to a white thread and night to a black one. It is an unusually forceful simile, called a kind of metaphor because the comparison term is folded into the image, though the phrase 'from dawn' makes the referent explicit.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r5.claim: When ʿAdī b. Ḥātim understood the threads literally, the Prophet replied that his pillow must be broad (another report says his nape was broad); another Companion reportedly made the same mistake.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r6.claim: A report says the clarification 'from dawn' came a full year after 'the white thread' and 'the black thread'; some Companions had meanwhile taken the image literally.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#4/r7.claim: The author explains why the expression is ultimately a simile rather than an unmarked metaphor: a metaphor needs contextual evidence, whereas the explicit dawn phrase supplies the comparison and some Companions read literally before it was added.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r1.claim: Fajr is the verbal noun of fajara/yafjuru, meaning to split or break open.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r2.claim: Ilā al-layl either marks the endpoint of completing the fast or is a circumstantial phrase; because night is outside the day, ilā does not include it.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r3.claim: Wa-antum ʿākifūn is circumstantial of the subject of 'do not approach'; the prohibition applies while one has undertaken mosque retreat, while intercourse in a mosque is forbidden even without retreat.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r4.claim: ʿUkūf is staying and remaining; the verb has both yaʿkufu and yaʿkifu forms, illustrated by readings of Q 7:138 and poetry by al-Farazdaq and al-Ṭirimmāḥ.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r5.claim: The source says iftiʿāl is used for the good and inﬁʿāl for the bad; legal iʿtikāf is a defined form of residence with conditions, analogous to the legal reality of prayer.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r6.speaker: قتادة
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r6.claim: Qatādah reads ʿakifūn, paralleling the forms ʿākif/ʿakif and bār/ barr.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r7.speaker: الأعمش
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#5/r7.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads 'in the mosque' in the singular, apparently intending the generic institution.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r1.claim: Tilka ḥudūd Allāh cannot refer only to the single intercourse prohibition; it encompasses the whole fasting passage's commands and prohibitions, with the plural limits reflecting their combined force.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r2.claim: Because a commanded act cannot be what 'do not approach them' prohibits, the plural limits include implied prohibitions generated by the preceding commands as well as the explicit final prohibition.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r3.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ supplies an omitted warning before the fāʾ; the author rejects treating fāʾ as extra, since that would require the following phrase to be accusative by the more idiomatic interlocking construction, contrary to the unanimous raised reading.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r4.claim: Ḥudūd means prevention and a boundary's endpoint; ḥaddād is a gatekeeper because he prevents passage, and a valid definition both excludes outsiders and includes what belongs within.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r5.claim: A ban on approaching is stronger than a ban on touching or mixing with the prohibited matter.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#6/r6.claim: This passage says 'do not approach' because an explicit prohibition immediately precedes it; Q 2:229 and 4:14 say 'do not transgress' after legal rulings, where crossing the prescribed limit is apt.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187#7/r1.claim: The kāf in kadhālika is accusative either as an adjective or circumstantial modifier of an omitted verbal noun meaning 'a clarification like this'; the latter reflects Sībawayh's view.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r1.claim: Laylata al-ṣiyām is an accusative adverb; its governor may be aḥilla (the common parsing, rejected because permission already existed), an implied verb from rafath, or rafath itself under an expansive view of adverbs.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r2.claim: The preferred repair is an implied verb, 'that you engage in rafath'; rafath itself cannot govern the preceding temporal phrase because a complement of a relative clause cannot precede its relative, so the poet's duplicated verbal noun illustrates the ellipsis.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r3.claim: A third analysis attaches the night phrase to rafath based on grammarians who allow temporal expansion with adverbs and prepositional phrases.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r4.claim: The iḍāfa of the night to fasting is licensed by loose association: the required intention is present at night, though fasting itself does not occur then.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r5.claim: Most read uḥilla passively, with God understood as agent; the active reading either omits 'God' or shifts to God's first-person voice, continuing the shift in lakum from third-person imperatives.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r6.claim: Rafath is followed by ilā because it is construed with the sense of ifḍāʾ, intimate approach: permission is for approaching wives through rafath.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r7.speaker: عبد الله
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r7.claim: ʿAbd Allāh's reading is al-rafūth rather than al-rafath.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r8.claim: Rafath lexically means indecent speech: it is the verbal noun of rafiṯa, while arfatha means to engage in such speech; al-ʿAjjāj provides a poetic usage.

SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r9.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:2:187/r9.claim: Al-Zajjāj, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, calls rafath a comprehensive expression for everything a man desires from a woman.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r1.claim: A report describes the earlier rule: people could eat, drink, and have sex until sleep; an Anṣārī named Ṣirma worked while fasting, slept without food after ʿIshāʾ, and woke fasting and exhausted; ʿUmar had intercourse after sleeping, and the verse then came down.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r2.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p499/r2.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that ʿĀshūrāʾ had been fasted, then after Ramadan fasting became obligatory, people could choose to fast it or break the fast; Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd report the same.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r1.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r1.claim: Al-Barāʾ says that during Ramadan people initially avoided women all month and some wronged themselves, prompting the phrase that God knew they had been betraying themselves and then pardoned them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that after ʿIshāʾ Muslims initially abstained from food and women until the next night; after some, including ʿUmar, broke the rule, they complained and the verse permitted intimacy.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r3.claim: In another report, before the fasting rule was changed people ate and had sex until sleep; ʿUmar had intercourse after sleeping, confessed to the Prophet, and the verse was revealed.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r4.claim: Abū Hurayra's report says ʿUmar had intercourse after ʿIshāʾ, while Ṣirma slept after sunset without a full meal and later ate after waking; the incident occasioned the verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r5.claim: In these reports, al-rafath means intercourse, and spouses are described as each other's covering while they had eaten, drunk, and had sex after ʿIshāʾ.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r6.claim: Abū Hurayra’s account concludes that the verse was revealed in response to companions’ infractions of the former night-time fasting restrictions.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510#2/r7.claim: Eating and drinking remain lawful until dawn becomes distinct, after which the fast is completed until night; this is God's pardon and mercy.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r1.claim: This verse relaxes the early rule, under which eating, drinking, and intercourse after breaking the fast stopped at ʿIshāʾ or sleep, whichever came first, a source of hardship.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، عطاء، مجاهد، سعيد بن جبير، طاوس، سالم بن عبد الله، عمرو بن دينار، الحسن، قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r2.claim: These authorities explain al-rafath here as sexual intercourse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r3.speaker: الزهري، الضحاك، إبراهيم النخعي، السدي، عطاء الخراساني، مقاتل بن حيان
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r3.claim: These authorities likewise interpret al-rafath as intercourse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r4.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، سعيد بن جبير، الحسن، قتادة، السدي، مقاتل بن حيان
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r4.claim: They explain spouses being garments for one another as each being a source of comfort and repose for the other.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r5.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r5.claim: Al-Rabīʿ gives a related metaphor: each spouse is the other's covering or blanket.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r6.claim: Because spouses mingle, touch, and lie together, allowing intercourse on Ramadan nights removes hardship and embarrassment.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r7.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r7.claim: An anonymous poetic line depicts the woman as her partner's garment when he embraces her, illustrating the metaphor.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r8.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p510/r8.claim: Al-Barāʾ recounts that Qays ibn Ṣirma worked in his field while fasting, fell asleep before eating, and collapsed the next day; after the Prophet was told, the verse was revealed and people rejoiced.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r1.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r1.claim: ʿUmar said that when he sought his wife after she had gone to sleep, she said she was asleep; he assumed she was making an excuse, had intercourse, and the verse was revealed concerning him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r2.claim: A report from Kaʿb ibn Mālik describes ʿUmar and Kaʿb having intercourse after sleep under the former rule; ʿUmar told the Prophet, and the verse followed. Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Qatāda also link it to ʿUmar, others like him, and Ṣirma.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p511/r3.claim: The ruling then allowed intercourse, food, and drink throughout the night as mercy, concession, and kindness.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r1.claim: Food, drink, and intercourse are permitted throughout the night until dawn; the white thread is daylight and the black thread is night, with “from dawn” removing ambiguity.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r2.speaker: سهل بن سعد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r2.claim: Sahl reports that some tied white and black strings to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them; the added words “from dawn” clarified that night and day were intended.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r3.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r3.claim: ʿAdī placed a black and a white cord under his pillow and could not distinguish them; the Prophet explained that the image meant night darkness and day whiteness, not literal cords.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512#2/r4.claim: The Prophet's remark that ʿAdī's pillow was broad refers to the cords spanning a width as broad as the east and west; another Bukhārī wording makes the explanation explicit.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة، ابن عباس، أنس، شريح القاضي، مجاهد، عكرمة، سعيد بن جبير، عطاء، الربيع بن أنس، السدي، زيد بن أسلم، الحكم بن عتبة، مقاتل بن حيان، الحسن البصري، الضحاك، قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r1.claim: These authorities interpret seeking what God has ordained as seeking offspring.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd instead interprets the phrase as referring to intercourse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the phrase refers to Laylat al-Qadr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r4.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r4.claim: Qatāda offers two broad readings: seek the concession God prescribed, or what God made lawful.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r5.claim: Asked whether to read wa-ibtaghū or wa-ittabiʿū, Ibn ʿAbbās allowed either but favored the first reading.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r6.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p512/r6.claim: Ibn Jarīr prefers the verse's wording to be understood broadly, encompassing all the reported interpretations.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r1.claim: Some took “your nape is broad” to mean dullness, but Ibn Kathīr calls that weak; it instead relates to the broad pillow and nape.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r2.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r2.claim: Asked whether the white and black threads were actual cords, the Prophet told ʿAdī that the intended contrast was night darkness and daylight.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r3.claim: Because the verse permits eating until dawn, taking the lawful concession makes the pre-dawn meal recommended; accepting concessions is beloved.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r4.speaker: أنس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r4.claim: The Prophet urged people to eat suḥūr, saying that it contains blessing.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r5.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r5.claim: The Prophet said the pre-dawn meal distinguishes the Muslim fast from the fast of the People of the Book.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r6.speaker: أبو سعيد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r6.claim: A report says suḥūr is blessed and should not be neglected, even if one only takes a sip of water; God and His angels bless those who eat it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r7.speaker: أنس، زيد بن ثابت
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p513/r7.claim: Anas and Zayd say they ate suḥūr with the Prophet, then went to prayer; the interval was about the time needed to recite fifty verses, showing it was delayed toward dawn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r1.speaker: أبو ذر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r1.claim: The Prophet said the community would remain in good condition while people hastened to break the fast and delayed suḥūr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r2.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r2.claim: Ḥudhayfa reports eating suḥūr with the Prophet when it seemed to be day though the sun had not risen; because ʿĀṣim alone transmitted it, Ibn Kathīr reads it as near dawn and cites 65:2's use of reaching a term for approaching it. Many early authorities allowed suḥūr close to dawn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r3.speaker: بعضهم، ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r3.claim: Ibn Jarīr reports an opinion that abstention begins only at sunrise; Ibn Kathīr rejects it as contrary to the verse's explicit dawn cutoff and says no scholar can firmly hold it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r4.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p514/r4.claim: The Prophet said not to let Bilāl's night call prevent suḥūr; eat until Ibn Umm Maktūm calls, since he waits until dawn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r1.speaker: طلق بن علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r1.claim: The Prophet described the true dawn as a horizontal red light across the horizon, not a vertical brightness rising upward.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r2.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r2.claim: Samura reports that neither Bilāl's call nor the vertically elongated dawn ends suḥūr; the relevant dawn spreads across the horizon.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r3.speaker: محمد بن عبد الرحمن بن ثوبان
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p515/r3.claim: A good mursal report distinguishes a harmless vertical dawn like a wolf's tail from the horizontal dawn that permits prayer and forbids food.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، عطاء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r1.claim: They distinguish two dawns: a vertical glow does not prohibit drink, begin prayer, or make pilgrimage time expire; only light spreading across mountain tops does so. Ibn Kathīr calls their chain sound and says other early authorities reported likewise.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r2.speaker: جمهور العلماء، الأئمة الأربعة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r2.claim: Because dawn ends the permission for intercourse, food, and drink, someone who wakes in a state of major ritual impurity may wash and complete the fast; the four imams and majority rely on reports that the Prophet did so.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p516/r3.claim: A report says that if dawn prayer is called while someone is sexually impure, he should not fast; Ibn Kathīr notes its good chain and transmissions in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r1.speaker: ابن حزم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r1.claim: Ibn Ḥazm says the report forbidding a fast after waking sexually impure was abrogated by this verse; Ibn Kathīr calls that remote because chronology is absent and apparently points the other way.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r2.claim: The closest and most comprehensive reconciliation reads “he has no fast” as denying its perfection, not its validity, preserving the permission established by ʿĀʾisha's and Umm Salama's reports.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r3.claim: The Prophet explained that a fast is considered ended when night advances from one side and day withdraws from the other, establishing sunset as the breaking point.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r4.speaker: سهل بن سعد الساعدي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r4.claim: The Prophet said people remain in good condition so long as they hasten to break the fast.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r5.claim: A divine report says God's most beloved servants are those who hasten to break their fast; al-Tirmidhī grades this report ḥasan gharīb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r6.speaker: ليلى امرأة بشير بن الخصاصية
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p517/r6.claim: When Laylā wanted to fast two days continuously, Bishr cited the Prophet's ban on continuous fasting and his instruction to finish at night and then break the fast; an Ibn ʿAsākir report adds that the Prophet's own continuous fast was a special exception and cites this verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r1.claim: The Prophet forbade joining one day's fast to the next without a break; when companions continued, he fasted with them for two days and nights, then said he could have extended it longer. The report is in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r2.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r2.claim: ʿĀʾisha says the Prophet forbade continuous fasting out of mercy for his followers, explaining that God fed and gave him drink.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r3.claim: Continuous fasting was a special prophetic capacity; Ibn Kathīr says the apparent feeding and drinking were spiritual rather than physical, citing a poem about memory distracting a lover from food and drink.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r4.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p518/r4.claim: The Prophet allowed anyone wishing to continue fasting to extend only until suḥūr, while explaining his own special capacity; another report invites a fasting woman to follow the Prophet's family's suḥūr-to-suḥūr practice.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says anyone in iʿtikāf in a mosque, in Ramadan or otherwise, is forbidden from sexual relations with women by night or day until the retreat ends.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r2.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says a person formerly could leave the mosque during retreat and have intercourse; the verse now forbids approaching wives while one remains in iʿtikāf, inside or outside the mosque. Mujāhid, Qatāda, and others agree that this practice preceded the verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود، محمد بن كعب، مجاهد، عطاء، الحسن، قتادة، الضحاك، السدي، الربيع بن أنس، مقاتل
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r3.claim: These early authorities agree that an iʿtikāf participant may not have intercourse with his wife during the retreat.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r4.claim: During iʿtikāf one may leave only as long as necessary for bodily needs; one may not kiss, embrace, occupy oneself with other matters, or visit the sick, though one may ask while passing.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r5.claim: Iʿtikāf has detailed rules, some agreed upon and others disputed, which Ibn Kathīr treated in the final part of his fasting book.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r6.claim: The Qur'an's placement of iʿtikāf after fasting points to retreat during fasting or in Ramadan's final part; the Prophet observed the last ten days yearly until death, and his wives continued afterward.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519#2/r7.claim: During iʿtikāf, Ṣafiyya visited the Prophet at night; he escorted her home, explained her identity to two Anṣārī men, and said Satan moves through Adam's bloodstream and he feared an evil thought might enter their hearts.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r1.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r1.claim: ʿAlī reports that the Prophet would continue fasting from one suḥūr to the next.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير، سلف آخرون
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r2.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr and other early Muslims continued for several days; Ibn Kathīr says they likely did so as self-discipline or understood the prohibition as compassionate guidance, not worship, because they had strength. Ibn al-Zubayr reportedly reached seven days.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r3.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p519/r3.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says fasting is prescribed during the day, while at night a person may eat or choose not to eat.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520#2/r1.claim: As God details fasting here, He clarifies other rulings through Muhammad so people can find guidance and obey; Ibn Kathīr links this to the verse about bringing people from darkness to light.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r1.speaker: الشافعي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r1.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says the Prophet clarified himself to prevent suspicion in a place where suspicion might arise, protecting the two men from falling into error; they were too pious to think ill of him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r2.claim: Direct marital contact forbidden during iʿtikāf includes intercourse and its preliminaries, such as kissing and embracing, but ordinary handling is permitted.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r3.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r3.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet let her comb his hair while she menstruated and entered the house only for a human need; she passed by a sick person to inquire about him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r4.claim: “God's limits” are the fasting rules, prohibitions, permissions, endpoints, concessions, and obligations He defined; “do not approach them” means do not exceed them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r5.speaker: الضحاك، مقاتل
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil specifically interpret God's limits here as the prohibition on sexual contact during iʿtikāf; Ibn Zayd instead refers to four limits spanning night intercourse through completing the fast at night.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r6.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p520/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd calls these four boundaries the sequence from night intimacy through completing the fast at night, as his elders taught him.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r1.claim: After recognizing God's nearness and recalling the sweetness of addressing Him, the fasting believers longed for ease; the verse answers their implied request concerning intimacy and eating at night.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r2.claim: Nighttime intercourse is permitted for the whole fasting night; rafath means sexual speech or intercourse, and the phrase 'to your wives' excludes other men's wives. The clothing metaphor either describes intimacy or spouses' mutual need.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r3.speaker: البراء
BIQAI-FULL:v1p350/r3.claim: Al-Bara reports that during Ramadan people initially avoided intercourse with their wives throughout the month, then some betrayed themselves before the permission was revealed.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r1.claim: A fasting man who slept before eating could not eat until the next night; Sirma b. Qays slept, fainted before midday, and the verse was revealed.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r2.claim: Al-Harali says God pardoned violations caused by human disposition, then eased the law to fit this community's nature; reports of one Emigrant and one Ansari show the mercy reached both groups.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r3.speaker: عائشة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r3.claim: Aisha told the Prophet that his Lord hastened to satisfy his desire, illustrating the special easing granted to the community through him.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r4.claim: The Prophet told Ali to ask God to make truth turn with him; the author also says wise leaders adapt commands to people's dispositions, like directing the brave to fight and restraining the coward.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r5.speaker: النبي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p351/r5.claim: The Prophet considered forbidding ghila, then refrained after learning that Persians and Romans practiced it without harm to their children; law should account for different human natures.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r1.claim: Forgiveness erases the trace of wrongdoing and hints that purification such as expiation might otherwise have been due; Ramadan fasting elevates the community beyond earlier separated days and nights.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r2.claim: Nighttime intercourse becomes obedience to God's command rather than mere appetite; 'what God prescribed' may mean offspring or a lawful place for sex, and some scholars favored marriage for the fasting person at night.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r3.speaker: النبي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r3.claim: The Prophet would break his fast with fresh dates, then dates, and if neither was available, sips of water; the author sees the order as following human appetite and need.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r4.claim: Making dawn's appearance the endpoint of permitted food and sex requires watching for dawn and supports intending the fast before it; intercourse continuing to dawn shows that ritual bathing may wait until daytime.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p352/r5.claim: The form yatabayyana suggests that the observer must exert effort to discern dawn; 'for you' indicates that legal judgments follow what is outwardly accessible and within human capacity.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r1.claim: The black thread is explained as the darkness at the end of night, likened to a black line beside the white dawn thread.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r2.claim: Al-Harali says 'from dawn' clarifies the metaphor by identifying its referent as a simile; Adi b. Hatim had misunderstood the image literally, so the added explanation prevents ambiguity.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r3.claim: The author says the verse was not left ambiguous or unexplained until the time of need, since the Prophet did not blame Adi for his misunderstanding; mentioning dawn instead of night is eloquent reliance on what is understood.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r4.claim: In his legal theory, al-Harali allows an initially general or ambiguous address whose binding clarification comes later; it still benefits gradual revelation and recitation, although the author elsewhere denies ambiguity here.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r5.claim: Al-Harali finds an Arabic rhetorical pattern in the third phrase returning semantically to the first while joining grammatically to the second, preserving the omitted night through implication.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r6.claim: Completing the fast until night makes abstention obligatory after dawn and signals the temporal gap between the permitted night and fasting day; some scholars inferred that i'tikaf begins before sunset.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r7.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p354/r7.claim: Al-Harali says daytime is for work and interaction, while night is rest and a time of divine manifestation; night eating is like being fed by God and does not negate the fast's spiritual reality.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r1.claim: Intercourse is forbidden throughout i'tikaf wherever the worshipper is; specifying mosques either honors the setting or, preferably, defines ritual i'tikaf as devotional confinement there. Combining i'tikaf and fasting strengthens the prohibition.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r2.claim: Al-Harali defines complete fasting as restraint from ordinary transactions, desires, and retaliation, with speech and conduct guarded; its inward reality matters more than abstaining from food alone.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p355/r3.claim: The author cites reports that Ramadan plus six days of Shawwal, or three days each month, equals fasting a lifetime; some Companions could say they were fasting in divine favor while eating as God's guests.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r1.claim: The demonstrative magnifies the divinely ordered rulings; calling them boundaries evokes barriers that prevent one thing entering another, and the pronoun restates their full meaning.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r2.claim: The command not to approach suits fasting and scrupulous restraint: it bars doubtful matters and the preliminaries to intercourse, since one who grazes near a protected boundary may cross it.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r3.claim: God explains His signs to all people, with complete power and knowledge, so understanding does not fundamentally differ between the less and more intelligent; the hope of piety hints that some will not attain it.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p357/r4.claim: The verse first permits intercourse because desire for it is strong and its month-long prohibition caused greater hardship, then permits eating as bodily sustenance before again forbidding intercourse in certain circumstances.

DURR-FULL:v1p427/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p427/r4.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v1p427/r4.claim: At first people could eat, drink, and have sex until sleeping; after sleep they abstained until the next night. The report says the verse followed Sirmah’s exhaustion and Umar’s intercourse after sleep.

DURR-FULL:v1p430/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r1.claim: The earlier rule prohibited food after sleep before eating and prohibited sex for the rest of that night; this verse granted a concession.

DURR-FULL:v1p430/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r2.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r2.claim: ʿĀshūrāʾ had been fasted; once Ramadan was revealed, fasting it became optional.

DURR-FULL:v1p430/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p430/r3.claim: The earlier restriction applied to the People of the Book and Muhammad’s companions; this verse abrogated the ban on food, drink, and sex after sleeping or the night prayer.

DURR-FULL:v1p474/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r5.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r5.claim: Previously, a fasting person who slept before breaking the fast could not eat that night or the next day. The verse allowing night intimacy was revealed after Sirmah slept without food and fainted from exhaustion.

DURR-FULL:v1p474/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r6.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r6.claim: When Ramadan fasting was first prescribed, men abstained from sex the entire month; some violated this, prompting the statement that they had betrayed themselves.

DURR-FULL:v1p474/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r7.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v1p474/r7.claim: A report with a sound chain says Umar and Kaʿb had intercourse after their wives slept under the old rule, and the verse was revealed about their self-betrayal.

DURR-FULL:v1p476/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r1.claim: Before this verse, eating, drinking, and sex were forbidden after the night prayer; after Umar and Sirmah reported their cases, the verse permitted night intimacy and food until dawn. In this report, rafath means intercourse, and what God wrote means offspring.

DURR-FULL:v1p476/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r2.claim: Muslims who had eaten the night prayer meal and then abstained until the next night complained after some violated the rule, and the verse permitted intercourse.

DURR-FULL:v1p476/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p476/r3.claim: A report has Umar confess that he had intercourse after sleeping; after the Prophet initially said he did not deserve a concession, revelation pardoned the act and allowed sex, eating, and drinking until dawn.

DURR-FULL:v1p477/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r1.speaker: ثابت
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r1.claim: Thābit reports that Umar had intercourse with his wife one Ramadan night, regretted it, and this verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v1p477/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r2.claim: Under the earlier rule, food, drink, and sex were forbidden after the night prayer; after a man violated it, God made this verse a concession and ease.

DURR-FULL:v1p477/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the instruction to eat and drink was revealed concerning Abū Qays ibn Ṣirmah of the Khazraj.

DURR-FULL:v1p477/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r4.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r4.claim: An account says Sirmah slept before eating and could not eat until the next night; Umar also admitted having sex after his wife slept, and the verse portions addressed each incident.

DURR-FULL:v1p477/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p477/r5.claim: Qatādah says an earlier fast involved three days per month and two daily prayers; when a faster slept, food and sex were prohibited until the next night, and some violated the rule.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r1.speaker: عثمان بن مظعون
