DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r1.claim: In the continuation of the report, the Prophet explains that spouses see one another unclothed; ʿUthmān remains reluctant, and the Prophet calls him modest and discreet.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r10.speaker: أم سلمة
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r10.claim: Umm Salamah likewise says the Prophet sometimes awoke ritually impure after intercourse, not a wet dream, and still fasted.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r2.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r2.claim: Takhūnū means that they had intercourse with their wives in breach of the rule.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses fa-l-āna bāshirūhunna as have intercourse with them.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says mubāshara means intercourse, but God uses a euphemism; Mujahid says the term means intercourse everywhere in the Qur’an.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r5.claim: One interpretation of seeking what God has written is seeking offspring, also reported from Mujahid, Qatādah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r6.claim: Another interpretation of what God has written is the Night of Decree; Anas also gives this interpretation.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r7.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r7.claim: Qatādah interprets the phrase as seeking the concession God has prescribed.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r8.claim: Asked whether the phrase is read wa-ibtaghū or wa-ittabiʿū, Ibn Abbas allows either but recommends the first reading.

DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r9.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p478#2/r9.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports that the Prophet could reach dawn in Ramadan in a state of major ritual impurity after intimacy, then bathe and fast.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r1.claim: Qatādah says people who ate or had sex after sleeping were described as betraying themselves, and the verse addressed that breach.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r2.claim: Mujahid says people could eat, drink, and have sex after sunset until sleeping; this verse pardoned them and permitted it throughout the night.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r3.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r3.claim: Early Muslims followed the People of the Book: after sleeping, they could not eat until the next day; this verse removed that rule.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r4.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r4.claim: The Prophet said the pre-dawn meal distinguishes Muslim fasting from the fasting of the People of the Book.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r5.claim: Al-rafath means sexual intercourse; the same meaning is transmitted from Ibn Umar.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas groups several terms for touching and intimacy as intercourse; in fasting rafath means intercourse, while in pilgrimage it means inciting desire.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r7.claim: The spouses being garments for one another means each is a source of repose for the other; Ibn Abbas cites Nabighah’s verse as Arabic usage for garment.

DURR-FULL:v1p478/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r8.speaker: سعد بن مسعود الكندي
DURR-FULL:v1p478/r8.claim: When ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn was ashamed to be seen naked by his wife, the Prophet said God had made each spouse a garment for the other and acknowledged his modesty.

DURR-FULL:v1p480/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r1.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r1.claim: When a man asked whether he could fast after waking ritually impure, the Prophet said he did so himself, urged by his own God-consciousness and knowledge of what to avoid.

DURR-FULL:v1p480/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r2.claim: The white thread is the brightness of day and the black thread the darkness of night; Ibn Abbas cites Umayya’s poetry to support the imagery.

DURR-FULL:v1p480/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r3.speaker: سهل بن سعد
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r3.claim: The first wording lacked min al-fajr, leading some to use literal black and white strings; its addition clarified that the intended contrast is night and day.

DURR-FULL:v1p480/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r4.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
DURR-FULL:v1p480/r4.claim: ʿAdī took the two threads literally, but the Prophet explained that the image means the whiteness of day against the darkness of night.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r1.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r1.claim: ʿAdī recounts tying literal white and black threads and asking about the verse; the Prophet clarified that dawn’s light emerges from the night’s darkness.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r2.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r2.claim: The Prophet again corrected the literal reading of the threads, defining them as night’s blackness and day’s whiteness.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r3.speaker: جابر الجعدي
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r3.claim: Jābir al-Juʿfī explains the white and black threads as day and night.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r4.claim: When asked when to stop the pre-dawn meal, Ibn Abbas said to keep eating when uncertain until dawn becomes clear.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r5.speaker: أبو الضحى
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r5.claim: People used to understand the relevant dawn as the light spreading across the sky.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas distinguishes two dawns: the vertical light in the sky changes no legal rule, whereas the dawn clearly appearing along mountain tops ends permission to drink.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r7.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r7.claim: The Prophet said neither Bilal’s call nor the vertically rising false dawn should stop the pre-dawn meal; only dawn spreading across the horizon does.

DURR-FULL:v1p481/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r8.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p481/r8.claim: Bilal called before dawn, so the Prophet said to continue eating until Ibn Umm Maktum called after dawn appeared.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r1.speaker: إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r1.claim: Ibrahim reports a saying that lying breaks a faster’s fast.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r10.claim: Intercourse invalidates a retreat, which must then be restarted.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r11.speaker: إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r11.claim: Ibrahim says a retreatant who has intercourse should restart the retreat, seek forgiveness, repent, and increase good works.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r12.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r12.claim: Mujahid says a retreatant who has intercourse should give two dinars in charity.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r13.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r13.claim: Al-Hasan treats intercourse during retreat like intercourse during Ramadan, apparently requiring the corresponding expiation.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r14.speaker: الزهري
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r14.claim: Al-Zuhrī says a retreatant who has sex owes the same expiation as one who has sex during Ramadan.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r2.speaker: أبو بكرة
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r2.claim: A prophetic report discourages claiming to have fasted and prayed all Ramadan; the narrator is unsure whether the reason is self-praise or that some sleep is inevitable.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r3.claim: In the prohibition on intimacy during retreat, direct contact can mean touching or intercourse, expressed euphemistically.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r4.claim: The prohibition applies to a man in retreat in Ramadan or outside it: he may not have sex at night or by day until completing the retreat.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r5.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says some people used to have sex while in retreat until the verse prohibited it.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r6.claim: Qatādah says a person who left the mosque during retreat could have intercourse, and the verse ended that practice.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r7.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r7.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says God forbade people who had been having sex with their wives during retreat.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says some retreatants used to have sex when leaving to relieve themselves, then bathe and return; they were forbidden to do so.

DURR-FULL:v1p484/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r9.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p484/r9.claim: Mujahid says sex in mosques was forbidden, where the Anṣār had practiced it.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r1.speaker: إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r1.claim: Ibrahim says a retreatant should not kiss or touch his spouse.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r2.claim: Mujahid says a retreatant should neither sell nor buy.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r3.speaker: الزهري
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r3.claim: A report attributed by some to ʿUrwa, but judged by al-Dāraquṭnī to be al-Zuhrī’s insertion, says the Prophet kept the last ten days of Ramadan in retreat and his wives did so after him; it lists retreat practices and requires a congregational mosque.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r4.claim: A weak prophetic report says retreat restrains a person from sins and earns the reward of all good deeds.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r5.claim: A report says helping a brother with a need is better than ten years of retreat and that a day of retreat for God’s sake creates three barriers from Hell; al-Hākim authenticated it while al-Bayhaqī weakened it.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r6.speaker: علي بن حسين
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r6.claim: A weak report from ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn, from his father, says ten days of Ramadan retreat equal two pilgrimages and two minor pilgrimages.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r7.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says each day of retreat counts as a pilgrimage; al-Bayhaqī notes he must have received this by report.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r8.speaker: زياد بن السكن
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r8.claim: Zubayd al-Yāmī and others retreated on Nowruz and Mihragān, contrasting the pagans’ observance with their own faith and asking forgiveness.

DURR-FULL:v1p485/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r9.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
DURR-FULL:v1p485/r9.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī compares the retreatant to a person in consecration who casts himself before the Merciful and pleads for mercy.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r1.speaker: الحسن بن علي
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r1.claim: Al-Hasan ibn Ali says walking with someone to meet a need is better than a month of retreat.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r10.claim: A prophetic report, authenticated by al-Ḥākim, says a retreatant need not fast unless he obligates himself to do so.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r11.speaker: علي
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r11.claim: ʿAlī says a retreatant may visit the sick, attend funerals and Friday prayer, and visit his family without sitting with them.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r2.claim: A very weak report says walking with a Muslim brother to fulfill a need is better than a month in the Prophet’s mosque and earns steadfastness on Judgment Day.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r3.speaker: محمد بن واسع الأزدي
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r3.claim: Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ attributes to the Prophet the statement that helping a brother for one day is better than a month of retreat.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r4.speaker: حذيفة
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r4.claim: Ḥudhayfa reports that retreat is valid in any mosque with a caller to prayer and an imam.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r5.speaker: المسيب
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r5.claim: Al-Musayyib says retreat is only valid in a mosque.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r6.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r6.claim: A report from ʿĀʾishah says retreat requires fasting.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r7.speaker: القاسم بن محمد ونافع مولى ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r7.claim: Al-Qāsim and Nāfiʿ say retreat requires fasting because the Qur’an mentions retreat alongside the fasting rules.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says a retreatant must fast; similar positions are attributed to ʿAlī and ʿĀʾishah.

DURR-FULL:v1p486/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r9.speaker: علي وابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v1p486/r9.claim: A different report from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd says fasting is not required unless the retreatant stipulates it for himself.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r1.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r1.claim: ʿĀʾishah says the Prophet, while in retreat, would extend his head into the house for her to comb and entered the home only when necessary.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r10.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r10.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses ka-dhālika as thus, explaining that God makes His signs clear in this way.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r2.claim: Ibn Umar reports that the Prophet kept retreat during the last ten days of Ramadan.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r3.claim: The Prophet retreated for ten days each Ramadan and for twenty in the year he died.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r4.speaker: أهل الفضل والدين
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r4.claim: Righteous people who observed the final ten days stayed in retreat until they attended the Eid prayer with everyone.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r5.speaker: إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r5.claim: Ibrahim says people recommended that a retreatant stay overnight in the mosque on the night before Eid.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r6.speaker: أبو مجلز
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r6.claim: Abū Mijlaz says he spent the night before Eid in the mosque where he had retreated, then went from there to the prayer ground.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r7.speaker: عمرو بن شعيب
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r7.claim: A report says seeing a brother after longing for him is better than a year of retreat in the Prophet’s mosque.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r8.claim: Ikrimah reports that one of the Prophet’s wives experienced irregular bleeding while in retreat.

DURR-FULL:v1p487/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p487/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God’s limits as obedience to God; al-Ḍaḥḥāk interprets them as the sin of intimacy during retreat, and Muqātil says the prohibited limit is intercourse.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r1.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r1.claim: Muadh reports that before this ruling people could eat, drink, and have intercourse until they slept; Qays ibn Sirma slept after the evening prayer without food and woke exhausted, while Umar had intercourse after sleeping and told the Prophet; the verse then came.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r2.speaker: author
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r2.claim: The report through Ibn Abi Layla from Muadh is well known, though Ibn Abi Layla did not hear directly from Muadh; it has corroborating reports.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r3.speaker: البراء
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r3.claim: Al-Bara reports that anyone who slept before breaking the fast could not eat that night or the next day; Qays's wife sought food while he worked, he slept, and he fainted the following day before the verse permitted night intimacy and food until dawn.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r4.speaker: البراء
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r4.claim: Al-Bara also reports that when Ramadan fasting was first prescribed, men abstained from women for the entire month and some betrayed themselves, prompting the clause about God forgiving them.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p34/r5.claim: Ka'b reports that after sleeping, Ramadan fasting forbade food, drink, and sex until the next sunset; Umar and Ka'b each had intercourse after sleep, and Umar informed the Prophet, after which the verse was revealed.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r1.claim: Sahl reports that the initial wording lacked “at dawn”; some tied white and black threads to their legs and kept eating until they could distinguish them, then the clarification showed that night and day were meant.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r2.speaker: قتادة
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p35/r2.claim: Qatada says a person in retreat could leave the mosque and have intercourse if he wished, prompting the prohibition on intimacy during retreat in mosques.

BURSEVI:v1p243/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p243/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p243/r7.claim: Placing the phrase 'on the night of the fast' first delays the expected ruling and makes the listener anticipate it, strengthening its effect when it arrives.

BURSEVI:v1p243/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p243/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p243/r8.claim: Rafath originally means obscene speech, then speech about intimacy, and by euphemism sexual intercourse; Ibn Abbas says it covers whatever a man desires from a woman, including touch and kissing.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r1.claim: Calling spouses garments explains permission: they are closely intertwined, and each covers the other and protects them from sexual wrongdoing.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r2.claim: A hadith says marriage secures two thirds of a person's religion.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r3.claim: An alternative reading understands spouses as each other's comfort or dwelling, like the verse saying that God made a mate so a person could find tranquility with her.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r4.claim: God's knowledge that people had been betraying themselves refers to His eternal knowledge.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r5.claim: Sex during prohibited fasting hours wrongs the self by risking punishment and losing reward; secretly disobeying a divine trust is treachery, as the cited warning says.

BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r6.speaker: صائب
BURSEVI:v1p244#2/r6.claim: A Persian couplet urges a trustee to guard God's entrusted jewel from thieves and not sleep.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r1.claim: God accepted their repentance and erased the trace of their earlier breach.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r2.claim: Now marks the time after the prohibition was repealed; intercourse means joining skin to skin and stands for sex and its preliminaries.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r3.claim: If the earlier ban on eating, drinking, and intercourse came from prophetic Sunnah, the verse proves scripture can abrogate Sunnah; it does not prove that if the ban came from an earlier revealed law.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r4.claim: What God has prescribed includes the offspring He decreed; intercourse should aim at children and continuity, the purpose of desire and marriage, not pleasure alone.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r5.claim: A prophetic saying urges marriage and reproduction so the Muslim community may be numerous before other nations on Judgment Day.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r6.claim: The white thread is the first thin line of dawn; the black thread is the dark remainder of night beside it as true dawn spreads across the horizon.

BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244#3/r7.claim: The phrase 'of dawn' explains the white thread, while the black thread is understood as being of night.

BURSEVI:v1p244/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244/r1.claim: The preposition إلى is used with rafath because the expression implies afḍā, 'to become intimate with,' as in the cited description of spouses becoming intimate.

BURSEVI:v1p244/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p244/r2.claim: At first, a Ramadan fast allowed food, drink, and sex only until the late prayer or sleep; then all three became forbidden until the next night.

BURSEVI:v1p244/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
BURSEVI:v1p244/r3.claim: After late prayer, Umar had intercourse with his wife, regretted it, and confessed to the Prophet; other men admitted the same lapse, and the verse brought relief to the community.

BURSEVI:v1p244/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p244/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p244/r4.claim: The Prophet told Umar that he had not been worthy of that lapse, before the new permission came.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r1.claim: Iʿtikāf is remaining in a mosque with the intention of worship and drawing near to God; it is an ancient religious practice, also mentioned in the command to purify the House for worshippers and retreatants.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r2.claim: The verse was revealed about retreatants who left the mosque to have sex and returned after washing; intercourse is forbidden and invalidates iʿtikāf.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r3.claim: The plural 'mosques' implies retreat is valid in any mosque, though a congregational mosque is better to avoid leaving for Friday prayer.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r4.claim: Sincere iʿtikāf is among the most honored acts because it empties the heart of everything besides God.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r5.speaker: عطاء
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r5.claim: ʿAṭāʾ compares a retreatant to someone who sits at a powerful patron's door, refusing to leave until the need is fulfilled; the retreatant waits in God's house for forgiveness.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r6.claim: A hadith likens helping a brother in need to twenty years of iʿtikāf and says one day of retreat places three trenches between a person and Hell, each farther apart than the horizons.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r7.claim: Retreat and seclusion spare people from one another's harm, humble the self, turn it from worldly concerns, and begin the path to sincerity.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r8.claim: Seclusion cultivates intimacy with God, reliance, and contentment with sufficiency; social dealings can lead people to blur lawful and unlawful limits.

BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245#2/r9.claim: The solitary also avoids ingratiating himself with people and many other sins that commonly arise through social mixing.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r1.claim: The dawn clause limits intercourse, eating, and drinking alike; allowing sex until dawn entails that one may delay ritual washing and still begin the fast while in a state of major impurity.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r2.claim: Fasting means continued abstention from intercourse, food, and drink throughout the daylight, ending when night begins at sunset.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p245/r3.claim: The fast-breaking time arrives when night comes, day departs, and the sun has set; the three signs clarify that the full disk must disappear or help observers who cannot see sunset.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r4.claim: Some infer daytime intention for Ramadan from the command to complete the fast: since fasting begins after dawn and entails intention, the command includes forming intention then.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r5.claim: Some infer that continuous fasting is excluded because night is the fast's endpoint and breaking the fast follows.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r6.claim: Others say the verse only marks the end of the duty; since the permission commands are concessions rather than obligations, it does not establish that fasting at night is forbidden or disprove continuous fasting.

BURSEVI:v1p245/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p245/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p245/r7.claim: Because people might compare retreat to fasting and assume sex is forbidden only by day, the passage clarifies that intercourse is prohibited for a person in retreat as well.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r1.speaker: افتاده أفندي
BURSEVI:v1p246/r1.claim: Tasawwuf means avoiding anything tainted by unlawfulness and guarding the tongue from idle speech; this discipline can be practiced among people, more firmly than through retreat alone.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r2.speaker: افتاده أفندي
BURSEVI:v1p246/r2.claim: The Prophetic and Companion path is not a prescribed forty-day retreat: the Prophet practiced retreat in Ramadan's last ten days, while Moses alone was appointed forty nights.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r3.speaker: افتاده أفندي
BURSEVI:v1p246/r3.claim: The Khalwati order derives its forty-day retreat from Moses' appointment, not from a Prophetic prescription.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p246/r4.claim: God's limits separate truth from falsehood and block violations; believers are told not even to approach them, which more strongly prevents transgression.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p246/r5.claim: The Prophet compares God's prohibitions to a king's protected pasture: grazing around it risks entering it.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p246/r6.claim: God's clear explanation of signs is guidance and mercy meant to lead people to obey His commands and avoid His prohibitions.

BURSEVI:v1p246/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p246/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p246/r7.claim: Taqwa proceeds by avoiding shirk first, then sins, then disordered desires.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r1.claim: A report from Kaʿb ibn Mālik says that Ramadan rules once prohibited food, drink, and sex after sleeping; ʿUmar and Kaʿb each approached a sleeping wife, then ʿUmar told the Prophet and this verse was revealed.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r10.claim: The two garment clauses are grammatically independent, not an explanatory rhetorical supplement; they explain the ruling by the spouses' little patience and difficulty avoiding one another, with the man's need placed first.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r11.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r11.claim: An unattributed report says there is no good in women and no patience without them; the honorable person may be overcome by them, which the quoted speaker prefers to being a base victor.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r2.claim: In Ibn ʿAbbās's account, ʿUmar confessed to the Prophet after his sleeping self prompted intercourse; God then sent an allowance in a Qurʾanic verse and ordered its placement in the middle hundred verses of al-Baqarah.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r3.claim: Laylat al-ṣiyām means the night before the day one fasts; the genitive is a loose association, and the phrase is generic. Rafath may govern it or be governed by an omitted word, or it may be an adverb of uhilla.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r4.claim: Rafath can mean obscene speech, but here it means intercourse, which commonly entails explicit speech; the verb's preposition reflects an incorporated sense of intimate approach.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, challenged about rafath while in ihram, said it means what occurs with women; his quoted verse can describe speech or conduct.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r6.claim: The explicit term is chosen instead of Qurʾanic euphemisms such as touching and entering because the point is intercourse itself and the wording rebukes their earlier conduct, later called betrayal.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r7.claim: Women is a plural of niswah or a non-form-based plural of imraʾah; the possessive marks the marital or owned relationship that makes intimacy lawful.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r8.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh has rafūth; the garment metaphor means spouses are repose for one another, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, or that they embrace and cover/protect one another.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v2p64/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās supports the garment metaphor with a verse by al-Nābighah describing a lover's embrace as a garment.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r1.claim: Here God's knowing means the attachment of His knowledge; ikhtiyān is either desire inclining a person to betrayal or intensive betrayal that diminishes the self and exposes it to punishment.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r10.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r10.claim: Qatādah interprets the command as seeking the concession God prescribed, since God loves that His concessions be accepted as His strict duties are; this reinforces the preceding permission.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r11.speaker: عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r11.claim: When ʿAṭāʾ asked Ibn ʿAbbās whether the reading is ibtaghū or attabiʿū, Ibn ʿAbbās allowed either but advised the first reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r12.claim: The white thread is the first horizontal light of true dawn; the black thread is the remaining night darkness alongside it. Taking it as the false vertical dawn is an error.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r13.claim: Some take min al-fajr as explaining the white thread alone, from which the black thread is understood; others explain both threads because dawn can encompass them, citing a poetic image of blue dawn preceding its white light.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r2.claim: The past and imperfect forms indicate that the people had persisted in the forbidden conduct before being informed of the allowance; the past-tense sequence conflicts with an eternal-knowledge interpretation adopted by some.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r3.claim: God's turning toward them follows their repentance; one interpretation distinguishes removal of the prohibition from forgiveness of the sin, while the two clauses may otherwise overlap.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r4.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes al-ān as the time when the ban on intercourse is lifted, linked to the dawn limit; it may also denote the near future as present or be literal with an implied 'We have permitted.'

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r5.claim: Mubāsharah literally means skin touching skin and is idiomatic for intercourse because intercourse entails it.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and others interpret 'what God wrote for you' as children decreed in the heavenly record; the command means praying for them despite not knowing one's decree.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r7.claim: The verse teaches that intercourse should seek preservation of human offspring, not merely satisfaction, just as appetite for food preserves individuals; pleasure alone suits beasts.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r8.claim: Some read 'what God wrote' as a prohibition of withdrawal or anal intercourse; others take it as seeking the prescribed ejaculation in its proper place, excluding those acts. The author notes juristic differences about consent to withdrawal.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r9.speaker: أنس
ALUSI-FULL:v2p65/r9.claim: Anas reportedly interprets 'what God wrote' as Laylat al-Qadr; the same interpretation is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r1.speaker: سهل بن سعد
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r1.claim: Sahl ibn Saʿd reports that some tied actual white and black threads to their legs and kept eating until the words 'from dawn' were revealed; al-Ālūsī says this does not prove the earlier wording was unintelligible or that explanation was delayed past need.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r2.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r2.claim: ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim says he placed a black cord and white cord under his pillow, could not distinguish them, and reported the mistake to the Prophet in the morning.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r3.claim: Once dawn is specified, the thread imagery functions as a simile rather than a sustained metaphor; min may be partitive because the first visible light is part of dawn.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p66/r4.claim: The first min is better attached to yatabayyan with the sense 'be distinguished': dawn must be separated from night haze; saying only 'dawn becomes clear' leaves multiple degrees and an unclear endpoint.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r1.claim: Until night is attached to completing the fast, or is a circumstantial phrase; it cannot be the limit of the obligation itself because the obligation is not temporally extended. Either reading excludes night from fasting and joining two days into one fast.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r2.claim: The Prophet is said to have inferred the prohibition of continuous fasting from the command to finish at night; Laylā, wife of Bashīr ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyyah, recounts that her husband stopped her two-day fast and relayed the Prophet's warning against imitating Christians.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r3.claim: The verse does not require an intervening meal before another fast, despite a claim to that effect; it directs people to break when night arrives.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r4.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that then complete the fast, coordinated with the earlier night commands, can allow intention during the day: the definite fast refers to the already described abstention, commanded after dawn and after the night has ended.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67#2/r5.claim: Because strict daytime intention from the verse and nighttime intention from the hadith cannot both be mandatory, consensus permits daytime intention for Ramadan, preserving both proofs; otherwise one would be discarded.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r1.claim: The suggestion that the verse was revealed before Ramadan in an ambiguous form requiring delayed explanation is criticized: explanation may follow the address only if it does not miss the time of need.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r10.claim: When ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim mistook the threads for literal cords, the Prophet said his pillow must be broad: the white and black mean daylight and night-darkness.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r2.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls the addition 'from dawn' abrogation because Companions acted on the apparent wording and it then became figurative; al-Ālūsī objects that abrogation requires independent speech.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r3.claim: If the earlier bans on intercourse, eating, and drinking came from Prophetic practice, the verse shows Scripture abrogating Sunna; the 'made lawful' wording supports this, though abrogation without a replacement is disputed.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r4.claim: The permission to have intercourse until dawn supports a valid fast begun while junub, since a person could be made junub at the last moment of night; some reject this argument based on contrary reports.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r5.claim: Emission after dawn from intercourse begun before it does not defeat the argument: the emission completes intercourse in daytime, whereas junub status is a necessary consequence of the nighttime act.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r6.claim: The verse also permits eating while one is unsure whether dawn has arrived, because the limit is the dawn's becoming clear; some jurists disagree about making up the fast if dawn had in fact begun.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r7.speaker: سعيد بن منصور
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r7.claim: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr transmits a similar view that no makeup is required when a person ate under uncertainty, but al-Ālūsī says this is not the stronger position.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r8.speaker: الأئمة الأربعة
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r8.claim: The four imams hold that the legal day starts at true dawn, making prohibited acts forbidden after it; al-Aʿmash instead starts it at sunrise, as do the Imāmīs, interpreting min as partitive and dawn as the final portion of night.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r9.speaker: الأعمش
ALUSI-FULL:v2p67/r9.claim: Al-Aʿmash argues that day begins at sunrise, citing a report that daytime prayer is silent and analogizing the dawn light before sunrise to evening light after sunset; al-Ālūsī replies that the report may use day colloquially.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r1.claim: The objection that a Qurʾanic command to complete the fast should defeat a solitary report is answered by noting that the verse's apparent force has already been qualified by consensus, leaving room for the report to explain it.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r10.speaker: الشافعي
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r10.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī requires neither a day nor fasting for iʿtikāf, citing a sound report from Ibn ʿAbbās that fasting is not required unless the worshipper imposes it on himself; similar reports are attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and two versions from ʿAlī differ.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r2.claim: Another Shāfiʿī argument for obligatory nighttime intention is rejected as unsupported; no fasting obligation begins before dawn that could require prior intention.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r3.claim: Iʿtikāf linguistically means confinement or staying; in law it is a specified period of residence, and the passage forbids intercourse with a spouse during it.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r4.claim: The intercourse prohibition does not itself settle whether touching or kissing is forbidden: they may be allowed without desire or prohibited with desire, with a Shāfiʿī majority holding invalidation in that case; the broader skin-contact reading conflicts with ʿĀʾishah's grooming report.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r5.speaker: عائشة
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r5.claim: ʿĀʾishah used to comb the Prophet's head while he was in iʿtikāf, a report against construing mubāsharah here as any skin contact.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r6.claim: Mentioning mosques as the setting for iʿtikāf indicates that it is valid only in a mosque; otherwise a home would count, contrary to consensus.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r7.speaker: الزهري
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r7.claim: The juristic reports restrict iʿtikāf to a congregational mosque according to al-Zuhrī, a mosque with a regular imam and muezzin according to Abū Ḥanīfah, and the three mosques according to Ḥudhayfah.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r8.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r8.claim: Further restrictions are attributed to ʿAlī (the Sacred Mosque only) and Ibn al-Musayyib (that mosque or the Prophet's Mosque); al-Shāfiʿī allows every mosque because the wording is unrestricted.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r9.speaker: نافع مولى ابن عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v2p68/r9.claim: Some infer that women may perform iʿtikāf outside mosques because women are not included in the masculine address, and that fasting is a condition and the minimum stay is a day; this is attributed to Nāfiʿ and ʿĀʾishah.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r1.claim: Although some infer intercourse invalidates iʿtikāf because a prohibition in worship entails invalidity, al-Ālūsī distinguishes an act prohibited within the ritual from a prohibited act merely coinciding with it.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r2.claim: The six preceding rulings are called God's boundaries, barriers between right and wrong; 'do not approach them' figuratively commands avoiding falsehood and is stronger than simply forbidding transgression.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r3.speaker: أبو مسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r3.claim: Abū Muslim interprets 'do not approach them' as not altering the rulings, like the prohibition on approaching an orphan's property; al-Ālūsī says this and other alternatives strain the wording.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r4.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects an interpretation that treats the rulings as forbidden for others to legislate or as a boundary between divinity and servitude, calling it far from the intended sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r5.claim: God's explanation of signs repeats the explanation given for fasting, or extends to all legal signs, so people may avoid disobeying commands and prohibitions; the parenthetical placement urges observance.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r6.claim: After fasting, the text turns to forbidding unlawful consumption, which could undermine acceptance of fasting and iʿtikāf.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r7.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r7.claim: Qatādah reports that men used to leave iʿtikāf to have intercourse with their wives and return, after which they were forbidden to do so.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p69/r8.claim: The inference that leaving the mosque permits intercourse outside it is answered by reading the rule as applying while one remains legally an iʿtikāf participant; leaving for a need does not end iʿtikāf.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r1.claim: At true dawn, stop eating and intercourse, then abstain completely until night; legal fasting is intentional abstention from food, drink, intercourse, and analogous bodily intake from dawn to the end of the legal day.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r10.speaker: Acemler (Ca‘feriyye mezhebinde bulunan)
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r10.claim: Persians of the Jaʿfarī school wait to see the stars before breaking the fast.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r11.claim: The lexical sense of fasting as abstention also suggests restraint by all outward and inward faculties: tongue from lies, slander, and idle speech; eye from doubtful sights; ear from entertainments; soul from desires; heart from love of the world; spirit from afterlife pleasures; and inner secret from witnessing anything besides God.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r12.claim: Although the verse can indicate these broader forms of abstinence, Elmalılı does not claim that every one is obligatory.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r13.claim: Given the preceding focus on eating, drinking, and intercourse, obligatory restraint is limited to these and analogous things entering the body; other restraint is recommended virtue and fasting etiquette.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r14.claim: Sexual relations are forbidden both day and night during mosque retreat, though otherwise lawful on fasting nights.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r15.claim: Linguistically iʿtikāf is staying confined in a place; legally it means remaining in a mosque with the intention of retreat, as the verse’s mosque qualification specifies.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r16.speaker: İmam Muhammed
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r16.claim: According to the apparent narration from Imam Muhammad, even a stay of one hour could count as legal iʿtikāf, which would mean fasting is not a condition and voluntary retreat can be done fasting or not.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r17.claim: From the verse’s context, Elmalılı infers that iʿtikāf entails fasting: the ban on intercourse particularizes the night permission, making fasting a condition and the retreat at least one day; this is proper legal iʿtikāf.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r18.claim: The hadith “There is no iʿtikāf except with fasting” supports making fasting a condition.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r19.speaker: İmam-ı A‘zam
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r19.claim: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says iʿtikāf is valid only in a congregational mosque or, at minimum, a mosque where the five daily prayers are held; a hadith’s mention of congregational mosque means mosques in their fullest sense.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r2.claim: This legal fast is a particular kind of lexical abstention defined by the additional limits and boundaries established by sacred law.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r20.claim: Women may perform iʿtikāf only in their home prayer place; the Prophet prohibited their retreat elsewhere.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r21.claim: A conditional or unconditional vow makes iʿtikāf obligatory; retreat during Ramadan’s last ten days is an emphasized Sunnah, and other times are recommended.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r22.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r22.claim: The two Ṣaḥīḥ collections report that the Prophet consistently observed iʿtikāf in Ramadan’s last ten days from his arrival in Medina until his death.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r23.claim: When ʿĀʾisha, Ḥafṣa, and Zaynab successively came to retreat in tents in the mosque, the Prophet stopped them, left iʿtikāf that Ramadan, and made it up in Shawwāl’s first ten days.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r24.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r24.speaker: Zührî
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r24.claim: Zuhri wondered how people could abandon iʿtikāf when the Prophet sometimes did and omitted other practices but never abandoned iʿtikāf until death.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r25.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r25.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r25.claim: The Prophet’s continued practice might suggest obligation, but companions who omitted it without rebuke show it is Sunnah rather than obligatory; his omission one Ramadan also indicates it was not individually obligatory, while making it up shows no year passed without it.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r26.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r26.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r26.claim: Without the evidence of companions’ omissions going unrebuked, the Prophet’s never missing iʿtikāf within a year would imply that at least one retreat each year was obligatory.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r27.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r27.speaker: Katâde
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r27.claim: Qatada reports that in an earlier religious law a man could leave iʿtikāf, have intercourse with his wife, and return; this verse prohibited that practice.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r28.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r28.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r28.claim: In Islamic law, intercourse with women invalidates iʿtikāf; the intended meaning of “mubashara” here is intercourse.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r29.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r29.speaker: İmam Şâfiî
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r29.claim: One report from al-Shāfiʿī takes the second occurrence of “mubashara” more broadly as skin-to-skin contact, so even touching a woman with desire invalidates iʿtikāf.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r3.claim: Fasting has three requirements: the proper time, intention, and abstention.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r4.claim: The fast lasts from true dawn to sunset, the legal day, rather than from sunrise to sunset as in ordinary or astronomical reckoning.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r5.claim: Intention must be associated with most of the day, while abstention must last through the entire day; eating after dawn makes the fast invalid.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r6.claim: The hadith “Actions are only by intentions” supports intention as a general legal condition for acts of worship.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r7.claim: No part of the night is fasting time, and every fast-breaking act is permitted throughout it.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r8.claim: Some wrongly infer that because legal morning starts at dawn, fasting must continue after sunset until twilight or even stars; the verse begins the day “from dawn” but ends it “at night,” and night begins with eastern darkness after sunset.

ELMALILI:2:187#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#2/r9.claim: Applying the dawn rule by analogy to twilight would alter the explicit text; the revelation context also indicates the former fast did not include the time from sunset to the evening prayer.

ELMALILI:2:187#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r1.claim: The mentioned rulings are either the limits God established or prohibited limits; believers must not even approach them, much less transgress them.

ELMALILI:2:187#3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r2.claim: A hadith compares God’s prohibitions to a ruler’s protected pasture: those who graze near it risk entering it; jurists derive the principle of blocking the means from this warning.

ELMALILI:2:187#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r3.claim: God explains the signs that guide people to His legislation clearly and eloquently so they may guard themselves by avoiding disobedience to His commands and prohibitions.

ELMALILI:2:187#3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187#3/r4.claim: After completing the fasts and learning not to approach forbidden limits, believers return to the permission to eat and drink for the festival, though the passage then continues.

ELMALILI:2:187/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r1.claim: Sexual relations with one’s wife are lawful at any hour of the fasting night; the earlier restriction after the evening prayer or sleep no longer applies.

ELMALILI:2:187/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r10.claim: A third interpretation of “seek what God wrote for you” is to seek the Night of Decree.

ELMALILI:2:187/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r11.claim: Mubashara literally denotes skin touching skin and is conventionally used for intercourse; intercourse is unanimously the intended meaning here.

ELMALILI:2:187/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r12.claim: The command to have relations, like the command to eat and drink, grants permission rather than imposing an obligation.

ELMALILI:2:187/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r13.claim: The following command to seek what God decreed indicates that the aim of intercourse should be offspring rather than mere gratification, since lawful sex and desire serve procreation and the continuation of the species.

ELMALILI:2:187/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r14.claim: Some interpret “seek what God wrote” as prohibiting coitus interruptus, but the text does not make this certain because its object is unstated; hadith nevertheless suggest disapproval.

ELMALILI:2:187/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r15.claim: Eating and drinking remain permitted until the white thread of true dawn becomes distinct from the black thread; this is the first light of dawn.

ELMALILI:2:187/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r16.claim: The phrase “until” excludes its endpoint, so fasting must already begin when the white thread becomes distinct; if uncertain, refraining is recommended, but eating does not require a make-up fast because distinction means certain knowledge.

ELMALILI:2:187/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r17.claim: A report says the clarification “from dawn” was revealed after some people used actual black and white threads to decide when to stop eating; it explains the familiar metaphor of the first dawn light and the legal day’s start.

ELMALILI:2:187/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r18.claim: Legal theory debates whether clarification came after it was needed; Elmalılı holds that delaying a clarification that changes the rule is impermissible, so on this report the verse must be abrogation rather than mere clarification.

ELMALILI:2:187/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r19.claim: True dawn is the true morning; false dawn is called dawn only with the qualifier “false,” and scholars unanimously place the legal day and fasting obligation at true dawn.

ELMALILI:2:187/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r2.claim: The former rule inferred from the earlier communities’ fasting and the previous rule taken from Prophetic practice were abrogated; Ramadan fasting abrogated the earlier fasts, showing that Scripture may abrogate Sunnah.

ELMALILI:2:187/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r20.claim: An objection says the white thread must be false dawn because its vertical column resembles a thread, whereas true dawn spreads horizontally, implying fasting should start earlier.

ELMALILI:2:187/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r21.claim: Elmalılı rejects that objection: the first true dawn is initially thin, so its horizontal spread does not prevent comparison to a thread; the forbidden amount of light is the first instant of true dawn.

ELMALILI:2:187/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r22.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r22.claim: Abū Hurayra and Hasan b. Ṣāliḥ b. Cinnī held that a person who reaches dawn in a state of major ritual impurity without bathing has no valid fast.

ELMALILI:2:187/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r23.claim: The majority holds that the fast is valid if one observes the fast on time despite remaining in major impurity at dawn, since this verse permits intercourse up to dawn and thus permits delaying the bath.

ELMALILI:2:187/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r3.claim: Rafath is obscene explicit speech about what should be stated indirectly, and by metonymy may mean intercourse; here it unanimously means physical intercourse, not verbal obscenity.

ELMALILI:2:187/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r4.claim: God wills ease for this community: He shortened the fasting period, removed the night restriction, and made sexual relations lawful at night.

ELMALILI:2:187/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r5.claim: Spouses are garments for one another: they embrace and cover each other, conceal faults, protect from heat and cold, guard chastity, and protect one another from fornication.

ELMALILI:2:187/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r6.claim: God knew that believers were betraying themselves by failing to restrain themselves and exposing themselves to loss of reward and punishment.

ELMALILI:2:187/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r7.claim: God accepted their repentance and erased the sin of sexual relations during the fasting night.

ELMALILI:2:187/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r8.claim: “Seek what God wrote for you” may mean seeking the offspring eternally decreed for you in the Preserved Tablet.

ELMALILI:2:187/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:187/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:187/r9.claim: A second interpretation of “seek what God wrote for you” is to seek the lawful place of intercourse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r1.claim: The verse shifts from fasting rules to acts permitted at certain Ramadan times that might be thought to conflict with fasting, so it is set apart from the prior sentences.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r2.speaker: أبو داود عن معاذ بن جبل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r2.claim: Abū Dāwūd reports from Muʿādh that after sleeping or praying ʿIshāʾ Muslims did not eat or have sex; ʿUmar went to his wife, who said she had slept, and he thought she was making an excuse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r3.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r3.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that Qays ibn Ṣirma came home at sunset, waited for food, fell asleep, then could not eat and fainted from hunger the next day.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r4.claim: A Bukhārī report from al-Barāʾ says men refrained from intercourse throughout Ramadan but some violated that restraint; the verse followed, and Kaʿb ibn Mālik had an event like ʿUmar's.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r5.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r5.claim: Most commentators say abstaining from food and sex after sleep or ʿIshāʾ had been established by Sunnah and was then abrogated.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p180#3/r6.claim: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī rejects that this abrogated an Islamic rule and says it abrogated a rule in Christian law.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r1.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects a prior Islamic night-long restriction: fasting was prescribed only by day, so this verse reports the existing night permission rather than creating it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r2.claim: The verse corrects some Muslims' mistaken belief that eating after sunset was allowed only until ʿIshāʾ or sleep, with only suḥūr food allowed, and that sleep barred sex and food until dawn.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r3.claim: Muslim reports that Abū Hurayra still held that restriction after the Prophet's death; Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests it may have spread from Jews, citing al-Suddī's route in al-Ṭabarī.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r4.speaker: ابن القاسم عن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r4.claim: Ibn al-Qāsim reports Mālik's account that early Muslims who slept before eating could not eat again that night until this verse allowed them to eat.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r5.claim: The wording 'God knew' indicates revelation clarified self-imposed hardship that Muslims had not openly reported; the Qays report may be a narrator's addition.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p181/r6.claim: A ban lasting nearly all night is implausible in a gradual easing of fasting: an annual day was followed by a month with a choice of fasting or feeding, which would not then become nearly night-and-day abstention.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r1.claim: Laylat al-ṣiyām means the night preceding the day of fasting, as Arabic normally associates a night with the following day; Laylat ʿArafa is an exception.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r2.claim: Rafath is speech about sexual pleasure with women, then a metonym for intercourse, though it may be literal for both; ilā specifies the intended intimacy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r3.claim: 'They are clothing for you' explains the permission: avoiding spouses at night would be severe hardship; the Qur'an revives an old image of close contact as clothing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r4.claim: The clothing metaphor parallels Imruʾ al-Qays's description of one garment slipping from another.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r5.speaker: الراغب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r5.claim: Al-Rāghib defines ikhtiyān as seeking to commit betrayal; the form derives from khawn with a vowel change.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r6.claim: Betraying oneself depicts imposing a burden not required, or waveringly treating permitted intimacy as forbidden; the wording may mean forcing one's self into betrayal or attributing betrayal to it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r7.speaker: الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p182/r7.claim: Al-Kashshāf says ikhtiyān is more intensive than khiyānah, like iktisāb compared with kasb; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes its use in another Qur'anic verse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r1.claim: Min al-fajr may mark origin—the streak arising from dawn—or be explanatory or partitive; Abū Duwād similarly says 'from morning.'

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r2.speaker: الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r2.claim: Al-Kashshāf calls the thread an emphatic simile, perhaps because he did not know the expression was well established; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers its direct, idiomatic meaning.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r3.claim: The Qur'an uses khayṭ as a well-established literal expression for dawn's light and darkness, not as an obscure simile.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r4.claim: Hattā yatabayyana sets the end of eating at perceptible true dawn and, by implication, the start of fasting; ending one period necessarily begins the other.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r5.claim: 'Complete the fast until night' gives the fast's endpoint; it says complete because the audience is already fasting.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r6.claim: Using ilā for night calls for promptly breaking the fast at sunset, since the endpoint does not extend into the night as it would with hattā.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183#2/r7.claim: Thumma marks rhetorical importance, not a time gap; he rejects Abū Jaʿfar al-Khubāz al-Samarqandī's use of it to permit delaying the intention until after dawn for Abū Ḥanīfa's view.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r1.claim: The command to approach spouses permits what has become clear now; it does not mean intimacy was newly legislated at that moment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r2.claim: 'What God wrote' can mean what He permitted outside fasting, or what He decreed as offspring; the latter encourages procreation and the community's continuation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r3.claim: The command to eat and drink is coordinated with the command for intimacy; khayṭ is a thread of linen or wool used to sew cloth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r4.speaker: أبو دؤاد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p183/r4.claim: The pre-Islamic poet Abū Duwād uses 'thread of dawn' for the streak of light extended through darkness, paired with the adjacent dark streak.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r1.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r1.claim: ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim reports that he put a black and a white cord beneath his pillow and watched for them to separate; the Prophet explained that the verse means night-darkness and day-whiteness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r2.speaker: سهل بن سعد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r2.claim: Sahl ibn Saʿd reports that before 'min al-fajr' was revealed, men tied white and black cords to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r3.claim: Since ʿAdī converted in year nine or ten, long after Ramadan became obligatory in year two, Ibn ʿĀshūr places Sahl's incident in an earlier voluntary or vow fast and ʿAdī's as a later recurrence of the mistake.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p184/r4.claim: The Sahl report's chain is sound, but its wording may be paraphrased and unclear; it appears in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections only through one route, whose wording says 'after' or 'after that.'

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r1.claim: There was no delayed clarification: khayṭ was clear Arabic, and a few people's misunderstanding of its familiar thread sense does not make the wording ambiguous.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r2.claim: Those confused took the common thread meaning and read min as causal; the Prophet's broad-pillow or broad-nape rebuke is a pointed metonym for dull perception.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r3.claim: The ban on intercourse while in iʿtikāf is coordinated with the permission to approach spouses so that a person in retreat remains fit for the rite.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r4.claim: Scholars agree iʿtikāf requires a mosque; he prefers the view that any mosque suffices over requiring a congregational mosque, following Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, and al-Shāfiʿī.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p185/r5.claim: 'Those are God's limits' summarizes the time and place restrictions, not permissions; crossing their boundaries leads from what is allowed into prohibition.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r1.claim: 'Do not approach them' warns against nearing limits, since proximity often leads to crossing them; he links the wording to other Qur'anic prohibitions and the hadith of grazing near a protected pasture.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r2.claim: As God clarifies fasting rulings, He clarifies all His signs for all people so they will not be confused.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p186/r3.claim: Laʿallahum yattaqūn may mean God intends to keep people from violations, or that clarity enables complete observance; on the second reading, excused ignorance still falls short of realizing the intended worship.

TABATABAI:2:187#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r1.claim: The alternative view says “made lawful” need not imply a prior ban, since sea game was not forbidden to those in consecration; it also interprets “betraying yourselves” as supposed sin or deprivation, with repentance and pardon not explicit proof of a prohibition.

TABATABAI:2:187#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r2.claim: He rejects the alternative because the wording strongly indicates a previous ban; “now approach them” follows a prohibition, and the Prophet could have conveyed fasting restrictions before this verse, allowing it to abrogate his ruling.

TABATABAI:2:187#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#2/r3.claim: An objection says that if spouses being clothing for each other explains permission for intercourse, it cannot explain an abrogation, since it applies both before and after the verse.

TABATABAI:2:187#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r1.claim: He answers that the clothing metaphor also applies during the day, when fasting prohibits intercourse; it therefore does not alone explain the rule’s limits.

TABATABAI:2:187#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r2.claim: He reads three conditions as nested rationales: marriage permits intimacy generally; fasting restricts it during the day; hardship and repeated violations justify restoring permission at night. Thus the rationale concerns only the new night-time concession.

TABATABAI:2:187#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r3.claim: The clothing relationship gives general permission for marital intimacy, fasting restricts that permission during the day, and the burden and recurring breaches justify a night concession; the verse restores only part of the general permission.

TABATABAI:2:187#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r4.claim: “Now approach them” follows a prohibition and therefore commands permission; “seek what God prescribed for you” means seeking offspring, which God wrote into human nature through sexual desire, as eating naturally serves life even when people seek pleasure.

TABATABAI:2:187#3/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#3/r5.claim: He finds the proposal that “what God prescribed” means a legal license unlikely, because the Qur’an does not use “writing” to mean permissibility or dispensation.

TABATABAI:2:187#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r1.claim: There are two dawns: the false dawn is a temporary vertical beam; the true dawn appears when the Sun is 18 degrees below the eastern horizon and spreads horizontally, announcing daylight.

TABATABAI:2:187#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r2.claim: The white thread is true dawn, “from” is explanatory, and the black thread is a metaphor for the adjoining darkness; the deadline is the first appearance of true dawn, before daylight erases both threads.

TABATABAI:2:187#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r3.claim: Because the dawn boundary is explicit, the verse concisely says to complete the fast until night; its use of “complete” treats fasting as one simple act, unlike “perfect,” which describes a composite whose parts each have an effect.

TABATABAI:2:187#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r4.claim: Iʿtikāf means remaining in a place; as a worship, it requires staying in a mosque, leaving only for need, and fasting, so the verse bars intercourse during it despite the general night permission.

TABATABAI:2:187#4/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#4/r5.claim: A “boundary” fundamentally prevents passage; “do not approach them” figuratively forbids either committing the listed acts or violating the fasting rules and sacred limits.

TABATABAI:2:187#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
