TABATABAI:2:187#5/r1.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r1.claim: A report attributed to al-Ṣādiq says intercourse was prohibited throughout Ramadan, while food was forbidden after sleeping; Khawwat b. Jubayr fell asleep before iftar, fainted while digging the trench next day, and the verse permitted night intercourse and food until dawn.

TABATABAI:2:187#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r2.claim: The phrase explaining the account beginning “and there was a man” is the narrator’s gloss; other reports in al-Kulayni and al-ʿAyyāshī likewise link the food rule to Khawwat and the sex concession to young men’s secret conduct.

TABATABAI:2:187#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r3.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r3.claim: A report says sleepers who missed iftar could not eat that night or the following day; Qays b. Ṣirma worked while fasting, slept before eating, then fainted, and the verse brought relief.

TABATABAI:2:187#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r4.claim: Versions vary on the name in Qays’s story, giving Abu Qubays b. Ṣirma or Ṣirma b. Mālik; the report is transmitted in multiple routes.

TABATABAI:2:187#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:2:187#5/r5.claim: A report says Muslims who had prayed ʿishāʾ were forbidden food and sex until the next evening; some, including ʿUmar, transgressed and complained, so “now approach them” meant have intercourse.

TABATABAI:2:187#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r1.claim: Most reports through Sunni transmitters say intercourse followed the same rule as food and drink: all were allowed early in the night but forbidden after sleep.

TABATABAI:2:187#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r2.claim: The first report says sex was forbidden throughout Ramadan, unlike food and drink, which were permitted before sleep; the verse’s syntax supports it because food has an explicit dawn limit while sex has none.

TABATABAI:2:187#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r3.claim: The claim that violations involved food and drink as well as intercourse conflicts with the verse’s order, which places “you were betraying yourselves” before the food permission.

TABATABAI:2:187#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r4.speaker: رسول الله
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r4.claim: A report distinguishes a wolf-tail-like false dawn, which changes no rule, from the horizontal dawn, which permits prayer and prohibits food.

TABATABAI:2:187#6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187#6/r5.claim: Reports from both Sunni and Shia routes are abundant on the two dawns and on the prohibition of intercourse during iʿtikāf.

TABATABAI:2:187/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r1.claim: Iḥlāl means making permissible. Rifth is explicit sexual speech, used here euphemistically for intercourse; the Qur’an and ordinary Arabic use other intercourse terms euphemistically too. The preposition ilā reportedly conveys approaching or giving oneself over.

TABATABAI:2:187/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r2.claim: “They are clothing for you” is a metaphor: spouses cover one another’s vulnerability and keep one another from public sexual wrongdoing. A spouse’s clothing cannot conceal that spouse from the other, fitting the permission for marital intimacy.

TABATABAI:2:187/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r3.claim: The repeated form of “you were betraying yourselves” suggests an ongoing practice; together, “repented” and “forgave” strongly imply that night intercourse had previously been forbidden, which this verse abrogated.

TABATABAI:2:187/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r4.claim: A group of commentators holds that the verse abrogated the former prohibition of intercourse during Ramadan nights.

TABATABAI:2:187/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r5.claim: An alternative view, supported by some Sunni reports, says Muslims inferred from the comparison with earlier communities that Ramadan fasting rules matched theirs: they could eat and have sex early at night but stopped after sleeping, a burden that led to secret violations and this concession.

TABATABAI:2:187/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:187/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:187/r6.claim: On that alternative, the comparison with earlier communities concerns the basic obligation to fast, not every detail of fasting law.

ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n159/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n159/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n159/r1.claim: Following Razi, Asad reads the phrase as referring to early Muslims' mistaken belief that sexual intercourse was forbidden during fasting even at night; the verse removes that misconception.

ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n160/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n160/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n160/r1.claim: The phrase about seeking what God ordained stresses that sexual life is willed by God.

ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n161/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n161/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n161/r1.claim: Arab philologists understand the black line as the darkness of night; the paired streaks denote day and night, according to Lane and Lisan al-'Arab.

ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n162/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n162/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:187#n162/r1.claim: The Prophet spent several days and nights in Ramadan, and sometimes at other times, in mosque prayer and meditation apart from worldly activity; he encouraged followers to do likewise, establishing optional i'tikaf, especially in Ramadan's last ten days.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r1.claim: Some Companions, perhaps influenced by Jewish and Christian customs, thought intercourse on Ramadan nights forbidden and suhur had to precede sleep; some secretly broke these assumed rules.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r10.claim: The permission to have intercourse is confined to night and does not extend into daytime; Arabic night begins at sunset.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r11.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r11.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r11.claim: Night may end at true dawn or sunrise, but here it means true dawn because the fasting prohibition is bounded by fajr and the white thread signals dawn breaking.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r12.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r12.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r12.claim: The cited hadith reports do not extend night to sunrise; they make dawn the end of night, and no jurist or exegete says fasting begins at sunrise.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r13.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r13.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r13.claim: When dawn is hard to determine, people may keep eating until sure; where modern tools identify dawn readily, fasting begins when dawn starts.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r14.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r14.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r14.claim: At latitudes where the sun does not rise or set for days or months, Muslims need a method for prayer and fasting times.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r15.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r15.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r15.claim: The author rejects the claim that places without normal daily times have no corresponding prayer or fasting obligations.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r16.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r16.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r16.claim: The divine address requires five daily prayers and a month of fasting within a 24-hour day; polar believers also need worship and reward, so they use an assumed 24-hour day as in ordinary regions.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r17.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r17.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r17.claim: Scholars propose either following the Mecca calendar or the calendar of the nearest region with normal day and night.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r18.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r18.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r18.claim: When Companions asked how to pray during the Dajjal's year-long day, the Prophet said to use the schedule of ordinary days, supporting the proposed high-latitude solution.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r19.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r19.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r19.claim: I'tikaf is retreating to a mosque for worship, temporarily leaving home, work, and ordinary social relations; even a short stay with worshipful intent qualifies.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r2.claim: Those who secretly had intercourse were described as betraying themselves because they privately violated the beliefs they professed to others.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r20.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r20.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r20.claim: The Prophet practiced i'tikaf in the mosque during Ramadan's last ten days and doubled it in his final year; some wives and Companions followed him.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r21.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r21.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r21.claim: During i'tikaf, leaving the mosque is forbidden except for natural or necessary needs, as is sexual intercourse with one's spouse.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r3.claim: The verse was revealed after early misunderstandings about fasting limits, clarifying that fasting begins when night ends and lasts until the next night.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r4.claim: Fasting is a daytime observance; after sunset, eating, drinking, intercourse, and other permitted acts are allowed throughout the night.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r5.claim: Although the forgiveness language might suggest an earlier prohibition, there is no Qur'anic or hadith evidence that such a ban existed.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r6.claim: The author reads betrayal, repentance, and forgiveness as referring to people who treated their own assumptions as prohibitions, then repented for violating them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r7.claim: Of the explanations for what God wrote for people to seek, the author prefers the natural fruit of permitted intimacy: asking God for a virtuous child.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r8.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r8.claim: There is agreement that the fast ends at sunset, while its start and observance where normal sunrise and sunset fail are disputed.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:187/r9.claim: The author says the verse clarifies the starting time: its first mention of night signals the beginning of fasting, and the later night marks its end.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r1.speaker: Many commentators
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r1.claim: Before this verse, fasting resumed after sleep: people could eat after sunset until the ʿishāʾ prayer, then sleep began the next day’s fast.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r10.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r10.claim: Reports say the Prophet spent Ramadan’s final ten days in mosque retreat.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r11.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r11.claim: During his final Ramadan, the Prophet spent twenty days in retreat.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r2.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r2.claim: Some say Muslims abstained from sex throughout Ramadan, even at night, though the source for this account is unclear.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r3.claim: The verse alleviates the earlier fasting requirements.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r4.speaker: Commentators
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r4.claim: Commentators report that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb admitted having intercourse with his wife after she said she had fallen asleep, then regretted it and sought recourse.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r5.speaker: Commentators
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r5.claim: Commentators recount that Qays ibn Ṣirmah fell asleep before eating after a hard day’s fasting and therefore continued fasting the following day.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r6.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r6.claim: IK lists possible senses of seeking what God prescribed: seeking children, obeying Quranic commands, seeking the Night of Power, accepting ritual latitude, or lawful intercourse.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r7.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r7.claim: The white thread and black thread signify dawn and night; Q explains the white thread as an idiom for daytime.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r8.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r8.claim: Hadiths discuss the dawn light that ends the night, including signs in the sky and illumination on mountain tops.

STUDYQURAN:2:187/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:187/r9.claim: Iʿtikāf is retreat in a mosque for a period devoted to prayer and remembrance.
